An 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for Counting Common Bases of Two Matroids

Xiaoyu Chen ††thanks: Email: xiaoyu@mit.edu, Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Supported by the NSF CAREER grant CCF-2443045, and the Reed Fund at MIT.    Kuikui Liu ††thanks: Email: liukui@mit.edu, Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Supported by the NSF CAREER grant CCF-2443045, and the Reed Fund at MIT.
Abstract

We design the first polynomial-time algorithms for approximately counting and uniformly sampling common bases of two matroids given by their independence oracles. Moreover, our algorithms generalize far beyond this to Hadamard products of two probability measures on the Boolean cube satisfying a simple nonnegative curvature condition. These algorithmic primitives have myriad applications in statistical physics, polyhedral combinatorics, the study of quantum many-body systems, and beyond.

Our approach has two key ingredients.

  • •

    We relax the intersection by imposing an overlap penalty on the product measure formed by the two input measures. We prove, via an integrated Bochner-type method, that this “soft intersection” satisfies a Poincaré Inequality uniformly over all external fields.

  • •

    We solve a dual maximum entropy convex program to compute external fields under which the hard constraint is satisfied with high probability under the soft intersection measure. We bound this success probability directly using the uniform Poincaré Inequality and smallness of the gradient norm.

AI Disclosure GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra and GPT-6 Astra Ultra were heavily used to develop the ideas in this paper. A more complete discussion is included in Section 1.5.

1 Introduction

In this paper, we design the first polynomial-time algorithms that solve the following fundamental problems in full generality: Let ℳ,𝒩{\mathcal{M}},{\mathcal{N}} be two matroids with the same rank rr on a common ground set 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} of size nn, both given via an independence oracle, and write ℬ⁡(ℳ){\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{M}}) (resp. ℬ⁡(𝒩){\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{N}})) for the collection of bases of ℳ{\mathcal{M}} (resp. 𝒩{\mathcal{N}}); for background on matroids, see Section 3.2.

  • Approximate Counting: Estimate the number |ℬ⁡(ℳ)∩ℬ⁡(𝒩)|\left|{{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{M}})\cap{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{N}})}\right| of common bases up to (1±ε)(1\pm\varepsilon)-multiplicative error, for any desired target accuracy 0<ε<10<\varepsilon<1. Note that exact counting is #​𝖯\#\mathsf{P}-hard and hence, unlikely to admit an efficient algorithm [Val79].

  • Approximate Sampling: Sample a common basis from the uniform distribution over ℬ⁡(ℳ)∩ℬ⁡(𝒩){\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{M}})\cap{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{N}}) up to ±ε\pm\varepsilon-additive total variation error, for any 0<ε<10<\varepsilon<1.

These are fundamental algorithmic problems in theoretical computer science that have abundant applications in statistical physics, high-dimensional statistics, and combinatorics; see Appendix C for a more comprehensive discussion.

Counting and sampling common bases of two matroids has received significant attention in the literature over the past several decades. For the moment, we highlight two landmark results that previously solved important special cases of the problem. Jerrum–Sinclair–Vigoda designed the first polynomial-time algorithms for counting and sampling (edge weighted) perfect matchings in bipartite graphs [JSV04]. As a result, they also obtained the first 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for estimating the permanent of any nonnegative matrix. Anari–Liu–Oveis Gharan–Vinzant gave the first polynomial-time algorithms for counting and sampling bases of a single matroid [Ana+19]. Both results are based on the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method.

Our algorithms are also based on MCMC and hence, are randomized. We note that randomization is necessary when the matroids can only be accessed via their independence oracles. Indeed, even for a single matroid ℳ{\mathcal{M}}, no efficient deterministic algorithm can approximate |ℬ⁡(ℳ)|\left|{{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{M}})}\right| to within a simply exponential multiplicative factor in the oracle model [ABF94]. This lower bound is nearly matched by the deterministic 2O⁡(r)2^{O(r)}-approximation algorithm of Anari–Oveis Gharan–Vinzant [AOV18], which also applies to common bases of two matroids.

Definition 1.1 (𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS}).

Let Z≥0Z\geq 0 be a quantity determined by an input instance. A fully polynomial-time randomized approximation scheme (𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS}) for ZZ is a randomized algorithm that, given the instance and an accuracy parameter 0<ε≤10<\varepsilon\leq 1, returns Z^≥0\widehat{Z}\geq 0 satisfying

𝐏𝐫[(1−ε)⋅Z≤Z^≤(1+ε)⋅Z]\displaystyle\mathbf{Pr}\left[(1-\varepsilon)\cdot Z\leq\widehat{Z}\leq(1+\varepsilon)\cdot Z\right] ≥34,\displaystyle\geq\frac{3}{4},

in time polynomial in the size of the instance and 1/ε1/\varepsilon.11 1 By the standard median trick, returning the median of O⁡(log⁡(1/δ))O(\log(1/\delta)) independent calls boosts the success probability to 1−δ1-\delta for any 0<δ<10<\delta<1. In the oracle model, each oracle call has unit cost.

Theorem 1.2 (Counting Common Bases).

There is an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} that, given independence oracles for two matroids ℳ,𝒩{\mathcal{M}},{\mathcal{N}} on a common ground set 𝒰{\mathcal{U}}, estimates the number |ℬ⁡(ℳ)∩ℬ⁡(𝒩)|\left|{{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{M}})\cap{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{N}})}\right| of common bases.

Remark 1.3.

The running time of our algorithm is O~​(n13/ε2)\widetilde{O}(n^{13}/\varepsilon^{2}), which certainly isn’t optimal. Since our goal is to present our algorithms and proofs in the simplest way possible, we made no attempt to optimize the running time.

All problems we consider in this paper will be self-reducible in the sense of [JVV86]. Hence, approximate counting and sampling are equivalent under polynomial-time reductions and we will move fluidly between them. In particular, Theorem 1.2 also implies a polynomial-time algorithm for approximately sampling a uniformly random common basis.

As a special case, Theorem 1.2 gives an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for counting strong orientations and undirected Euler tours, resolving the approximate counting questions in [Jer24, Section 3.5] and [GŠ10], respectively; see Sections C.1 and C.2. A variant of Theorem 1.2 for weighted common bases (proved below) applies to network reliability, where the goal is to estimate the probability of directed root-to-all reachability, or of an unpaired vertex-disjoint linkage between two terminal sets, under independent edge failures; see Sections C.4 and C.3. The former settles the general directed reachability question in [GJ19, Section 7]; the latter extends the two-terminal result of [FFG26] to multiple disjoint paths. Finally, we mention that Theorem 1.2 also yields a new 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for perfect matchings in bipartite graphs (and the permanent of nonnegative matrices more generally).

1.1 Subset Convolution of Log-Concave Measures

Theorem 1.2 is an important special case of “intersections” of multi-affine log-concave measures, which we now describe. Let μ:2𝒰→ℝ≥0\mu:2^{{\mathcal{U}}}\to{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0} be a nonnegative weight function, which need not be normalized to sum to 11, and define its multi-affine generating polynomial with variables {xu:u∈𝒰}\{x_{u}:u\in{\mathcal{U}}\} by

gμ​(𝒙)≔∑S⊆𝒰μ⁡(S)⋅𝒙S,\displaystyle g_{\mu}(\bm{x})\coloneqq\sum_{S\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}}\mu(S)\cdot\bm{x}^{S}, (1)

where 𝒙S≔∏u∈Sxu\bm{x}^{S}\coloneqq\prod_{u\in S}x_{u}. We write [𝒙S]​gμ\left[{\bm{x}^{S}}\right]g_{\mu} for the coefficient μ⁡(S)\mu(S) of 𝒙S\bm{x}^{S} in the polynomial gμg_{\mu}.

Definition 1.4 (Subset Convolution; [Bjö+07]).

Let μ,ν:2𝒰→ℝ≥0\mu,\nu:2^{{\mathcal{U}}}\to{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0} be two nonnegative weight functions. We define their subset convolution by the quantity

(μ∗ν)​(T)\displaystyle(\mu\ast\nu)(T) ≔∑S⊆Tμ⁡(S)⋅ν⁡(T∖S)=[𝒙T]​(gμ​(𝒙)⋅gν​(𝒙)),∀T⊆𝒰.\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{S\subseteq T}\mu(S)\cdot\nu(T\setminus S)=\left[{\bm{x}^{T}}\right]\left({g_{\mu}(\bm{x})\cdot g_{\nu}(\bm{x})}\right),\qquad\forall T\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}.
Definition 1.5 (Log-Concave Polynomial; [Gur09, AOV18, BH20]).

A nonzero polynomial gg with nonnegative coefficients is log-concave on ℝ≥0𝒰\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{{\mathcal{U}}} if

∇2​log​g​(𝒙)⪯0,∀𝒙∈ℝ>0𝒰.\displaystyle\nabla^{2}\log g(\bm{x})\preceq 0,\qquad\forall\bm{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}_{>0}^{{\mathcal{U}}}.

We will design an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for the subset convolution (and a natural generalization of it) of two nonnegative weight functions μ,ν\mu,\nu assuming gμ,gνg_{\mu},g_{\nu} are log-concave on ℝ≥0n{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n}. To bound the running time, let us also define the coefficient range ℛμ{\mathcal{R}}_{\mu} for a weight function μ\mu as

ℛμ≔maxS∈supp⁡(μ)⁡μ⁡(S)minS∈supp⁡(μ)⁡μ⁡(S)≥1.\displaystyle{\mathcal{R}}_{\mu}\coloneqq\frac{\max_{S\in\supp(\mu)}\mu(S)}{\min_{S\in\supp(\mu)}\mu(S)}\geq 1. (2)

To guarantee that our algorithms run in polynomial-time, we will only require that ℛμ,ℛν≤exp⁡(𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)){\mathcal{R}}_{\mu},{\mathcal{R}}_{\nu}\leq\exp\left({\mathsf{poly}(n)}\right), which is easily satisfied in most applications of interest. The algorithms below take these parameters as input; upper bounds supplied by the user may be used instead, with the same replacement in the running-time bounds.

Theorem 1.6 (𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for Log-Concave Subset Convolution).

Let μ,ν:2𝒰→ℝ≥0\mu,\nu:2^{{\mathcal{U}}}\to{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0} be two nonnegative weight functions given by evaluation oracles,22 2 This means that there is a black-box that returns the weight μ⁡(S)\mu(S) (resp. ν⁡(S)\nu(S)) on input S⊆𝒰S\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}. The number of calls to this black-box is counted in the overall running time of our algorithms. and suppose gμ,gνg_{\mu},g_{\nu} are log-concave. Assume initial sets S0,T0⊆𝒰S_{0},T_{0}\subseteq{\mathcal{U}} satisfying μ⁡(S0)>0,ν⁡(T0)>0\mu(S_{0})>0,\nu(T_{0})>0, upper bounds on ℛμ,ℛν{\mathcal{R}}_{\mu},{\mathcal{R}}_{\nu}, and an error parameter 0<ε≤10<\varepsilon\leq 1 are given. Then there is an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for any specified coefficient

Z𝜶≔[𝒙𝜶]​(gμ​(𝒙)⋅gν​(𝒙)),𝜶∈{0,1,2}𝒰\displaystyle Z_{\bm{\alpha}}\coloneqq\left[{\bm{x}^{\bm{\alpha}}}\right]\left({g_{\mu}(\bm{x})\cdot g_{\nu}(\bm{x})}\right),\qquad\bm{\alpha}\in\{0,1,2\}^{{\mathcal{U}}}

that uses at most

O~​(n11⋅(n+log⁡(ℛμ⋅ℛν))2ε2)\displaystyle\widetilde{O}\left({\frac{n^{11}\cdot\left({n+\log({\mathcal{R}}_{\mu}\cdot{\mathcal{R}}_{\nu})}\right)^{2}}{\varepsilon^{2}}}\right)

arithmetic operations and evaluation oracle calls.

Proof of Theorem 1.2.

This is an immediate corollary of Theorem 1.6 in the case 𝜶=𝟏\bm{\alpha}=\mathbf{1} by setting μ(S)=𝟏[S∈ℬ(ℳ)]\mu(S)=\mathbf{1}[S\in{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{M}})] and ν(T)=𝟏[𝒰∖T∈ℬ(𝒩)]\nu(T)=\mathbf{1}[{\mathcal{U}}\setminus T\in{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{N}})], both of which can be evaluated given independence oracles for ℳ,𝒩{\mathcal{M}},{\mathcal{N}}. Log-concavity of gμ,gνg_{\mu},g_{\nu} was established in [AOV18, BH20], and we can find initializing sets S0,T0S_{0},T_{0} by greedy algorithms. ∎

We highlight three further applications of the more general Theorem 1.6 that aren’t captured directly by Theorem 1.2. Each admits an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS}; precise definitions and reductions appear in Appendix C.

  • •

    Mixed discriminants. Approximate the mixed discriminant of positive semidefinite matrices, a generalization of the permanent [Cel+17]; see Section C.5. This resolves the mixed-discriminant question in [Gur07, Section 4, Problem 2], disproving the conjectured nonexistence of an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS}.

  • •

    The six-vertex model. Estimate its partition function on loopless 44-regular multigraphs when the nonnegative weights satisfy a≤b+ca\leq b+c, b≤a+cb\leq a+c, and c≤a+bc\leq a+b; see Section C.6. For positive weights, this completes the general-graph approximation classification left open by [CLL19, Section 6].

  • •

    Quantum Max-Cut and the EPR model. Estimate the optimal value of Quantum Max-Cut on bipartite graphs and of the EPR model on arbitrary graphs, with nonnegative edge weights; see Section C.7. This resolves the bipartite complexity question in [Gha23, Open question 3.4] and proves the EPR-in-𝖡𝖯𝖯\mathsf{BPP} conjecture of [MS26, Conjecture 1].

1.2 Counting and Sampling for Hadamard Products via Curvature

The key input into our approximate counting and sampling algorithms is a Poincaré Inequality for the Hadamard product of two probability measures μ,ν\mu,\nu assumed to satisfy suitable “curvature” conditions. For the Hadamard-product dynamics and Poincaré inequality below, let μ,ν:2𝒰→ℝ≥0\mu,\nu:2^{{\mathcal{U}}}\to{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0} have a common nonempty support Ω\Omega. For weights with different supports, first restrict both to their support intersection and set them to zero outside it.

Definition 1.7 (Hadamard Product).

Let ρ=μ⊙ν\rho=\mu\odot\nu denote the probability measure supported on Ω\Omega defined by (μ⊙ν)​(S)∝μ⁡(S)⋅ν⁡(S)(\mu\odot\nu)(S)\propto\mu(S)\cdot\nu(S) for all S⊆𝒰S\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}.

Let us now introduce a natural local Markov chain that samples from ρ=μ⊙ν\rho=\mu\odot\nu. Write S+u≔S∪{u}S+u\coloneqq S\cup\{u\} and S−u≔S∖{u}S-u\coloneqq S\setminus\{u\}. For each u∈𝒰u\in{\mathcal{U}}, define the Laplacian ℒu{\mathscr{L}}_{u} via the following operator on functions f:2𝒰→ℝf:2^{{\mathcal{U}}}\to{\mathbb{R}}, evaluated at S∈ΩS\in\Omega:

(ℒu​f)​(S)=ru​(S)⋅(f⁡(S+u)−f⁡(S−u))​where​ru​(S)≔{−μ(S+u)/μ(S−u),if ​u∉Sν⁡(S−u)/ν⁡(S+u),if ​u∈S\displaystyle({\mathscr{L}}_{u}f)(S)=r_{u}(S)\cdot\left({f(S+u)-f(S-u)}\right)\kern 5.0pt\text{where}\kern 5.0ptr_{u}(S)\coloneqq\begin{cases}-\mu(S+u)/\mu(S-u),&\quad\text{if }u\notin S\\ \nu(S-u)/\nu(S+u),&\quad\text{if }u\in S\end{cases}

gives the relative birth and death rates. The operator ℒu{\mathscr{L}}_{u} encodes the updates at coordinate uu. The full Laplacian is defined as

ℒ\displaystyle{\mathscr{L}} ≔∑u∈𝒰ℒu.\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{u\in{\mathcal{U}}}{\mathscr{L}}_{u}. (3)

It acts on S∈ΩS\in\Omega with infeasible additions and deletions omitted.

Fact 1.8.

ℒu{\mathscr{L}}_{u} is reversible with respect to ρ\rho for all u∈𝒰u\in{\mathcal{U}}, i.e. ⟨f,ℒu​g⟩ρ=⟨ℒu​f,g⟩ρ\langle f,{\mathscr{L}}_{u}g\rangle_{\rho}=\langle{\mathscr{L}}_{u}f,g\rangle_{\rho} for all functions f,g:2𝒰→ℝf,g:2^{{\mathcal{U}}}\to{\mathbb{R}}. Moreover, ℒu{\mathscr{L}}_{u} is positive semidefinite, i.e. ⟨f,ℒu​f⟩ρ≥0\langle f,{\mathscr{L}}_{u}f\rangle_{\rho}\geq 0 for all f:2𝒰→ℝf:2^{{\mathcal{U}}}\to{\mathbb{R}}.

The resulting transition matrix is P=I−ℒ/(2​n​B)P=I-{\mathscr{L}}/(2nB), which is lazy and reversible with respect to ρ\rho, and its spectral gap is that of ℒ{\mathscr{L}} divided by 2​n​B2nB. Having defined the dynamics, let us now introduce the local “curvature” criterion that will be used to deduce a Poincaré Inequality for ℒ{\mathscr{L}}.

Definition 1.10 ((Upward) κ\kappa-Spectral Curvature).

Fix a parameter κ∈ℝ\kappa\in{\mathbb{R}}. For a nonnegative weight function μ:2𝒰→ℝ≥0\mu:2^{{\mathcal{U}}}\to{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0} that is not identically zero, and each S∈supp⁡(μ)S\in\supp(\mu), define the 𝒰×𝒰{\mathcal{U}}\times{\mathcal{U}} (upward) κ\kappa-curvature matrix33 3 Note that the only nonzero entries ASμA_{S}^{\mu} come from elements in 𝒰∖S{\mathcal{U}}\setminus S.

ASμ,κ​(u,v)≔{μ​(S+v)2μ​(S)2−κ⋅μ⁡(S+v)μ⁡(S),if ​u,v∉S,u=vμ⁡(S+u)μ⁡(S)⋅μ⁡(S+v)μ⁡(S)−μ⁡(S+u+v)μ⁡(S),if ​u,v∉S,u≠v0,otherwise\displaystyle A_{S}^{\mu,\kappa}(u,v)\coloneqq\begin{cases}\frac{\mu(S+v)^{2}}{\mu(S)^{2}}-\kappa\cdot\frac{\mu(S+v)}{\mu(S)},&\quad\text{if }u,v\notin S,u=v\\ \frac{\mu(S+u)}{\mu(S)}\cdot\frac{\mu(S+v)}{\mu(S)}-\frac{\mu(S+u+v)}{\mu(S)},&\quad\text{if }u,v\notin S,u\neq v\\ 0,&\quad\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

We say μ\mu has (upward) κ\kappa-spectral curvature if ASμ,κ⪰0A_{S}^{\mu,\kappa}\succeq 0 for every S∈supp⁡(μ)S\in\supp(\mu).

Remark 1.11.

In this paper, we are primarily interested in the κ≥0\kappa\geq 0 regime. However, we note that κ\kappa can be any real number; see Section A.7 for examples.

Remark 1.12.

Unlike the influence/correlation/covariance matrices appearing in the theory of spectral independence [ALO20] and localization schemes [CE22], whose entries are #​𝖯\#\mathsf{P}-hard to compute exactly, the entries of ASμ,κA_{S}^{\mu,\kappa} are straightforward to compute for any S∈supp⁡(μ)S\in\supp(\mu). Hence, for many applications, verifying spectral curvature can be done easily by hand.

The notion of curvature appearing in Definition 1.10 has previously appeared in the literature in various guises; we discuss these connections in greater depth in Section 1.3. Before we continue, note that we can also define a “downward” analog of κ\kappa-spectral curvature by considering the (upward) κ\kappa-spectral curvature of the dual μ∗\mu^{*}, defined as follows.

Definition 1.13 (Dual).

Let μ:2𝒰→ℝ≥0\mu:2^{{\mathcal{U}}}\to{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0} be nonzero. We define its dual μ∗:2𝒰→ℝ≥0\mu^{*}:2^{{\mathcal{U}}}\to{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0} by μ∗​(S)≔μ⁡(𝒰∖S)\mu^{*}(S)\coloneqq\mu({\mathcal{U}}\setminus S) for all S⊆𝒰S\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}.

We elaborate on the role of the “downward” analog of κ\kappa-spectral curvature in Section 4. Our main technical theorem is the following.

Theorem 1.14 (Main Poincaré Inequality).

Let μ,ν:2𝒰→ℝ≥0\mu,\nu:2^{{\mathcal{U}}}\to{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0} have a common nonempty support Ω\Omega, connected under single-element additions and deletions, and let ρ=μ⊙ν\rho=\mu\odot\nu be their Hadamard product, which is supported on Ω\Omega. If μ\mu has η\eta-spectral curvature and ν∗\nu^{*} has κ\kappa-spectral curvature, where η,κ∈ℝ\eta,\kappa\in{\mathbb{R}} satisfy η+κ>0\eta+\kappa>0, then ρ\rho obeys the Poincaré Inequality

(η+κ)⋅𝐕𝐚𝐫ρ​[f]≤⟨f,ℒ​f⟩ρ,∀f:Ω→ℝ.\displaystyle(\eta+\kappa)\cdot\mathbf{Var}_{\rho}\left[f\right]\leq\langle f,{\mathscr{L}}f\rangle_{\rho},\qquad\forall f:\Omega\to{\mathbb{R}}.

A family ℱ⊆2W\mathcal{F}\subseteq 2^{W} is downward closed if it contains every subset of each of its members, and upward closed if it contains every superset contained in WW of each of its members.

Remark 1.15.

By Lemma A.1, a positive spectral-gap bound from Theorem 1.14 forces Ω\Omega to be upward or downward closed after removing coordinates that are constant on Ω\Omega.

Through Theorem 1.14, we can design an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for the subset convolution of a pair of downward closed measures that satisfy nonnegative curvature.

Theorem 1.16.

Suppose μ,ν:2𝒰→ℝ≥0\mu,\nu:2^{{\mathcal{U}}}\to{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0} have downward closed supports and upward spectral curvatures η,κ\eta,\kappa, with η+κ≥0\eta+\kappa\geq 0. Put γ≔max⁡{η,κ}\gamma\coloneqq\max\{\eta,\kappa\}; if γ>0\gamma>0, let χ≥1\chi\geq 1 be a supplied bound, polynomial in nn, such that, for each ω∈{μ,ν}\omega\in\{\mu,\nu\},

ω⁡(S+u)\displaystyle\omega(S+u) ≤χ⋅γ⋅ω⁡(S),∀S∈supp⁡ω,∀u∉S.\displaystyle\leq\chi\cdot\gamma\cdot\omega(S),\qquad\forall S\in\supp\omega,\,\forall u\notin S.

In all other cases, take χ=1\chi=1 without imposing this bound. Given value oracles for μ,ν\mu,\nu, upper bounds on ℛμ,ℛν{\mathcal{R}}_{\mu},{\mathcal{R}}_{\nu}, and an error parameter 0<ε<10<\varepsilon<1, there is an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for any specified coefficient

Z𝜶\displaystyle Z_{\bm{\alpha}} ≔[𝒙𝜶]​(gμ​(𝒙)⋅gν​(𝒙)),𝜶∈{0,1,2}𝒰\displaystyle\coloneqq[\bm{x}^{\bm{\alpha}}]\bigl(g_{\mu}(\bm{x})\cdot g_{\nu}(\bm{x})\bigr),\qquad\bm{\alpha}\in\{0,1,2\}^{{\mathcal{U}}}

that uses at most

O~​(n11​(n+log⁡(ℛμ​ℛν))2ε2+n5​χ​(n+log⁡(ℛμ​ℛν))ε3)\displaystyle\widetilde{O}\left({\frac{n^{11}(n+\log({\mathcal{R}}_{\mu}{\mathcal{R}}_{\nu}))^{2}}{\varepsilon^{2}}+\frac{n^{5}\chi(n+\log({\mathcal{R}}_{\mu}{\mathcal{R}}_{\nu}))}{\varepsilon^{3}}}\right)

arithmetic operations and evaluation oracle calls.

Remark 1.17.

Theorem 1.16 can be viewed as a generalization of Theorem 1.6. For log-concave measures, translating gμ​(𝒙),gν​(𝒙)g_{\mu}(\bm{x}),g_{\nu}(\bm{x}) to gμ​(𝟏+𝒙),gν​(𝟏+𝒙)g_{\mu}(\mathbf{1}+\bm{x}),g_{\nu}(\mathbf{1}+\bm{x}) gives downward-closed measures with zero curvature by Proposition 1.22. After reducing to homogeneous polynomials whose degrees sum to nn (see Section A.1), these translations preserve the coefficient of 𝒙𝒰\bm{x}^{{\mathcal{U}}}. The translated weights, i.e. the coefficients of gμ​(𝟏+𝒙),gν​(𝟏+𝒙)g_{\mu}(\mathbf{1}+\bm{x}),g_{\nu}(\mathbf{1}+\bm{x}), are respectively

μ^​(S)=∑T⊇Sμ⁡(T),ν^​(S)=∑T⊇Sν⁡(T).\widehat{\mu}(S)=\sum_{T\supseteq S}\mu(T),\qquad\widehat{\nu}(S)=\sum_{T\supseteq S}\nu(T).

These sums each admit an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} since μ,ν\mu,\nu are log-concave [Ana+19]. Using sufficiently accurate estimates of the queried weights and controlling the accumulated sampling error gives the reduction, with additional polynomial overhead. We state Theorem 1.6 separately to give a direct algorithm using the original evaluation oracles and a sharper running-time bound.

Remark 1.18 (Optimality of the curvature threshold).

The condition η+κ≥0\eta+\kappa\geq 0 in Theorem 1.16 is optimal among constant lower bounds on the curvature sum. For every fixed δ>0\delta>0, there is no 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} under the weaker condition η+κ>−δ\eta+\kappa>-\delta, unless 𝖭𝖯=𝖱𝖯\mathsf{NP}=\mathsf{RP}. This holds even when μ=ν\mu=\nu have downward-closed support, polynomial-time value oracles, and log⁡(ℛμ​ℛν)=O⁡(n​log⁡n)\log({\mathcal{R}}_{\mu}{\mathcal{R}}_{\nu})=O(n\log n). The proof is deferred to Section A.3.

Additional Applications of Theorem 1.16.

As noted in Remark 1.17, Theorem 1.16 generalizes Theorem 1.6. However, we highlight a couple interesting applications of the former that aren’t captured by the latter. In particular, we show that each of the following approximate counting problems on simple graphs admits an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS}. Both counts include all sizes; precise definitions and proofs appear in Section C.11.

  • •

    Rainbow matchings. Count matchings with no repeated edge color, for an arbitrary edge coloring; see Corollary C.24. This counts all sizes and does not address the rainbow perfect-matching enumeration studied by [PS13].

  • •

    Degree-constrained forests. Count forests satisfying prescribed upper bounds on the vertex degrees. When every bound is two, this counts unions of vertex-disjoint paths; see Corollary C.25. This adds vertex-degree bounds to the forest-counting result of [Ana+19].

1.3 Connections with Previous Notions

We compare the spectral curvature condition in Definition 1.10 with earlier notions that appeared in the literature.

Trickle-Down Condition for Field Dynamics

Previous work of [Che+25] derived a sufficient condition for the so-called field dynamics [Che+24] to satisfy a Poincaré Inequality based on a certain “pairwise dependency matrix”. This matrix turns out to be equivalent to the curvature matrix appearing in Definition 1.10 up to a simple transformation, which we now describe.

Let μ:2𝒰→ℝ≥0\mu:2^{{\mathcal{U}}}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} be a nonzero weight function with downward closed support. For each S∈supp⁡(μ)S\in\supp(\mu), put

DS≔diag(μ⁡(S+u)μ⁡(S):u∉S,μ(S+u)>0).\displaystyle D_{S}\coloneqq\diag\left({\frac{\mu(S+u)}{\mu(S)}:u\notin S,\mu(S+u)>0}\right).

The matrices below are indexed by the feasible additions u∉Su\notin S with μ⁡(S+u)>0\mu(S+u)>0.

Definition 1.19 (Pairwise dependency matrix [Che+25]).

Let S∈supp⁡(μ)S\in\supp(\mu). The pairwise dependency matrix of μ\mu at SS is the symmetric matrix MSM_{S} with entries

MS​(u,v)\displaystyle M_{S}(u,v) ≔{μ⁡(S+u+v)⋅μ⁡(S)μ⁡(S+u)⋅μ⁡(S+v)−1,u≠v,0,u=v.\displaystyle\coloneqq\begin{cases}\dfrac{\mu(S+u+v)\cdot\mu(S)}{\mu(S+u)\cdot\mu(S+v)}-1,&u\neq v,\\ 0,&u=v.\end{cases}

A straightforward calculation reveals the identity

ASμ,κ\displaystyle A_{S}^{\mu,\kappa} =DS⋅(I−MS−κ​DS−1)⋅DS.\displaystyle=D_{S}\cdot\left({I-M_{S}-\kappa D_{S}^{-1}}\right)\cdot D_{S}.

Here we restrict ASμ,κA_{S}^{\mu,\kappa} to the feasible additions; downward closure makes all other rows and columns zero. Thus the trickle-down criterion for field dynamics MS⪯I+(1−δ)​DS−1M_{S}\preceq I+(1-\delta)D_{S}^{-1} for every SS, with 0<δ<10<\delta<1, in [Che+25, Theorems 1.9 and 1.14] is exactly upward (δ−1)(\delta-1)-spectral curvature. The stronger condition MS⪯IM_{S}\preceq I is the case κ=0\kappa=0.

A shorter proof of the spectral gap bound under the aforementioned trickle-down criterion appears in [Göb+26], which is based on an integrated Bochner method. Our proof of Theorem 1.14 is a direct generalization of their argument.

Remark 1.20.

For δ>0\delta>0, the δ\delta-ultra-log-concavity of [CW26, Definition 3.5] extends this criterion to measures on ℕ𝒰\mathbb{N}^{{\mathcal{U}}} with downward-closed support. On the Boolean cube, it is exactly upward (δ−1)(\delta-1)-spectral curvature; the case δ=1\delta=1 corresponds to zero upward curvature.

Log-concave polynomials.

Log-concavity of the generating polynomial gives another way to bound spectral curvature.

Definition 1.21 (Fractional log-concavity [Ali+21]).

Let 0<α≤10<\alpha\leq 1, and let p∈ℝ⁡[x1,…,xn]p\in\mathbb{R}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] be a nonzero polynomial with nonnegative coefficients. We say that pp is α\alpha-fractionally log-concave if 𝒙↦log⁡p⁡(x1α,…,xnα)\bm{x}\mapsto\log p(x_{1}^{\alpha},\ldots,x_{n}^{\alpha}) is concave on ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}.

For multiaffine pp, this gives a curvature bound for the coefficients of p⁡(𝟏+𝒙)p(\mathbf{1}+\bm{x}).

Proposition 1.22.

Let pp be nonzero, multiaffine, and α\alpha-fractionally log-concave, with nonnegative coefficients and 0<α≤10<\alpha\leq 1. The coefficient measure μ^\widehat{\mu} defined by gμ^​(𝐱)≔p⁡(𝟏+𝐱)g_{\widehat{\mu}}(\bm{x})\coloneqq p(\mathbf{1}+\bm{x}) has downward-closed support and upward (1−α−1)(1-\alpha^{-1})-spectral curvature.

The proof is given in Section A.6.

Remark 1.23.

Lorentzian polynomials extend the theory of multi-affine homogeneous log-concave polynomials to polynomials with M\mathrm{M}-convex supports [BH20, Theorems 2.30 and 3.10]. For a nonzero multiaffine Lorentzian polynomial pp, Proposition 1.22 with α=1\alpha=1 gives zero upward spectral curvature for the coefficient measure of p⁡(𝟏+𝒙)p(\mathbf{1}+\bm{x}).

00-spectral curvature is closely related to log-concavity through the trickle-down principle [Opp18] and analogous local-to-global results for polynomials [Ana+19, BH20]. These polynomial results are stated for homogeneous polynomials, meaning that every monomial has the same degree. [Che+25] gives a direct extension to generating polynomials that need not be homogeneous, for measures with downward-closed support, yielding the following result.

Proposition 1.24 ([Che+25, Proposition 3.8]).

Let μ:2𝒰→ℝ≥0\mu:2^{{\mathcal{U}}}\to{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0} have downward closed support. If μ\mu has (upward) 00-spectral curvature, then gμg_{\mu} is log-concave.

1.4 Prior Work

Trickle-down and field dynamics.

Trickle-down arguments grew out of earlier local-to-global ideas [Gar73, KM17, DK17] and establish rapid mixing of “global” random walks by analyzing related “local” random walks, which are usually easier to study [Opp18, KO20, AL20, Ana+19, ALO20]. Refinements and extensions appear in [GM20, ALO21, AO23, GK23, AKV24, LLO25, LO25, GZ26, BLO26]. Related sampling results appear in [CLV23, CLV21, Fen+22, Bla+22, Liu21, Ana+24]. Field dynamics [Che+24] provides a mechanism for reducing sampling from a “hard” distribution to sampling from relatively “easier” conditional distributions with smaller external fields. This approach and related methods [Eld13, EKZ22, CE22, Che+22] have led to rapid-mixing results for the hardcore model (and more general antiferromagnetic two-spin systems) in the tree-uniqueness regime and at the uniqueness threshold [Che+25a, Che+26a]. Our curvature condition builds on top of a criterion that lies between these two lines of work [Che+25].

Bochner-Type Methods.

Bochner-type methods bound the spectral gap of random walks by relating it to the local “curvature” of the underlying space. The terminology originates from Bochner’s formula in Riemannian geometry [Boc46, Lic58], and its application to continuous diffusions in high-dimensional probability is classical [BÉ85]; see also [BGL14]. Adaptations of these techniques to discrete spaces appear in [Bou+06, CP07, Cap08, CDP09, KKO13, DP13, Joh17, JY17, WZ21, Ped25]. A recent flurry of work, starting with [Göb+26], applies a variant of this method and closely related arguments for spin systems on random regular and planar graphs [Göb+26, GZ26], the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model [Wan26, BLO26], graph colorings [CL26, Haq26], and “ultra-log-concave” distributions [CW26]. It also gives simpler proofs of known trickle-down results; see [CL26a] and references therein. Our proof of Theorem 1.14 uses this method.

Geometry of polynomials.

Properties of generating polynomials have been used to prove inequalities for combinatorial counts and probabilities [BBL09, Gur09, Huh12, HK12, HW17, AHK18, AOV18, Ana+18, BH20].

Gurvits capacity and related entropy maximization programs connect these inequalities to approximate counting and optimization [Gur06, Gur07, NS16, SV17, GL21]. Applications include permanents [LSW00, Gur06], bases and common bases of matroids [AO17, SV17, AOV18], contingency tables and integer flows [Bar09, BLP23], and lattice points in bounded totally unimodular polytopes [LM26]. These methods often give polynomial-time algorithms with exponential approximation ratios. Recent work has improved deterministic approximation guarantees for the permanent [Ana26, KLM26, DJ26].

For sampling and randomized counting on matroids, earlier algorithms covered special classes [FM92, JS02, AOR16]. Later advances based on log-concavity handled general matroids and improved the running times [Ana+19, CGM21, Ana+21, AD20].

Annealing and adjusting weights.

The Markov-chain approach to approximating the permanent was initiated by Broder [Bro86] and developed by Jerrum and Sinclair [JS89]. Jerrum, Sinclair, and Vigoda [JSV04] gave the first 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for the permanent of an arbitrary nonnegative matrix. This algorithm and subsequent 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS}es for the permanent [Bez+08, CVY26, Che+26] and two-terminal reliability [FFG26] add extra configurations to make sampling easier, and gradually change the input weights (annealing; see [ŠVV09, Guo+26]) while learning weights that keep desired configurations, such as perfect matchings, from becoming rare. Those algorithms learn correction weights along a carefully designed annealing path; our method chooses fields directly by stochastic gradient descent. The resulting fields make the desired pairs frequent. We then estimate the total weight using the standard reduction from sampling to counting [JVV86]. See Section 2.3 for a detailed discussion.

AI Disclosure

For transparency, we detail the progression of this project and the role AI tools played. While the authors did provide many high level directions, we emphasize that AI contributions were critical to the success of this project.

This project began with a much more modest problem, namely establishing rapid mixing of Glauber dynamics for sampling from the distribution μ⁡(S)∝λ|S|\mu(S)\propto\lambda^{\left|{S}\right|} for common independent sets SS of all sizes (see Section D.1). Although the authors were unaware of any previous work formulating this specific problem, it is a somewhat obvious generalization of the monomer-dimer model on all matchings of a graph, for which Glauber dynamics provably mixes rapidly for all λ\lambda [JS89, CLV21, Che+25b, MY26, CCZ26]. Based on this, as well as rapid mixing for a similar distribution over all independent sets of a single matroid, the authors conjectured that no dynamical phase transition occurs, and that the mixing time remains polynomial for every fixed λ≥0\lambda\geq 0. This conjecture was previously posed by the authors, for instance, during “The geometry of polynomials in combinatorics and sampling” workshop at the American Institute of Mathematics in early March 2025. The main motivation for studying this specific problem was two-fold:

  • •

    Its resolution would provide a first stepping stone towards an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for common bases of two matroids, paralleling the chronological development of the first 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for the permanent of nonnegative matrices.

  • •

    Independent of whether or not it would eventually lead to an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for common bases of two matroids, the authors believed this problem was interesting because all previously known techniques for proving rapid mixing appear to fail for this model: There are simple examples of pairs of matroids for which the spectral-independence parameter of the resulting distribution on common independent sets is Ω⁡(𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n))\Omega(\mathsf{poly}(n)).44 4 For example, at λ=1\lambda=1, the monomer–dimer model on an even cycle of length Θ⁡(n1/3)\Theta(n^{1/3}) with each edge replaced by Θ⁡(n2/3)\Theta(n^{2/3}) parallel edges has Θ⁡(n1/3)\Theta(n^{1/3})-spectral-independence, where nn is the total number of edges; see [Che+25c] for the parallel-edge construction. This bipartite graph’s matchings are exactly the common independent sets of two partition matroids. It is also believed that constructing canonical paths or flows with polynomial congestion would be hard in general.

In light of recent exciting work of [Göb+26], the authors suspected that (integrated) Bochner-type methods had a chance of overcoming these obstacles. The authors instructed GPT 5.6 Sol Ultra to take inspiration from [Göb+26] and prove rapid mixing for all λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 using an integrated Bochner-type argument. Initially, GPT 5.6 Sol Ultra worked on this task for 17 hours without success. Fortuitously, GPT 6 Astra Ultra was released at this time, and it was able to solve the problem with an additional 3 hours. The result was a fairly short and simple proof, parts of which are reproduced in Section 4, that was tailored to this specific problem. During the process of digesting this proof, the authors independently realized that the argument works much more generally for intersections of probability measures satisfying suitable “curvature” conditions, and that this notion of “curvature” is essentially equivalent to a notion contained in prior work of [Che+25]. This is how we came to the formulation of Theorem 1.14.

Our progress on sampling common independent sets of matroids led us to ask whether similar ideas could give an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for common bases. To explore this question, we provided ChatGPT Pro with several separate drafts:

  • •

    a revised note on sampling common independent sets;

  • •

    a revised note on a common framework for recent progress on Bochner-type methods;

  • •

    a draft on a faster 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for the permanent [Che+26].

ChatGPT first identified an obstruction to obtaining an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} directly from our sampler for common independent sets. We replied that this was understandable and suggested an annealing approach, as in algorithms for the permanent. It agreed, and after a further prompt to “keep trying,” it found a solution.

While studying the proof produced by ChatGPT, we recognized the underlying stochastic gradient descent framework (Section 2.3). With further help from ChatGPT, we generalized the 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for common bases to subset convolution, both for measures with log-concave generating polynomials and for measures with downward closed supports satisfying our nonnegative curvature condition (Theorems 1.6 and 1.16). We also used ChatGPT to search for reductions of other known problems to these subset-convolution problems (see Appendix C).

2 Technical Overview

2.1 Poincaré Inequality via an Integrated Bochner Method

We prove Theorem 1.14 in Section 4 by an integrated Bochner-type method, which bounds the spectral gap of a Laplacian using its square. The following abstract criterion holds for the Laplacian ℒ{\mathcal{L}} of any irreducible reversible Markov chain; see Section 3.3 for the notation and proof.

Proposition 2.1.

Let ℒ{\mathcal{L}} be the Laplacian of an irreducible reversible Markov chain on a finite state space Ω\Omega, with stationary distribution π\pi. Then its spectral gap satisfies

γ≔inff​ nonconstant⟨f,ℒ​f⟩π𝐕𝐚𝐫π​[f]\displaystyle\gamma\coloneqq\inf_{f\text{ nonconstant}}\frac{\langle f,{\mathcal{L}}f\rangle_{\pi}}{\mathbf{Var}_{\pi}\left[f\right]} =inff​ nonconstant⟨ℒ​f,ℒ​f⟩π⟨f,ℒ​f⟩π.\displaystyle=\inf_{f\text{ nonconstant}}\frac{\langle{\mathcal{L}}f,{\mathcal{L}}f\rangle_{\pi}}{\langle f,{\mathcal{L}}f\rangle_{\pi}}.

We apply Proposition 2.1 to the Laplacian ℒ{\mathscr{L}} defined in Eq. 3. The common support Ω\Omega is connected under single-element additions and deletions, and every feasible transition has positive rate, so the chain with Laplacian ℒ{\mathscr{L}} is irreducible. Thus, to prove γ≥η+κ\gamma\geq\eta+\kappa, it suffices to show

⟨ℒ​f,ℒ​f⟩ρ≥(η+κ)⋅⟨f,ℒ​f⟩ρ∀f:Ω→ℝ.\displaystyle\langle{\mathscr{L}}f,{\mathscr{L}}f\rangle_{\rho}\geq(\eta+\kappa)\cdot\langle f,{\mathscr{L}}f\rangle_{\rho}\qquad\forall f:\Omega\to{\mathbb{R}}.

We prove this by writing ⟨f,(ℒ2−(η+κ)⋅ℒ)​f⟩ρ\langle f,({\mathscr{L}}^{2}-(\eta+\kappa)\cdot{\mathscr{L}})f\rangle_{\rho} as a sum-of-squares (Proposition 4.2), taking heavy inspiration from [Göb+26]. The spectral-curvature conditions make the terms involving the curvature matrices nonnegative, and the remaining terms are squared second differences of ff with nonnegative weights.

2.2 Reduction to the Homogeneous Log-Concave Case

The following special case of Theorem 1.6 (and Theorem 1.16) is the most interesting case. It is also, in some sense, the most difficult.

Theorem 2.2 (Simplified version of Theorem 5.1).

Let μ:(𝒰a)→ℝ≥0\mu:\binom{{\mathcal{U}}}{a}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} and ν:(𝒰b)→ℝ≥0\nu:\binom{{\mathcal{U}}}{b}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}, extended by zero to 2𝒰2^{{\mathcal{U}}}, where a,b≥0a,b\geq 0 are integers with a+b=n≔|𝒰|≥1a+b=n\coloneqq|{\mathcal{U}}|\geq 1. Suppose gμ,gνg_{\mu},g_{\nu} are log-concave. Given value oracles for μ,ν\mu,\nu, the coefficient ranges ℛμ,ℛν{\mathcal{R}}_{\mu},{\mathcal{R}}_{\nu}, and one set in the support of each measure, there is an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for the subset-convolution value

Z∩\displaystyle Z_{\cap} ≔(μ∗ν)​(𝒰)=[𝒙𝒰]​(gμ​(𝒙)⋅gν​(𝒙))=∑S⊆𝒰μ⁡(S)⋅ν⁡(𝒰∖S).\displaystyle\coloneqq(\mu\ast\nu)({\mathcal{U}})=[\bm{x}^{{\mathcal{U}}}]\bigl(g_{\mu}(\bm{x})\cdot g_{\nu}(\bm{x})\bigr)=\sum_{S\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}}\mu(S)\cdot\nu({\mathcal{U}}\setminus S).

In this subsection, we describe how we reduce Theorem 1.16 (which generalizes Theorem 1.6 as mentioned in Remark 1.17) to Theorem 2.2 and Theorem 1.14. A pictorial representation is provided in Fig. 1, with detailed proofs deferred to Section A.1. Throughout this subsection, we focus on the case of convolution where 𝜶=𝟏\bm{\alpha}=\mathbf{1}; this is essentially without loss of generality, as one can simply pin the coordinates with exponent 00 or 22 for a general 𝜶∈{0,1,2}𝒰\bm{\alpha}\in\{0,1,2\}^{{\mathcal{U}}}. We briefly explain our reductions as follows:

  • •

    For Theorem 1.16 with max⁡{η,κ}>0\max\{\eta,\kappa\}>0, we apply an external field to the measure with higher curvature. This external field is of magnitude O⁡(1/n)O(1/n) away from 11, which is enough to make the Poincaré constant in Theorem 1.14 at least Ω⁡(1/n)\Omega(1/n), but small enough so that the new partition function remains ε\varepsilon-multiplicatively close to the original. We then apply the standard self-reduction [JVV86].

  • •

    For Theorem 1.6, which includes Theorem 1.16 with η=κ=0\eta=\kappa=0, we split by degree into at most n+1n+1 homogeneous pairs and apply Theorem 2.2 to each.

2.3 From Poincaré to Counting via Convex Programming and Softening

In this section, we outline the proof of Theorem 2.2. The algorithm and its proof of correctness provide a general framework to turn sampling from a “soft” intersection of two measures on sets into approximate counting for the corresponding “hard” intersection. This method may be of independent interest, and is based on the following general principle: A Poincaré inequality that holds uniformly over external fields turns subset convolution into a dual maximum entropy convex program. Variants of this principle based on stronger assumptions (e.g. log-concavity of the generating polynomial) with significantly weaker approximation guarantees have previously appeared in the literature [Gur06, AO17]. We discuss this in greater detail in Remark 2.7.

Let μ,ν:2𝒰→ℝ≥0\mu,\nu:2^{{\mathcal{U}}}\to{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0} be nonzero, put n≔|𝒰|n\coloneqq|{\mathcal{U}}|, and consider

Z∩\displaystyle Z_{\cap} ≔∑S⊆𝒰μ⁡(S)⋅ν⁡(𝒰∖S).\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{S\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}}\mu(S)\cdot\nu({\mathcal{U}}\setminus S).

When Z∩>0Z_{\cap}>0, the direct target measure μ⊙ν∗\mu\odot\nu^{*}, with weights proportional to μ⁡(S)​ν​(𝒰∖S)\mu(S)\nu({\mathcal{U}}\setminus S), can be poorly connected under natural local moves: the hard constraint T=𝒰∖ST={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S forces changes to the two sets to be coordinated. To bypass this, it is natural to consider a variant of μ⊙ν∗\mu\odot\nu^{*} in which the hard constraint T=𝒰∖ST={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S is “softened”.

For penalty vectors 𝒕∈(0,1]𝒰\bm{t}\in(0,1]^{{\mathcal{U}}}, write 𝒕R≔∏u∈Rtu\bm{t}^{R}\coloneqq\prod_{u\in R}t_{u}. For external fields 𝒛∈ℝ>0𝒰\bm{z}\in{\mathbb{R}}_{>0}^{{\mathcal{U}}}, the soft intersection is the distribution on supp⁡μ×supp⁡ν\supp\mu\times\supp\nu given by

π𝒕,𝒛​(S,T)\displaystyle\pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}(S,T) ∝μ⁡(S)⋅ν⁡(T)⋅𝒛S​𝒛T⋅𝒕S∩T,\displaystyle\propto\mu(S)\cdot\nu(T)\cdot\bm{z}^{S}\bm{z}^{T}\cdot\bm{t}^{S\cap T},

that is, the Hadamard product

π𝒕,𝒛\displaystyle\pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}} =(μ𝒛⊗ν𝒛)⊙ψ𝒕,\displaystyle=(\mu_{\bm{z}}\otimes\nu_{\bm{z}})\odot\psi_{\bm{t}}, μ𝒛​(S)\displaystyle\mu_{\bm{z}}(S) ≔μ⁡(S)⋅𝒛S,ν𝒛​(T)≔ν⁡(T)⋅𝒛T,ψ𝒕​(S,T)≔𝒕S∩T.\displaystyle\coloneqq\mu(S)\cdot\bm{z}^{S},\quad\nu_{\bm{z}}(T)\coloneqq\nu(T)\cdot\bm{z}^{T},\quad\psi_{\bm{t}}(S,T)\coloneqq\bm{t}^{S\cap T}.

Let

Z𝒕,𝒛≔∑S,T⊆𝒰μ⁡(S)⋅ν⁡(T)⋅𝒛S​𝒛T⋅𝒕S∩T\displaystyle Z_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}\coloneqq\sum_{S,T\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}}\mu(S)\cdot\nu(T)\cdot\bm{z}^{S}\bm{z}^{T}\cdot\bm{t}^{S\cap T}

be its partition function. When all penalties equal a scalar t∈(0,1]t\in(0,1], we write a subscript tt for the uniform penalty vector 𝒕=t⋅𝟏\bm{t}=t\cdot\mathbf{1}.

Note that π𝒕,𝒛\pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}} penalizes pairs (S,T)(S,T) where S,TS,T have a large intersection. On the other hand, complementary pairs T=𝒰∖ST={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S carry no penalty. Moreover, all such complementary pairs have the common factor 𝒛𝒰\bm{z}^{{\mathcal{U}}}, so

Z∩\displaystyle Z_{\cap} =Z𝒕,𝒛𝒛𝒰⋅π𝒕,𝒛​(T=𝒰∖S),∀𝒛∈ℝ>0𝒰.\displaystyle=\frac{Z_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}}{\bm{z}^{{\mathcal{U}}}}\cdot\pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}(T={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S),\qquad\forall\bm{z}\in{\mathbb{R}}_{>0}^{{\mathcal{U}}}.

Note that in our application, since μ\mu and ν\nu are log-concave measures, so is μ⊗ν\mu\otimes\nu. Hence, the down-up walk (a.k.a. the basis exchange walk) on μ⊗ν\mu\otimes\nu is rapidly mixing [Ana+19]. μ⊗ν\mu\otimes\nu corresponds to the case t=1t=1, and we can hope that when tt is not too close to 00, local Markov chains for sampling from πt,𝒛\pi_{t,\bm{z}} remain rapidly mixing. In the later part of the proof, we will formally prove this by an application of Theorem 1.14 and show that there is an efficiently implementable Markov chain that samples from πt,𝒛\pi_{t,\bm{z}} in polynomial time provided t≳1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)t\gtrsim 1/\mathsf{poly}(n). This also allows us to approximate Zt,𝒛Z_{t,\bm{z}} by standard counting-to-sampling reductions [JVV86].

All that remains is to estimate πt,𝒛​(T=𝒰∖S)\pi_{t,\bm{z}}(T={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S) with good relative error, since putting it together with an accurate estimate of Zt,𝒛Z_{t,\bm{z}} yields an accurate estimate of Z∩Z_{\cap}. The naïve Monte Carlo method can work well as long as πt,𝒛​(T=𝒰∖S)≳1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)\pi_{t,\bm{z}}(T={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S)\gtrsim 1/\mathsf{poly}(n). The problem is that choosing tt to be as small as 1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1/\mathsf{poly}(n) does not automatically make πt,𝒛​(T=𝒰∖S)\pi_{t,\bm{z}}(T={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S) large. See Remark 2.3 for an example.

Remark 2.3.

An inverse-polynomial tt need not give complementary pairs inverse-polynomial probability when 𝒛=𝟏\bm{z}=\mathbf{1}. Consider the following ladder of Jerrum, Sinclair, and Vigoda [JSV04, Figure 2]. Blue SS and orange B=𝒰∖TB={\mathcal{U}}\setminus T are bases of the partition matroids on filled and hollow vertices, respectively; shared edges are drawn twice above and once below.

The pendant edges force a unique perfect matching MM. Leaving both leaves unmatched gives exponentially many near-perfect matchings CC, with two choices per shaded block. Completing CC as shown gives a distinct soft configuration with |S∩T|=|S∖B|=1|S\cap T|=|S\setminus B|=1, hence only one factor of tt. Their total weight makes the perfect matching exponentially unlikely.

Since Z∩Z_{\cap} isn’t affected by the choice of 𝒛\bm{z} and tt, the hope is that we can still make πt,𝒛​(T=𝒰∖S)≳1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)\pi_{t,\bm{z}}(T={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S)\gtrsim 1/\mathsf{poly}(n) by finding a good 𝒛∈ℝ>0𝒰\bm{z}\in{\mathbb{R}}_{>0}^{{\mathcal{U}}}. To find such a 𝒛\bm{z}, it is natural to consider the following dual maximum entropy convex program.

Definition 2.4.

Fix t∈(0,1]t\in(0,1]. Write the external field as 𝒛=e𝒚\bm{z}=\mathrm{e}^{\bm{y}}, where 𝒚∈ℝ𝒰\bm{y}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{{\mathcal{U}}} gives its logarithmic coordinates, and define

Φ⁡(𝒚)\displaystyle\Phi(\bm{y}) ≔log⁡Zt,𝒛−∑u∈𝒰yu,\displaystyle\coloneqq\log Z_{t,\bm{z}}-\sum_{u\in{\mathcal{U}}}y_{u}, ∂uΦ⁡(𝒚)\displaystyle\partial_{u}\Phi(\bm{y}) =πt,𝒛​(u∈S)−πt,𝒛​(u∉T).\displaystyle=\pi_{t,\bm{z}}(u\in S)-\pi_{t,\bm{z}}(u\notin T). (4)

We consider the following convex program:

inf𝒚∈ℝ𝒰Φ⁡(𝒚).\displaystyle\inf_{\bm{y}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{{\mathcal{U}}}}\Phi(\bm{y}). (5)

The quantity exp⁡(inf𝒚∈ℝ𝒰Φ⁡(𝒚))=Cap𝟏⁡(Zt,𝒙)\exp(\inf_{\bm{y}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{{\mathcal{U}}}}\Phi(\bm{y}))=\operatorname{Cap}_{\mathbf{1}}(Z_{t,\bm{x}}) is the Gurvits capacity of Zt,𝒙Z_{t,\bm{x}}, viewed as a polynomial in 𝒙\bm{x}; see Remark 2.7 for the definition and its connection to earlier work. The potential Φ\Phi is convex because its Hessian is the covariance matrix of 𝟏S+𝟏T−𝟏\mathbf{1}_{S}+\mathbf{1}_{T}-\mathbf{1} for (S,T)∼πt,e𝒚(S,T)\sim\pi_{t,\mathrm{e}^{\bm{y}}}. When Z∩>0Z_{\cap}>0, it holds that

πt,e𝒚​(T=𝒰∖S)\displaystyle\pi_{t,\mathrm{e}^{\bm{y}}}(T={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S) =Z∩⋅exp⁡(−Φ⁡(𝒚)).\displaystyle=Z_{\cap}\cdot\exp\left(-\Phi(\bm{y})\right).

Hence, minimizing Φ\Phi maximizes the probability πt,e𝒚​(T=𝒰∖S)\pi_{t,\mathrm{e}^{\bm{y}}}(T={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S).

The next lemma shows that, under suitable Poincaré inequality assumptions, any near stationary point 𝒚\bm{y} (i.e., points with ‖∇Φ​(𝒚)‖∞\left\|{\nabla\Phi(\bm{y})}\right\|_{\infty} small) make πt,e𝒚​(T=𝒰∖S)\pi_{t,\mathrm{e}^{\bm{y}}}(T={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S) large when tt is sufficiently small. By Eq. 4, the gradient of Φ\Phi can be estimated by sampling. Thus, we can find such a near stationary point by using standard stochastic gradient descent algorithms.

Lemma 2.5.

Let γ>0\gamma>0. Suppose that for every 𝐭∈(0,1]𝒰\bm{t}\in(0,1]^{{\mathcal{U}}} and 𝐳∈ℝ>0𝒰\bm{z}\in{\mathbb{R}}_{>0}^{{\mathcal{U}}}, there is an irreducible continuous-time Markov chain reversible with respect to π𝐭,𝐳\pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}, with spectral gap at least γ\gamma. Each move updates only one of the two sets S,TS,T. Whenever u∈S⊕Tu\in S\oplus T, the total rate of moves removing its unique copy is at most 11. Then for every scalar t∈(0,1]t\in(0,1] and every 𝐳∈ℝ>0𝒰\bm{z}\in{\mathbb{R}}_{>0}^{{\mathcal{U}}}, with 𝐲=log⁡𝐳\bm{y}=\log\bm{z},

πt,𝒛​(T≠𝒰∖S)\displaystyle\pi_{t,\bm{z}}(T\neq{\mathcal{U}}\setminus S) ≤n⁡(‖∇Φ​(𝒚)‖∞+4​tγ).\displaystyle\leq n\left(\|\nabla\Phi(\bm{y})\|_{\infty}+\frac{4\sqrt{t}}{\gamma}\right). (6)

The proof is deferred to Section 5.2.

To summarize, we choose a small scalar penalty t≍1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)t\asymp 1/\mathsf{poly}(n) and implement stochastic gradient descent on Φ\Phi, seeking logarithmic coordinates 𝒚\bm{y} with small ∇Φ​(𝒚)\nabla\Phi(\bm{y}) and setting 𝒛=e𝒚\bm{z}=\mathrm{e}^{\bm{y}}. Note that by Eq. 4, each gradient coordinate can be efficiently estimated as the difference of two empirical frequencies from random samples of πt,𝒛\pi_{t,\bm{z}}. With an inverse-polynomial lower bound on γ\gamma, taking ‖∇Φ​(𝒚)‖∞≤1/poly⁡(n)\|\nabla\Phi(\bm{y})\|_{\infty}\leq 1/\operatorname{poly}(n) sufficiently small makes complementary pairs occur with constant probability, by Lemma 2.5. We can therefore estimate this probability πt,𝒛​(T=𝒰∖S)\pi_{t,\bm{z}}(T={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S) from polynomially many samples as desired.

Application to the Homogeneous Log-Concave Case

We apply the previous framework under the hypotheses of Theorem 2.2, with degrees a,ba,b and a+b=na+b=n. Here πt,𝒛\pi_{t,\bm{z}} is supported on (𝒰a)×(𝒰b)\binom{{\mathcal{U}}}{a}\times\binom{{\mathcal{U}}}{b}, and we call it the bases pair law; see Definition 5.4. The key input we need to verify is the Poincaré Inequality for πt,𝒛\pi_{t,\bm{z}} required by Lemma 2.5. We describe here the argument at a high level; the formal argument is provided in Section 5.1.

We first extend the measures to downward-closed set families. Define the weights μ^𝒛,ν^𝒛\widehat{\mu}_{\bm{z}},\widehat{\nu}_{\bm{z}} through their generating polynomials by

gμ^𝒛​(𝒙)\displaystyle g_{\widehat{\mu}_{\bm{z}}}(\bm{x}) ≔gμ​(𝟏+𝒛​𝒙),\displaystyle\coloneqq g_{\mu}(\mathbf{1}+\bm{z}\bm{x}), gν^𝒛​(𝒙)\displaystyle g_{\widehat{\nu}_{\bm{z}}}(\bm{x}) ≔gν​(𝟏+𝒛​𝒙),𝒛​𝒙≔(zu​xu)u∈𝒰.\displaystyle\coloneqq g_{\nu}(\mathbf{1}+\bm{z}\bm{x}),\qquad\bm{z}\bm{x}\coloneqq(z_{u}x_{u})_{u\in{\mathcal{U}}}.

The independent-set pair law on 2𝒰×2𝒰2^{{\mathcal{U}}}\times 2^{{\mathcal{U}}} (Definition 5.2) is the normalized Hadamard product

π^t,𝒛\displaystyle\widehat{\pi}_{t,\bm{z}} ≔(μ^𝒛⊗ν^𝒛)⊙ψt.\displaystyle\coloneqq(\widehat{\mu}_{\bm{z}}\otimes\widehat{\nu}_{\bm{z}})\odot\psi_{t}.

Conditioning π^t,𝒛\widehat{\pi}_{t,\bm{z}} on (𝒰a)×(𝒰b)\binom{{\mathcal{U}}}{a}\times\binom{{\mathcal{U}}}{b} gives exactly πt,𝒛\pi_{t,\bm{z}}, and π^t,λ​𝒛\widehat{\pi}_{t,\lambda\bm{z}} converges to πt,𝒛\pi_{t,\bm{z}} as λ→∞\lambda\to\infty. The first factor has 00-spectral curvature, and the dual of the second factor has 11-spectral curvature (Observations 5.8 and 5.9). Thus Theorem 1.14 gives a Poincaré bound with constant 11 for π^t,λ​𝒛\widehat{\pi}_{t,\lambda\bm{z}}, uniformly in λ\lambda. Taking λ→∞\lambda\to\infty transfers this bound to an exchange chain for πt,𝒛\pi_{t,\bm{z}} (Lemma 5.5), yielding an efficient sampler using only the original value oracles.

Connections and Additional Intuition

Remark 2.6 (Partition-matroid interpretation).

The penalty ψ𝒕\psi_{\bm{t}} can be understood as an analogue of the random-cluster model, where there is a soft penalty for non-independent sets. Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} be the partition matroid on 𝒰×{1,2}{\mathcal{U}}\times\{1,2\} allowing at most one copy of each uu, and set X≔(S×{1})∪(T×{2})X\coloneqq(S\times\{1\})\cup(T\times\{2\}). For uniform penalties tu=t∈(0,1]t_{u}=t\in(0,1],

ψt​𝟏​(S,T)=t|S∩T|=t|X|−𝗋𝗄𝒫​(X).\psi_{t\mathbf{1}}(S,T)=t^{|S\cap T|}=t^{|X|-{\mathsf{rk}_{\mathcal{P}}}(X)}.
Remark 2.7 (Gurvits capacity).

For a nonzero finitely supported measure ww on ℤ≥0n\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}, write gw​(𝒙)=∑𝒌w⁡(𝒌)​𝒙𝒌g_{w}(\bm{x})=\sum_{\bm{k}}w(\bm{k})\bm{x}^{\bm{k}}. Its Gurvits capacity at 𝜶∈ℝ≥0n\bm{\alpha}\in{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n} is

Cap𝜶⁡(gw)≔inf𝒙∈ℝ>0ngw​(𝒙)𝒙𝜶.\operatorname{Cap}_{\bm{\alpha}}(g_{w})\coloneqq\inf_{\bm{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}_{>0}^{n}}\frac{g_{w}(\bm{x})}{\bm{x}^{\bm{\alpha}}}.

The Gurvits capacity at 𝜶∈supp⁡w\bm{\alpha}\in\supp w is always an upper bound on w⁡(𝜶)w(\bm{\alpha}). To see this, define the distribution p𝒛​(𝒌)=w⁡(𝒌)​𝒛𝒌/gw​(𝒛)p_{\bm{z}}(\bm{k})=w(\bm{k})\bm{z}^{\bm{k}}/g_{w}(\bm{z}). If 𝜶∈supp⁡w\bm{\alpha}\in\supp w, then

Cap𝜶⁡(gw)=w⁡(𝜶)sup𝒛>0p𝒛​(𝜶)≥w⁡(𝜶).\operatorname{Cap}_{\bm{\alpha}}(g_{w})=\frac{w(\bm{\alpha})}{\sup_{\bm{z}>0}p_{\bm{z}}(\bm{\alpha})}\geq w(\bm{\alpha}).

Intuitively, it gives the best possible approximation of w⁡(𝜶)w(\bm{\alpha}) that we can get by only tuning external fields applied to the base measure.

After taking logarithms, the optimization over external fields above has a dual formulation as a minimum KL\KL-divergence convex program with prescribed mean, or equivalently, a weighted maximum-entropy convex program [SV14]. For 𝜶∈supp⁡w\bm{\alpha}\in\supp w, let

q∗=arg​minq:𝔼q​[𝑿]=𝜶DKL(q∥p𝟏),q^{*}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{q:\,\mathbb{E}_{q}[\bm{X}]=\bm{\alpha}}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q\,\middle\|\,p_{\mathbf{1}}\right),

where qq ranges over probability distributions on supp⁡w\supp w, p𝟏=w/gw​(𝟏)p_{\mathbf{1}}=w/g_{w}(\mathbf{1}) is the normalized measure, and DKLD_{\mathrm{KL}} denotes Kullback–Leibler divergence. Entropy duality and the KL Pythagorean identity [CS04, Theorem 3.2] give

log⁡Cap𝜶⁡(gw)w⁡(𝜶)=DKL​(δ𝜶∥q∗)=−log⁡q∗​(𝜶),\log\frac{\operatorname{Cap}_{\bm{\alpha}}(g_{w})}{w(\bm{\alpha})}=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\delta_{\bm{\alpha}}\,\middle\|\,q^{*}\right)=-\log q^{*}(\bm{\alpha}),

where δ𝜶\delta_{\bm{\alpha}} is the point mass at 𝜶\bm{\alpha}. In other words, we adjust the original distribution as little as possible in KL divergence to obtain mean 𝜶\bm{\alpha}. The approximation ratio is the reciprocal of the probability that this distribution assigns to 𝜶\bm{\alpha} itself.

For every homogeneous real stable polynomial gg of degree nn in nn variables with nonnegative coefficients,

n!nnCap𝟏(g)≤[x1⋯xn]g≤Cap𝟏(g).\frac{n!}{n^{n}}\operatorname{Cap}_{\mathbf{1}}(g)\leq[x_{1}\cdots x_{n}]g\leq\operatorname{Cap}_{\mathbf{1}}(g).

The upper bound follows from the definition of capacity. Gurvits [Gur06] proves the lower bound, showing that capacity overestimates the coefficient by at most a factor nn/n!n^{n}/n!. For the permanent of a nonnegative matrix AA, he uses the polynomial g⁡(𝒙)=∏i=1n(∑j=1nAi​j​xj)g(\bm{x})=\prod_{i=1}^{n}(\sum_{j=1}^{n}A_{ij}x_{j}); for mixed discriminants, he uses g⁡(𝒙)=det(∑i=1nxi​Ai)g(\bm{x})=\det(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}A_{i}), where the AiA_{i} are positive semidefinite. This approach has since been extended to other settings; see Section 1.4.

In our setting, the target coefficient [𝒙𝒰]​Zt,𝒙=Z∩[\bm{x}^{{\mathcal{U}}}]Z_{t,\bm{x}}=Z_{\cap} is independent of tt. For fixed tt, the Gurvits capacity is

Cap𝟏⁡(Zt,𝒙)=inf𝒙∈ℝ>0𝒰Zt,𝒙𝒙𝒰=exp⁡(inf𝒚∈ℝ𝒰Φ⁡(𝒚)).\operatorname{Cap}_{\mathbf{1}}(Z_{t,\bm{x}})=\inf_{\bm{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}_{>0}^{{\mathcal{U}}}}\frac{Z_{t,\bm{x}}}{\bm{x}^{{\mathcal{U}}}}=\exp\left(\inf_{\bm{y}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{{\mathcal{U}}}}\Phi(\bm{y})\right).

When Z∩>0Z_{\cap}>0, the probability interpretation above gives the approximation ratio

Cap𝟏⁡(Zt,𝒙)Z∩=1sup𝒛>0πt,𝒛​(T=𝒰∖S).\frac{\operatorname{Cap}_{\mathbf{1}}(Z_{t,\bm{x}})}{Z_{\cap}}=\frac{1}{\sup_{\bm{z}>0}\pi_{t,\bm{z}}(T={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S)}.

Under the hypotheses of Lemma 2.5, this ratio satisfies

1≤Cap𝟏⁡(Zt,𝒙)Z∩≤(1−4​n​tγ)−1,4​n​t<γ.1\leq\frac{\operatorname{Cap}_{\mathbf{1}}(Z_{t,\bm{x}})}{Z_{\cap}}\leq\left(1-\frac{4n\sqrt{t}}{\gamma}\right)^{-1},\qquad 4n\sqrt{t}<\gamma.

Indeed, Φ\Phi is bounded below and has a globally bounded Hessian, so it admits points 𝒚\bm{y} with arbitrarily small gradient; applying Lemma 2.5 to the corresponding fields 𝒛=e𝒚\bm{z}=\mathrm{e}^{\bm{y}} gives the upper bound on the ratio. Thus decreasing tt makes the capacity bound nearly tight.

Remark 2.8 (Comparison with permanent algorithms).

The permanent algorithm of Jerrum–Sinclair–Vigoda [JSV04] learns correction weights along an annealing schedule to balance the total weight of perfect matchings with that of each near-perfect class, indexed by its pair of unmatched vertices. Our framework chooses external fields directly by stochastic gradient descent. It can serve as a black box for a broad class of counting problems admitting the above formulation, once the sampling and uniform Poincaré hypotheses are verified.

3 Preliminaries

3.1 Notation

For a finite ground set 𝒰{\mathcal{U}}, write n≔|𝒰|n\coloneqq|{\mathcal{U}}| and (𝒰r)≔{S⊆𝒰:|S|=r}\binom{{\mathcal{U}}}{r}\coloneqq\{S\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}:|S|=r\}. We use S+u≔S∪{u}S+u\coloneqq S\cup\{u\}, S−u≔S∖{u}S-u\coloneqq S\setminus\{u\}, and S⊕T≔(S∖T)∪(T∖S)S\oplus T\coloneqq(S\setminus T)\cup(T\setminus S). The symbol 𝟏​[⋅]\mathbf{1}[\cdot] denotes an indicator, 𝟏S\mathbf{1}_{S} the indicator vector of SS, and 𝟏\mathbf{1} the all-ones vector.

Vectors are written in bold. Products 𝒛​𝒙\bm{z}\bm{x}, exponentials e𝒚\mathrm{e}^{\bm{y}}, and logarithms log⁡𝒛\log\bm{z} are taken coordinatewise. We write 𝒛S≔∏u∈Szu\bm{z}^{S}\coloneqq\prod_{u\in S}z_{u} for S⊆𝒰S\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}, and 𝒛𝜶≔∏u∈𝒰zuαu\bm{z}^{\bm{\alpha}}\coloneqq\prod_{u\in{\mathcal{U}}}z_{u}^{\alpha_{u}} for 𝜶∈ℤ≥0𝒰\bm{\alpha}\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}^{{\mathcal{U}}}. For a polynomial pp, [𝒛𝜶]​p[\bm{z}^{\bm{\alpha}}]p denotes the coefficient of 𝒛𝜶\bm{z}^{\bm{\alpha}} in pp. For symmetric matrices, A⪰BA\succeq B means that A−BA-B is positive semidefinite.

A nonnegative set measure μ:2𝒰→ℝ≥0\mu:2^{{\mathcal{U}}}\to{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0} need not be normalized. Its support is supp⁡μ≔{S⊆𝒰:μ⁡(S)>0}\supp\mu\coloneqq\{S\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}:\mu(S)>0\}. An external field is a vector 𝒛∈ℝ>0𝒰\bm{z}\in{\mathbb{R}}_{>0}^{{\mathcal{U}}}. Applying it to μ\mu gives the unnormalized measure

μ𝒛​(S)≔μ⁡(S)​𝒛S.\mu_{\bm{z}}(S)\coloneqq\mu(S)\bm{z}^{S}.

When μ\mu is nonzero, the corresponding probability distribution is μ𝒛/gμ​(𝒛)\mu_{\bm{z}}/g_{\mu}(\bm{z}). We write 𝒚=log⁡𝒛\bm{y}=\log\bm{z} for the logarithmic coordinates of the external field, so 𝒛=e𝒚\bm{z}=\mathrm{e}^{\bm{y}}. The product weights (μ⊗ν)​(S,T)=μ⁡(S)​ν​(T)(\mu\otimes\nu)(S,T)=\mu(S)\nu(T) are also unnormalized; μ⊙ν\mu\odot\nu denotes the normalized Hadamard product of Definition 1.7.

Logarithms are natural unless a base is specified. O~​(⋅)\widetilde{O}(\cdot) hides polylogarithmic factors.

3.2 Matroids

A matroid ℳ{\mathcal{M}} on 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} has a family ℐ⁡(ℳ)⊆2𝒰{\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{M}})\subseteq 2^{{\mathcal{U}}} of independent sets satisfying:

  • •

    ∅∈ℐ⁡(ℳ)\varnothing\in{\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{M}}).

  • •

    If I∈ℐ⁡(ℳ)I\in{\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{M}}) and J⊆IJ\subseteq I, then J∈ℐ⁡(ℳ)J\in{\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{M}}).

  • •

    If I,J∈ℐ⁡(ℳ)I,J\in{\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{M}}) and |I|<|J||I|<|J|, then I∪{e}∈ℐ⁡(ℳ)I\cup\{e\}\in{\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{M}}) for some e∈J∖Ie\in J\setminus I.

A basis is a maximal independent set; write ℬ⁡(ℳ){\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{M}}) for the family of bases. The rank of S⊆𝒰S\subseteq{\mathcal{U}} is

𝗋𝗄ℳ(S)≔max{|I|:I⊆S,I∈ℐ(ℳ)}.\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{M}}}(S)\coloneqq\max\{|I|:I\subseteq S,\ I\in{\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{M}})\}.

All bases have size 𝗋𝗄ℳ​(𝒰)\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{M}}}({\mathcal{U}}). An independence oracle tests membership in ℐ⁡(ℳ){\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{M}}). Greedily adding elements of SS while preserving independence finds a largest independent subset of SS, and hence its rank, with at most |S||S| oracle queries. The dual matroid ℳ∗{\mathcal{M}}^{*} is the matroid on 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} whose independent sets are the sets I⊆𝒰I\subseteq{\mathcal{U}} such that 𝒰∖I{\mathcal{U}}\setminus I contains a basis of ℳ{\mathcal{M}}. Equivalently, ℬ⁡(ℳ∗)={𝒰∖B:B∈ℬ⁡(ℳ)}{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{M}}^{*})=\{{\mathcal{U}}\setminus B:B\in{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{M}})\}; see [Oxl11] for further background.

The basis generating polynomial gℳ​(𝒙)≔∑B∈ℬ⁡(ℳ)𝒙Bg_{{\mathcal{M}}}(\bm{x})\coloneqq\sum_{B\in{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{M}})}\bm{x}^{B} is log-concave [AOV18, BH20]. Additional matroid terminology and operations used in the applications are recalled in Appendix B.

3.3 Markov chains and mixing time

Let Ω\Omega be a finite state space and π\pi a probability law on Ω\Omega with π⁡(x)>0\pi(x)>0 for every x∈Ωx\in\Omega. For f,g:Ω→ℝf,g:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}, define

⟨f,g⟩π\displaystyle\langle f,g\rangle_{\pi} ≔∑x∈Ωπ⁡(x)​f​(x)​g​(x),\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{x\in\Omega}\pi(x)f(x)g(x), ‖f‖π2\displaystyle\|f\|_{\pi}^{2} ≔⟨f,f⟩π,\displaystyle\coloneqq\langle f,f\rangle_{\pi}, 𝐕𝐚𝐫π​[f]\displaystyle\mathbf{Var}_{\pi}\left[f\right] ≔‖f−𝔼π​[f]‖π2.\displaystyle\coloneqq\|f-\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[f\right]\|_{\pi}^{2}.

Let r⁡(x,y)≥0r(x,y)\geq 0, x≠yx\neq y, be transition rates on Ω\Omega. These define a continuous-time Markov chain (Xt)t≥0(X_{t})_{t\geq 0}: assign each directed edge x→yx\to y an independent Poisson clock of rate r⁡(x,y)r(x,y). When its clock rings, the chain moves to yy if it is currently at xx; otherwise, nothing happens. We assume the rates satisfy the detailed balance equations

π⁡(x)​r​(x,y)\displaystyle\pi(x)\,r(x,y) =π⁡(y)​r​(y,x)for all ​x≠y∈Ω.\displaystyle=\pi(y)\,r(y,x)\qquad\text{for all }x\neq y\in\Omega. (7)

We then say that the chain is reversible with respect to π\pi. All Markov chains used in this paper are finite and reversible. The positive Laplacian and Dirichlet form associated with these rates are

(ℒr​f)​(x)\displaystyle({\mathcal{L}}_{r}f)(x) ≔∑y≠xr⁡(x,y)⋅(f⁡(x)−f⁡(y)),\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{y\neq x}r(x,y)\cdot\bigl(f(x)-f(y)\bigr), (8)
ℰr​(f,g)\displaystyle{\mathcal{E}}_{r}(f,g) ≔⟨f,ℒr​g⟩π=12​∑x,y∈Ωx≠yπ⁡(x)​r​(x,y)⋅(f⁡(y)−f⁡(x))⋅(g⁡(y)−g⁡(x)).\displaystyle\coloneqq\langle f,{\mathcal{L}}_{r}g\rangle_{\pi}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x,y\in\Omega\\ x\neq y\end{subarray}}\pi(x)r(x,y)\cdot\bigl(f(y)-f(x)\bigr)\cdot\bigl(g(y)-g(x)\bigr). (9)

The second equality in Eq. 9 follows from detailed balance. The chain has generator −ℒr-{\mathcal{L}}_{r}, so its transition matrix Pt​(x,y)≔𝐏𝐫⁡[Xt=y∣X0=x]P_{t}(x,y)\coloneqq\mathbf{Pr}\left[X_{t}=y\mid X_{0}=x\right] satisfies

Pt\displaystyle P_{t} =exp⁡(−t​ℒr),t≥0.\displaystyle=\exp(-t{\mathcal{L}}_{r}),\qquad t\geq 0.

We omit the subscript of ℒr{\mathcal{L}}_{r} when the rates are clear, and note that ℰc⋅r​(⋅,⋅)=c⋅ℰr​(⋅,⋅){\mathcal{E}}_{c\cdot r}(\cdot,\cdot)=c\cdot{\mathcal{E}}_{r}(\cdot,\cdot) for c>0c>0. We use ℒ{\mathcal{L}} for a general Laplacian and reserve ℒ{\mathscr{L}} for the Laplacian defined in Eq. 3.

Spectral gap and Poincaré inequalities.

The chain is irreducible if, for every x,y∈Ωx,y\in\Omega, there is a sequence x=x0,…,xk=yx=x_{0},\ldots,x_{k}=y such that r⁡(xj−1,xj)>0r(x_{j-1},x_{j})>0 for 1≤j≤k1\leq j\leq k. In this case, its spectral gap is

γ⁡(ℒr)\displaystyle\gamma({\mathcal{L}}_{r}) ≔inff​ nonconstantℰr​(f,f)𝐕𝐚𝐫π​[f],\displaystyle\coloneqq\inf_{f\text{ nonconstant}}\frac{{\mathcal{E}}_{r}(f,f)}{\mathbf{Var}_{\pi}\left[f\right]}, (10)

the smallest nonzero eigenvalue of ℒr{\mathcal{L}}_{r}; see [LP17, Lemma 13.7]. Thus γ⁡(ℒr)≥γ\gamma({\mathcal{L}}_{r})\geq\gamma if and only if the following Poincaré inequality holds:

γ⋅𝐕𝐚𝐫π​[f]\displaystyle\gamma\cdot\mathbf{Var}_{\pi}\left[f\right] ≤ℰr​(f,f)for every ​f:Ω→ℝ.\displaystyle\leq{\mathcal{E}}_{r}(f,f)\qquad\text{for every }f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}. (11)

Mixing time.

The continuous-time chain PtP_{t} has a lazy discrete-time implementation: choose R>0R>0 with R≥max⁡∑y≠xx⁡r⁡(x,y)R\geq\max_{x}\sum_{y\neq x}r(x,y) and set P≔I−ℒr/(2​R)P\coloneqq I-{\mathcal{L}}_{r}/(2R). Applying PP at the rings of an independent Poisson clock of rate 2​R2R gives the chain PtP_{t}. For sampling from π\pi, we run PP for a fixed number of steps, bounded as follows. For probability laws ρ,ν\rho,\nu on Ω\Omega, their total variation distance is

‖ρ−ν‖TV≔12​∑x∈Ω|ρ⁡(x)−ν⁡(x)|.\|\rho-\nu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\coloneqq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x\in\Omega}|\rho(x)-\nu(x)|.

For 0<ε<10<\varepsilon<1, the mixing time of PP is

tmix​(ε)\displaystyle t_{\mathrm{mix}}(\varepsilon) ≔min⁡{k∈ℤ≥0:maxx∈Ω⁡‖Pk​(x,⋅)−π‖TV≤ε}.\displaystyle\coloneqq\min\left\{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}:\max_{x\in\Omega}\|P^{k}(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\leq\varepsilon\right\}.

Write πmin≔minx∈Ω⁡π⁡(x)\pi_{\min}\coloneqq\min_{x\in\Omega}\pi(x). Under Eq. 11 with γ>0\gamma>0, the standard spectral mixing bound [LP17, Theorem 12.4] gives

tmix​(ε)\displaystyle t_{\mathrm{mix}}(\varepsilon) ≤⌈2​Rγ​log⁡1ε​πmin⌉.\displaystyle\leq\left\lceil\frac{2R}{\gamma}\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon\pi_{\min}}\right\rceil. (12)

Running PP for this many steps from any starting state gives a sample within total variation distance ε\varepsilon of π\pi. Thus an efficient implementation of each step gives an efficient sampler whenever this mixing-time bound is polynomial.

Proof of Proposition 2.1.

Since the chain is reversible, ℒ{\mathcal{L}} is self-adjoint and positive semidefinite with respect to ⟨⋅,⋅⟩π\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\pi}; since it is irreducible, its kernel consists of the constant functions. Hence ℒ{\mathcal{L}} is positive definite on 𝟏⟂\mathbf{1}^{\perp} (the functions with mean zero under π\pi), and ℒ1/2{\mathcal{L}}^{1/2} is a bijection of 𝟏⟂\mathbf{1}^{\perp}. Both ratios are unchanged when a constant is added to ff, so we may take f∈𝟏⟂∖{0}f\in\mathbf{1}^{\perp}\setminus\{0\}, for which 𝐕𝐚𝐫π​[f]=⟨f,f⟩π\mathbf{Var}_{\pi}\left[f\right]=\langle f,f\rangle_{\pi}. Substituting g≔ℒ1/2​fg\coloneqq{\mathcal{L}}^{1/2}f gives

⟨ℒ​f,ℒ​f⟩π⟨f,ℒ​f⟩π\displaystyle\frac{\langle{\mathcal{L}}f,{\mathcal{L}}f\rangle_{\pi}}{\langle f,{\mathcal{L}}f\rangle_{\pi}} =⟨g,ℒ​g⟩π⟨g,g⟩π,\displaystyle=\frac{\langle g,{\mathcal{L}}g\rangle_{\pi}}{\langle g,g\rangle_{\pi}},

and gg ranges over 𝟏⟂∖{0}\mathbf{1}^{\perp}\setminus\{0\} as ff does. Hence the two infima coincide. ∎

3.4 Sampling to counting

We record below the standard reduction from counting to sampling due to Jerrum, Valiant, and Vazirani [JVV86].

Lemma 3.1 ([JVV86]).

Let m≥1m\geq 1, let w:{0,1}m→ℝ≥0w:\{0,1\}^{m}\to{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0} be nonzero, and write Z≔∑σw⁡(σ)Z\coloneqq\sum_{\sigma}w(\sigma) and π⁡(σ)≔w⁡(σ)/Z\pi(\sigma)\coloneqq w(\sigma)/Z. For every nonempty conditional law obtained by fixing coordinates, suppose a sampler, given any starting state in its support and an accuracy 0<τ<10<\tau<1, returns a sample in that support whose distribution is within total variation distance τ\tau of the conditional law, using fresh independent randomness. Given an evaluation oracle for ww, a state σ0∈supp⁡w\sigma_{0}\in\supp w, and 0<ε,δ<10<\varepsilon,\delta<1, one can compute Z^\widehat{Z} satisfying

𝐏𝐫[(1−ε)Z≤Z^≤(1+ε)Z]≥1−δ.\mathbf{Pr}\left[(1-\varepsilon)Z\leq\widehat{Z}\leq(1+\varepsilon)Z\right]\geq 1-\delta.

On every execution, the algorithm uses Q=O⁡(m3​ε−2​log⁡(2​m/δ))Q=O(m^{3}\varepsilon^{-2}\log(2m/\delta)) sampler calls, each with total variation distance at most τ=ε/(16​m)\tau=\varepsilon/(16m), one evaluation of ww, and O⁡(Q)O(Q) additional arithmetic operations. It supplies a starting state for every call.

3.5 Stochastic Coordinate-Descent

Stochastic coordinate descent finds a point with small gradient using noisy gradient estimates: it averages fresh estimates and steps along any coordinate whose averaged estimate is large. The analysis combines the coordinate-descent estimate of Nutini et al. [Nut+15, Section 3, equation (2)] with concentration bounds for the noise. We state it with two guarantees that are convenient when the gradient oracle is implemented by sampling: every iterate stays in a bounded region, and the cost is bounded on every execution.

Theorem 3.2.

Fix d≥1d\geq 1, 𝐱0∈ℝd\bm{x}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, L,σ>0L,\sigma>0, and H0≥0H_{0}\geq 0. Assume the following.

  1. (i)

    Function. The function f:ℝd→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} is convex and differentiable, and for all 𝒙∈ℝd\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, u∈ℝu\in\mathbb{R}, and 1≤i≤d1\leq i\leq d,

    f⁡(𝒙+u​𝒆i)\displaystyle f(\bm{x}+u\bm{e}_{i}) ≤f⁡(𝒙)+u​∂if⁡(𝒙)+L​u2/2,\displaystyle\leq f(\bm{x})+u\partial_{i}f(\bm{x})+Lu^{2}/2, (13)
    f⁡(𝒙)\displaystyle f(\bm{x}) ≥f⁡(𝒙0)−H0.\displaystyle\geq f(\bm{x}_{0})-H_{0}. (14)

    Here (𝒆i)j≔𝟏{i=j}(\bm{e}_{i})_{j}\coloneqq\mathbf{1}_{\{i=j\}}.

  2. (ii)

    Gradient oracle. Each query at 𝒙\bm{x} uses fresh independent randomness and costs at most T≥dT\geq d. Its output 𝑮⁡(𝒙)\bm{G}(\bm{x}) is unbiased with coordinatewise σ\sigma-sub-Gaussian noise: for all 𝒙,u,i\bm{x},u,i as above,

    𝔼⁡[𝑮⁡(𝒙)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\bm{G}(\bm{x})\right] =∇f​(𝒙),\displaystyle=\nabla f(\bm{x}),
    𝔼⁡[exp⁡(u⁡(Gi​(𝒙)−∂if⁡(𝒙)))]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\bigl(u(G_{i}(\bm{x})-\partial_{i}f(\bm{x}))\bigr)\right] ≤exp⁡(σ2​u2/2).\displaystyle\leq\exp(\sigma^{2}u^{2}/2).

For any 0<η≤10<\eta\leq 1 and 0<δ<10<\delta<1, a stochastic coordinate-descent algorithm has the following guarantees.

  1. (a)

    Output and queries. With probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, it returns 𝒙\bm{x} with ‖∇f​(𝒙)‖∞≤η\|\nabla f(\bm{x})\|_{\infty}\leq\eta. On every execution, every queried or returned point 𝒚\bm{y} satisfies

    ‖𝒚−𝒙0‖1\displaystyle\|\bm{y}-\bm{x}_{0}\|_{1} =O⁡(H0η+ηL).\displaystyle=O\left(\frac{H_{0}}{\eta}+\frac{\eta}{L}\right). (15)
  2. (b)

    Cost. On every execution, it uses O⁡(Q)O(Q) oracle calls and total time O⁡(T​Q)O(TQ), where

    Q\displaystyle Q ≔(1+σ2η2)​(1+L​H0η2)​log⁡[2​dδ​(1+L​H0η2)].\displaystyle\coloneqq\left(1+\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\eta^{2}}\right)\left(1+\frac{LH_{0}}{\eta^{2}}\right)\log\left[\frac{2d}{\delta}\left(1+\frac{LH_{0}}{\eta^{2}}\right)\right]. (16)

For instance, if each coordinate of 𝑮⁡(𝒙)\bm{G}(\bm{x}) takes values in an interval of length at most 2​σ2\sigma, the noise condition holds by Hoeffding’s lemma [Hoe63]; centered Gaussian errors of variance at most σ2\sigma^{2} are also allowed. The algorithm and its analysis are given in Section A.4.

Remark 3.3.

If the jjth oracle output, conditional on the history, is within total variation distance ξj\xi_{j} of its prescribed law, then the conclusion of Theorem 3.2(a) holds with probability at least 1−δ−∑jξj1-\delta-\sum_{j}\xi_{j}, and the remaining guarantees hold on every execution. Indeed, coupling each output with an exact one, the two runs agree except with probability at most ∑jξj\sum_{j}\xi_{j}.

4 Global Mixing via Local Curvature

In this section, we prove Theorem 1.14. We begin by setting up some notation. We extend functions on Ω\Omega by zero on 2𝒰∖Ω2^{{\mathcal{U}}}\setminus\Omega.

Definition 4.1 (Discrete Gradient).

For each u∈𝒰u\in{\mathcal{U}} and f:2𝒰→ℝf:2^{{\mathcal{U}}}\to{\mathbb{R}}, let

(∇uf)​(S)≔f⁡(S+u)−f⁡(S−u).\displaystyle(\nabla_{u}f)(S)\coloneqq f(S+u)-f(S-u).

Further define the upper and lower discrete derivatives via

(∇u+f)(S)≔(∇uf)(S)⋅𝟏[u∉S]and(∇u−f)(S)≔(∇uf)(S)⋅𝟏[u∈S].\displaystyle(\nabla_{u}^{+}f)(S)\coloneqq(\nabla_{u}f)(S)\cdot\mathbf{1}[u\notin S]\qquad\text{and}\qquad(\nabla_{u}^{-}f)(S)\coloneqq(\nabla_{u}f)(S)\cdot\mathbf{1}[u\in S].

Note that (∇f)​(S),(∇+f)​(S),(∇−f)​(S)(\nabla f)(S),(\nabla^{+}f)(S),(\nabla^{-}f)(S) are vectors in ℝ𝒰{\mathbb{R}}^{{\mathcal{U}}}.

It will also be notationally convenient define a “downward” analog of spectral curvature. For each S∈supp⁡(μ)S\in\supp(\mu), let

DSμ,κ​(u,v)\displaystyle D_{S}^{\mu,\kappa}(u,v) ≔A𝒰∖Sμ∗,κ​(u,v)={μ​(S−v)2μ​(S)2−κ⋅μ⁡(S−v)μ⁡(S),if ​u,v∈S,u=vμ⁡(S−u)μ⁡(S)⋅μ⁡(S−v)μ⁡(S)−μ⁡(S−u−v)μ⁡(S),if ​u,v∈S,u≠v0,otherwise.\displaystyle\coloneqq A_{{\mathcal{U}}\setminus S}^{\mu^{*},\kappa}(u,v)=\begin{cases}\frac{\mu(S-v)^{2}}{\mu(S)^{2}}-\kappa\cdot\frac{\mu(S-v)}{\mu(S)},&\quad\text{if }u,v\in S,u=v\\ \frac{\mu(S-u)}{\mu(S)}\cdot\frac{\mu(S-v)}{\mu(S)}-\frac{\mu(S-u-v)}{\mu(S)},&\quad\text{if }u,v\in S,u\neq v\\ 0,&\quad\text{otherwise}\end{cases}.

This is a 𝒰×𝒰{\mathcal{U}}\times{\mathcal{U}} matrix supported only on SS. The (downward) κ\kappa-spectral curvature is then the condition that DSμ,κ⪰0D_{S}^{\mu,\kappa}\succeq 0.

We will use the following Bochner-type identity to prove Theorem 1.14.

Proposition 4.2.

Under the hypotheses of Theorem 1.14, for every function f:2𝒰→ℝf:2^{{\mathcal{U}}}\to{\mathbb{R}}, we have the identity,

⟨f,(ℒ2−(η+κ)⋅ℒ)​f⟩ρ\displaystyle\left\langle{f,\left({\mathscr{L}^{2}-(\eta+\kappa)\cdot\mathscr{L}}\right)f}\right\rangle_{\rho} =∑S∈Ωρ⁡(S)⋅(∇+f)​(S)⊤⋅ASμ,η⋅(∇+f)​(S)\displaystyle=\sum_{S\in\Omega}\rho(S)\cdot(\nabla^{+}f)(S)^{\top}\cdot A_{S}^{\mu,\eta}\cdot(\nabla^{+}f)(S)
+∑S∈Ωρ(S)⋅(∇−f)(S)⊤⋅DSν,κ⋅(∇−f)(S)\displaystyle+\sum_{S\in\Omega}\rho(S)\cdot(\nabla^{-}f)(S)^{\top}\cdot D_{S}^{\nu,\kappa}\cdot(\nabla^{-}f)(S)
+1Z∑S∈Ω∑u,v∉S:u≠vS+u+v∈Ωμ(S+u+v)⋅ν(S)⋅(Δu​vf)(S)2,\displaystyle+\frac{1}{Z}\sum_{S\in\Omega}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}u,v\notin S:u\neq v\\ S+u+v\in\Omega\end{subarray}}\mu(S+u+v)\cdot\nu(S)\cdot(\Delta_{uv}f)(S)^{2},

where

(Δu​v​f)​(S)≔(∇u∇v​f)​(S)=f⁡(S+u+v)−f⁡(S+u−v)−f⁡(S−u+v)+f⁡(S−u−v),\displaystyle(\Delta_{uv}f)(S)\coloneqq(\nabla_{u}\nabla_{v}f)(S)=f(S+u+v)-f(S+u-v)-f(S-u+v)+f(S-u-v),

Proposition 4.2 is proved in Section 4.1 below.

Proof of Theorem 1.14.

In Proposition 4.2, the term (Δu​v​f)​(S)2(\Delta_{uv}f)(S)^{2} is non-negative automatically; and, by the spectral-curvature conditions, the first two terms are also non-negative. Hence ⟨ℒ​f,ℒ​f⟩ρ≥(η+κ)⋅⟨f,ℒ​f⟩ρ\langle{\mathscr{L}}f,{\mathscr{L}}f\rangle_{\rho}\geq(\eta+\kappa)\cdot\langle f,{\mathscr{L}}f\rangle_{\rho} for all ff. The chain generated by −ℒ-{\mathscr{L}} is reversible with respect to ρ\rho and irreducible on Ω\Omega, since Ω\Omega is connected under single-element additions and deletions and every feasible transition has positive rate. Thus Proposition 2.1 gives spectral gap γ≥η+κ\gamma\geq\eta+\kappa, which is the desired Poincaré inequality. ∎

The gradient ∇uf\nabla_{u}f is unchanged when uu is added or removed, and similarly for ∇vf\nabla_{v}f. Thus Observation 4.3 gives, for each group,

∑X∈{S,S+u,S+v,T}ρ⁡(X)​BX​(u,v)​(∇uf)​(X)​(∇vf)​(X)\displaystyle\sum_{X\in\{S,S+u,S+v,T\}}\rho(X)B_{X}(u,v)(\nabla_{u}f)(X)(\nabla_{v}f)(X)
=w⋅((∇uf)​(T)−(∇uf)​(S))​((∇vf)​(T)−(∇vf)​(S))=w⋅(Δu​v​f)​(S)2.\displaystyle=w\cdot\bigl((\nabla_{u}f)(T)-(\nabla_{u}f)(S)\bigr)\bigl((\nabla_{v}f)(T)-(\nabla_{v}f)(S)\bigr)=w\cdot(\Delta_{uv}f)(S)^{2}.

5 Subset Convolution for Homogeneous Log-Concave Measures

In this section, we prove the following formal version of Theorem 2.2.

Theorem 5.1.

Let μ:(𝒰a)→ℝ≥0\mu:\binom{{\mathcal{U}}}{a}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} and ν:(𝒰b)→ℝ≥0\nu:\binom{{\mathcal{U}}}{b}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}, extended by zero to 2𝒰2^{{\mathcal{U}}}, where a,b≥0a,b\geq 0 are integers with a+b=n≔|𝒰|≥1a+b=n\coloneqq|{\mathcal{U}}|\geq 1. Given value oracles for μ,ν\mu,\nu, the coefficient ranges ℛμ,ℛν{\mathcal{R}}_{\mu},{\mathcal{R}}_{\nu} in Eq. 2, and sets S0,T0S_{0},T_{0} with μ⁡(S0)>0\mu(S_{0})>0 and ν⁡(T0)>0\nu(T_{0})>0, there is an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for the subset-convolution value (μ∗ν)​(𝒰)(\mu*\nu)({\mathcal{U}}), namely

Z∩\displaystyle Z_{\cap} ≔[𝒙𝒰]​(gμ​(𝒙)​gν​(𝒙))=∑S⊆𝒰μ⁡(S)​ν​(𝒰∖S),𝒙𝒰≔∏u∈𝒰xu.\displaystyle\coloneqq[\bm{x}^{{\mathcal{U}}}]\bigl(g_{\mu}(\bm{x})g_{\nu}(\bm{x})\bigr)=\sum_{S\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}}\mu(S)\nu({\mathcal{U}}\setminus S),\qquad\bm{x}^{{\mathcal{U}}}\coloneqq\prod_{u\in{\mathcal{U}}}x_{u}. (17)

For every 0<ε≤10<\varepsilon\leq 1, it uses at most

O⁡(n10​(n+log⁡(ℛμ​ℛν))2​ε−2​log2​2​(n+log⁡(ℛμ​ℛν))ε)\displaystyle O\left(n^{10}(n+\log({\mathcal{R}}_{\mu}{\mathcal{R}}_{\nu}))^{2}\varepsilon^{-2}\log^{2}\frac{2(n+\log({\mathcal{R}}_{\mu}{\mathcal{R}}_{\nu}))}{\varepsilon}\right) (18)

arithmetic operations and value-oracle calls on every execution.

Throughout this section, μ,ν\mu,\nu satisfy the hypotheses of Theorem 5.1, with degrees a,ba,b and a+b=na+b=n. We extend the measures to downward-closed set families by translating their generating polynomials.

Definition 5.2 (Independent-Set Pair Law).

Let μ,ν\mu,\nu be as in Theorem 5.1, 𝒕=(tu)u∈𝒰∈(0,1]𝒰\bm{t}=(t_{u})_{u\in{\mathcal{U}}}\in(0,1]^{{\mathcal{U}}}, and 𝒛∈ℝ>0𝒰\bm{z}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{{\mathcal{U}}}. The independent-set pair law on 2𝒰×2𝒰2^{{\mathcal{U}}}\times 2^{{\mathcal{U}}} is the normalized Hadamard product

π^𝒕,𝒛\displaystyle\widehat{\pi}_{\bm{t},\bm{z}} ≔(μ^𝒛⊗ν^𝒛)⊙ψ𝒕.\displaystyle\coloneqq(\widehat{\mu}_{\bm{z}}\otimes\widehat{\nu}_{\bm{z}})\odot\psi_{\bm{t}}.

Explicitly, for S,T⊆𝒰S,T\subseteq{\mathcal{U}},

Definition 5.4 (Bases Pair Law).

With μ,ν,𝒕,𝒛\mu,\nu,\bm{t},\bm{z} as in Definition 5.2, set Ω≔(𝒰a)×(𝒰b)\Omega\coloneqq\binom{{\mathcal{U}}}{a}\times\binom{{\mathcal{U}}}{b}. The bases pair law is π^𝒕,𝒛\widehat{\pi}_{\bm{t},\bm{z}} conditioned on Ω\Omega. Its partition function and probability mass function are

π𝒕,𝒛​(S,T)\displaystyle\pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}(S,T) ≔μ⁡(S)​ν​(T)​𝒕S∩T​𝒛S​𝒛TZ𝒕,𝒛.\displaystyle\coloneqq\frac{\mu(S)\nu(T)\bm{t}^{S\cap T}\bm{z}^{S}\bm{z}^{T}}{Z_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}}.
