We recall the induced-chain construction and its Poincaré comparison.

Definition 5.10 (Induced chain).

Let (Xs)s≥0(X_{s})_{s\geq 0} be an irreducible continuous-time Markov chain on a finite state space Ω\Omega, with off-diagonal rates r⁡(x,y)r(x,y), and let ∅≠B⊆Ω\varnothing\neq B\subseteq\Omega. Its induced chain on BB is the chain obtained by deleting all time spent outside BB. Writing τB≔inf{s≥0:Xs∈B}\tau_{B}\coloneqq\inf\{s\geq 0:X_{s}\in B\}, its off-diagonal rates are

rB​(x,y)\displaystyle r^{B}(x,y) ≔r(x,y)+∑u∈Ω∖Br(x,u)𝐏𝐫[XτB=y∣X0=u](x,y∈B,x≠y).\displaystyle\coloneqq r(x,y)+\sum_{u\in\Omega\setminus B}r(x,u){\mathbf{Pr}\left[X_{\tau_{B}}=y\mid X_{0}=u\right]}\qquad(x,y\in B,\ x\neq y).
Proposition 5.11 ([LP17, Theorem 13.16]).

In the setting of Definition 5.10, suppose the chain is reversible with stationary law π\pi and has spectral gap at least γ>0\gamma>0. Then the induced chain is reversible with respect to πB​(x)≔π⁡(x)/π⁡(B)\pi_{B}(x)\coloneqq\pi(x)/\pi(B) for x∈Bx\in B, and for every f:B→ℝf:B\to\mathbb{R},

γ​𝐕𝐚𝐫πB​[f]\displaystyle\gamma\mathbf{Var}_{\pi_{B}}\left[f\right] ≤ℰrB​(f,f).\displaystyle\leq{\mathcal{E}}_{r^{B}}(f,f).

The proof of [LP17, Theorem 13.16] is for discrete-time Markov chains but extends directly to the continuous-time setting. For the reader’s convenience, we include a proof in Section A.8.

Proof of Lemma 5.5.

We pass to the induced chain on pairs of bases and show that its rates converge to Eq. 19. Singleton support is immediate. Recall from Eq. 3 that the chain with generator −ℒ-{\mathscr{L}} has rates

q^λ​((S,T),(S+u,T))\displaystyle\widehat{q}_{\lambda}\bigl((S,T),(S+u,T)\bigr) =wλ​(S+u,T)wλ​(S,T)=μ^λ​𝒛​(S+u)μ^λ​𝒛​(S)\displaystyle=\frac{w_{\lambda}(S+u,T)}{w_{\lambda}(S,T)}=\frac{\widehat{\mu}_{\lambda\bm{z}}(S+u)}{\widehat{\mu}_{\lambda\bm{z}}(S)} (u∉S),\displaystyle(u\notin S),
q^λ​((S,T),(S−u,T))\displaystyle\widehat{q}_{\lambda}\bigl((S,T),(S-u,T)\bigr) =ψ𝒕​(S−u,T)ψ𝒕​(S,T)=tu−𝟏[u∈T]\displaystyle=\frac{\psi_{\bm{t}}(S-u,T)}{\psi_{\bm{t}}(S,T)}=t_{u}^{-\mathbf{1}[u\in T]} (u∈S).\displaystyle(u\in S).

The rates updating TT are symmetric; unsupported additions are omitted and all other off-diagonal rates are zero.

Let qλindq_{\lambda}^{\mathrm{ind}} be the rates of the chain induced on supp⁡π𝒕,𝒛\supp\pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}} from Definition 5.10. Conditioning π^𝒕,λ​𝒛\widehat{\pi}_{\bm{t},\lambda\bm{z}} on pairs of bases cancels the common factor λn\lambda^{n}, giving exactly π𝒕,𝒛\pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}. By Propositions 5.11 and 5.7, the induced chain is therefore reversible with stationary law π𝒕,𝒛\pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}} and has spectral gap at least one.

It remains to identify the limiting rates. After deleting u∈Su\in S from a pair of bases (S,T)(S,T), put S′≔S−uS^{\prime}\coloneqq S-u. At (S′,T)(S^{\prime},T), additions have positive total rate proportional to λ\lambda, whereas the total deletion rate is at most n/mini⁡tin/\min_{i}t_{i}. Thus the next jump is an addition with probability 1−O⁡(λ−1)1-O(\lambda^{-1}). Every such addition returns to a pair of bases, and its conditional reinsertion law is

𝐏𝐫⁡[reinsert ​v∣next jump is an addition]\displaystyle\mathbf{Pr}\left[\text{reinsert }v\mid\text{next jump is an addition}\right] =zv​μ​(S′+v)∑w∉S′zw​μ​(S′+w)(v∉S′).\displaystyle=\frac{z_{v}\mu(S^{\prime}+v)}{\sum_{w\notin S^{\prime}}z_{w}\mu(S^{\prime}+w)}\qquad(v\notin S^{\prime}).

Multiplying by the initial deletion rate tu−𝟏[u∈T]t_{u}^{-\mathbf{1}[u\in T]} gives Eq. 19 in the limit. The same argument applies to deletions from TT; excursions with a further deletion have probability O⁡(λ−1)O(\lambda^{-1}). Hence qλind​(X,Y)→q⁡(X,Y)q_{\lambda}^{\mathrm{ind}}(X,Y)\to q(X,Y) for every distinct pair X,Y∈supp⁡π𝒕,𝒛X,Y\in\supp\pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}.

Reversibility passes to the limit. Since the state space is finite, passing to the limit in the induced chains’ Poincaré inequalities gives, for every ff,

𝐕𝐚𝐫π𝒕,𝒛​[f]\displaystyle\mathbf{Var}_{\pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}}\left[f\right] ≤limλ→∞ℰqλind​(f,f)=ℰq​(f,f).∎\displaystyle\leq\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}{\mathcal{E}}_{q_{\lambda}^{\mathrm{ind}}}(f,f)={\mathcal{E}}_{q}(f,f).\qed

Corollary 5.12.

Under the hypotheses of Theorem 5.1, put

t\displaystyle t ≔1256​n2,\displaystyle\coloneqq\frac{1}{256n^{2}}, B\displaystyle B ≔2​n+⌈log2⁡(ℛμ​ℛν)⌉.\displaystyle\coloneqq 2n+\lceil\log_{2}({\mathcal{R}}_{\mu}{\mathcal{R}}_{\nu})\rceil.

If Z∩>0Z_{\cap}>0, with probability at least 31/3231/32 it returns a field satisfying

πt,𝒛​(T=𝒰∖S)\displaystyle\pi_{t,\bm{z}}(T={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S) ≥12.\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{2}.

On every execution, it uses O⁡(n10​B2​log⁡(2​B))O(n^{10}B^{2}\log(2B)) arithmetic operations and value-oracle calls, and every queried or returned field satisfies

‖log⁡𝒛‖1\displaystyle\|\log\bm{z}\|_{1} =O⁡(n​B).\displaystyle=O(nB). (23)
Proof.

By Lemma 2.5, it suffices to find 𝒚\bm{y} with ‖∇Φ​(𝒚)‖∞≤η≔1/(4​n)\|\nabla\Phi(\bm{y})\|_{\infty}\leq\eta\coloneqq 1/(4n) and return 𝒛≔exp⁡(𝒚)\bm{z}\coloneqq\exp(\bm{y}): then n⁡(η+4​t)=1/2n(\eta+4\sqrt{t})=1/2. We apply Theorem 3.2 with d=nd=n, L=σ=1L=\sigma=1, H0=BH_{0}=B, and 𝒙0=𝟎\bm{x}_{0}=\bm{0}. For (S,T)∼πt,exp⁡(𝒚)(S,T)\sim\pi_{t,\exp(\bm{y})}, the vector 𝑮≔𝟏S+𝟏T−𝟏\bm{G}\coloneqq\mathbf{1}_{S}+\mathbf{1}_{T}-\mathbf{1} satisfies

∇Φ​(𝒚)\displaystyle\nabla\Phi(\bm{y}) =𝔼⁡[𝑮],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\bm{G}\right], ∇2Φ​(𝒚)\displaystyle\nabla^{2}\Phi(\bm{y}) =Cov⁡(𝑮)⪰0,\displaystyle=\operatorname{Cov}(\bm{G})\succeq 0,
∂u2Φ⁡(𝒚)\displaystyle\partial_{u}^{2}\Phi(\bm{y}) =𝐕𝐚𝐫⁡[Gu]≤1,\displaystyle=\mathbf{Var}\left[G_{u}\right]\leq 1, 𝑮\displaystyle\bm{G} ∈[−1,1]n.\displaystyle\in[-1,1]^{n}.

When Z∩>0Z_{\cap}>0, every complementary pair contributes its unchanged weight to exp⁡(Φ⁡(𝒚))\exp(\Phi(\bm{y})). Writing M≔maxS⁡μ⁡(S)​maxT⁡ν⁡(T)M\coloneqq\max_{S}\mu(S)\max_{T}\nu(T), we therefore have

Φ⁡(𝒚)\displaystyle\Phi(\bm{y}) ≥log⁡Z∩≥log⁡Mℛμ​ℛν,\displaystyle\geq\log Z_{\cap}\geq\log\frac{M}{{\mathcal{R}}_{\mu}{\mathcal{R}}_{\nu}}, Φ⁡(𝟎)\displaystyle\Phi(\bm{0}) ≤log⁡(4n​M).\displaystyle\leq\log(4^{n}M).

5.3 Wrapping Up

Proof of Theorem 5.1.

The cases a=0a=0 or b=0b=0 are evaluated directly, so assume n≥2n\geq 2. We choose fields making complementary pairs frequent, then estimate the two unknown factors in

Z∩\displaystyle Z_{\cap} =Zt,𝒛𝒛𝒰×πt,𝒛​(T=𝒰∖S).\displaystyle=\frac{Z_{t,\bm{z}}}{\bm{z}^{{\mathcal{U}}}}\times\pi_{t,\bm{z}}(T={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S). (24)

Let B,tB,t be as in Corollary 5.12, and put β≔ε/4\beta\coloneqq\varepsilon/4 and δ0≔1/64\delta_{0}\coloneqq 1/64. Apply Corollary 5.12; if it reports failure, return zero. Otherwise fix the returned field 𝒛\bm{z}. When Z∩>0Z_{\cap}>0, with probability at least 1−2​δ01-2\delta_{0}, this field satisfies πt,𝒛​(T=𝒰∖S)≥1/2\pi_{t,\bm{z}}(T={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S)\geq 1/2.

Estimating the normalizer.

For any returned field 𝒛\bm{z}, we apply Lemma 3.1 to the 2​n2n membership bits of (S,T)(S,T), with weight

W⁡(S,T)\displaystyle W(S,T) ≔μ⁡(S)​ν​(T)​t|S∩T|​𝒛S​𝒛T.\displaystyle\coloneqq\mu(S)\nu(T)t^{|S\cap T|}\bm{z}^{S}\bm{z}^{T}.

The supplied pair (S0,T0)(S_{0},T_{0}) is a valid starting state.

Each conditional law is obtained by restricting μ,ν\mu,\nu to the prescribed inclusions and exclusions, with the same t,𝒛t,\bm{z}. We keep the original ground set and the forced elements in each set, so the degrees remain a,ba,b. Inclusion replaces a generating polynomial by its coordinate derivative times that variable; exclusion sets the variable to zero. These operations preserve log-concavity, and the coefficient ranges do not increase. For every nonempty conditional law, both measures are nonzero. Thus Corollary 5.6 applies to every conditional law.

Lemma 3.1, with relative error β\beta and failure probability δ0\delta_{0}, therefore gives an estimate Z^\widehat{Z} of Zt,𝒛Z_{t,\bm{z}} using O⁡(n3​β−2​log⁡(2​n/δ0))O(n^{3}\beta^{-2}\log(2n/\delta_{0})) conditional samples, each within total variation distance β/(32​n)\beta/(32n) of its law. The sample counts and running times are bounded on every execution.

Combining the estimates.

Independently draw m=⌈8​β−2​log⁡(2/δ0)⌉m=\lceil 8\beta^{-2}\log(2/\delta_{0})\rceil pairs from πt,𝒛\pi_{t,\bm{z}}, each to total variation error β/4\beta/4, and let p^\widehat{p} be the fraction that are complementary. Conditional on the returned fields, Hoeffding’s inequality gives |p^−πt,𝒛​(T=𝒰∖S)|≤β/2|\widehat{p}-\pi_{t,\bm{z}}(T={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S)|\leq\beta/2 except with probability δ0\delta_{0}: the sampling bias is at most β/4\beta/4, as is the fluctuation of the empirical average. Return

Z^∩\displaystyle\widehat{Z}_{\cap} ≔p^​Z^/𝒛𝒰.\displaystyle\coloneqq\widehat{p}\,\widehat{Z}/\bm{z}^{{\mathcal{U}}}.

When the returned field satisfies πt,𝒛​(T=𝒰∖S)≥1/2\pi_{t,\bm{z}}(T={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S)\geq 1/2 and both preceding estimation bounds hold, this is a product of two estimates, each with relative error at most β\beta. These conditions hold jointly with probability at least 1−4​δ0>3/41-4\delta_{0}>3/4, so

(1−β)2\displaystyle(1-\beta)^{2} ≤Z^∩/Z∩≤(1+β)2,\displaystyle\leq\widehat{Z}_{\cap}/Z_{\cap}\leq(1+\beta)^{2},

which implies relative error ε\varepsilon. If Z∩=0Z_{\cap}=0, every supported pair fails the complementary-pair test. Thus every execution returns zero, either at the field-finding step or because p^=0\widehat{p}=0.

Running time.

Finding the field costs O⁡(n10​B2​log⁡(2​B))O(n^{10}B^{2}\log(2B)) by Corollary 5.12. Throughout the self-reduction, the coefficient ranges do not increase, and n​log⁡(zmax/zmin)=O⁡(n2​B)n\log(z_{\max}/z_{\min})=O(n^{2}B) by Eq. 23. Each restricted oracle uses one original query and O⁡(n)O(n) operations to check the prescribed memberships. Thus Corollary 5.6, with t−1=256​n2t^{-1}=256n^{2}, bounds the cost of a conditional sample by

O⁡(n5​(n2​B+log⁡nε)).\displaystyle O\left(n^{5}\left(n^{2}B+\log\frac{n}{\varepsilon}\right)\right).

Self-reduction uses O⁡(n3​ε−2​log⁡(2​n))O(n^{3}\varepsilon^{-2}\log(2n)) such samples. Estimating the complementary-pair probability takes O⁡(ε−2)O(\varepsilon^{-2}) additional samples and is covered by the same bound. Since B=Θ⁡(n+log⁡(ℛμ​ℛν))B=\Theta(n+\log({\mathcal{R}}_{\mu}{\mathcal{R}}_{\nu})), the total cost is

O⁡(n10​B2​ε−2​log2​2​Bε),\displaystyle O\left(n^{10}B^{2}\varepsilon^{-2}\log^{2}\frac{2B}{\varepsilon}\right),

as required by Eq. 18. ∎

Appendix A Deferred Proofs

A.1 Proofs of the convolution theorems

We prove Theorems 1.6 and 1.16 by a common reduction to the coefficient [𝒙𝒰]​(gμ​gν)[\bm{x}^{\mathcal{U}}](g_{\mu}g_{\nu}), followed by separate arguments for the two hypotheses. We first record three lemmas about supports and homogeneous components; proofs of the first two are deferred to Section A.2.

Lemma A.1.

Let ω\omega be a nonzero nonnegative measure on 2𝒰2^{{\mathcal{U}}} whose support Ω\Omega is connected under single-element additions and deletions, and put V≔⋃S∈ΩSV\coloneqq\bigcup_{S\in\Omega}S. If ω\omega has upward spectral curvature κ>0\kappa>0, then Ω\Omega is upward closed in 2V2^{V}. In particular, if Ω\Omega is also downward closed, then Ω=2V\Omega=2^{V}, where V={u:ω⁡({u})>0}V=\{u:\omega(\{u\})>0\}.

Lemma A.2.

Let gω​(𝐱)=∑A⊆𝒰ω⁡(A)​𝐱Ag_{\omega}(\bm{x})=\sum_{A\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}}\omega(A)\bm{x}^{A} be nonzero and log-concave, with nonnegative coefficients, and put n≔|𝒰|n\coloneqq|{\mathcal{U}}|. Given a value oracle for ω\omega, a set A0∈supp⁡ωA_{0}\in\supp\omega, and disjoint C,O⊆𝒰C,O\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}, an algorithm using O⁡(n3)O(n^{3}) queries can:

  • •

    certify that no A∈supp⁡ωA\in\supp\omega contains CC and avoids OO; or

  • •

    find, for every size at which such a set exists, a set A∈supp⁡ωA\in\supp\omega containing CC and avoiding OO.

Lemma A.3 ([RSJ19, Corollary 28]).

Let gg be a multiaffine log-concave polynomial with nonnegative coefficients. For each degree kk, the sum of the degree-kk terms of gg is either zero or log-concave.

Reduce to the coefficient [𝒙𝒰]​(gμ​gν)[\bm{x}^{\mathcal{U}}](g_{\mu}g_{\nu}).

Put C≔{u:αu=2}C\coloneqq\{u:\alpha_{u}=2\}, W≔{u:αu=1}W\coloneqq\{u:\alpha_{u}=1\}, and O≔{u:αu=0}O\coloneqq\{u:\alpha_{u}=0\}. In a pair contributing to Z𝜶Z_{\bm{\alpha}}, both sets contain CC and avoid OO, while each element of WW belongs to exactly one of them. Define measures μ′,ν′\mu^{\prime},\nu^{\prime} on 2W2^{W} by

μ′​(A)\displaystyle\mu^{\prime}(A) ≔μ⁡(C∪A),\displaystyle\coloneqq\mu(C\cup A), ν′​(A)\displaystyle\nu^{\prime}(A) ≔ν⁡(C∪A),A⊆W.\displaystyle\coloneqq\nu(C\cup A),\qquad A\subseteq W.

Then

Z𝜶\displaystyle Z_{\bm{\alpha}} =∑A⊆Wμ′​(A)​ν′​(W∖A).\displaystyle=\sum_{A\subseteq W}\mu^{\prime}(A)\nu^{\prime}(W\setminus A).

If W=∅W=\varnothing, return Z𝜶=μ⁡(C)​ν​(C)Z_{\bm{\alpha}}=\mu(C)\nu(C) directly. Henceforth assume W≠∅W\neq\varnothing. We check that these measures satisfy the assumptions needed for the reduction.

A.2 Proofs of the support lemmas

We now prove Lemmas A.1 and A.2.

Proof of Lemma A.1.

Fix u∈Vu\in V. We show that uu can be added to every supported set that does not already contain it. The key observation is that, along an edge between two such sets, uu can be added at both endpoints or at neither.

To see this, let S,S+v∈ΩS,S+v\in\Omega with distinct u,v∉Su,v\notin S, and put

a=ω⁡(S+u)ω⁡(S),b=ω⁡(S+v)ω⁡(S)>0,c=ω⁡(S+u+v)ω⁡(S).a=\frac{\omega(S+u)}{\omega(S)},\qquad b=\frac{\omega(S+v)}{\omega(S)}>0,\qquad c=\frac{\omega(S+u+v)}{\omega(S)}.

The principal submatrix of ASω,κA_{S}^{\omega,\kappa} on u,vu,v is

M=(a2−κ​aa​b−ca​b−cb2−κ​b)⪰0.M=\begin{pmatrix}a^{2}-\kappa a&ab-c\\ ab-c&b^{2}-\kappa b\end{pmatrix}\succeq 0.

If a=0a=0, the first diagonal entry is zero, so positive semidefiniteness forces the off-diagonal entry to vanish, giving c=0c=0. If a>0a>0, positive semidefiniteness also gives

0≤(b,−a)​M​(b,−a)𝖳=a​b​(2​c−κ⁡(a+b)),0\leq(b,-a)M(b,-a)^{\mathsf{T}}=ab\bigl(2c-\kappa(a+b)\bigr),

so c≥κ⁡(a+b)/2>0c\geq\kappa(a+b)/2>0. Thus a>0a>0 if and only if c>0c>0, proving the observation.

Now take any S∈ΩS\in\Omega with u∉Su\notin S. Since u∈Vu\in V and Ω\Omega is connected, there is a path in Ω\Omega from SS to a set containing uu. Stop at the first such set. The last step adds uu, so uu can be added to the preceding set. Every earlier edge has both endpoints omitting uu; by the observation, working backwards along the path shows that uu can also be added to SS. Since u∈Vu\in V was arbitrary, Ω\Omega is upward closed in 2V2^{V}.

If Ω\Omega is also downward closed, then ∅∈Ω\varnothing\in\Omega. Upward closure now gives Ω=2V\Omega=2^{V}, and the description of VV as the set of elements uu with ω⁡({u})>0\omega(\{u\})>0 follows. ∎

Proof of Lemma A.2.

Let P≔conv⁡{𝟏A:A∈supp⁡ω}P\coloneqq\operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf{1}_{A}:A\in\supp\omega\}, where 𝟏A\mathbf{1}_{A} is the incidence vector of AA. This convex hull is the Newton polytope of gωg_{\omega}. Its vertices are precisely the incidence vectors of sets in supp⁡ω\supp\omega, and an edge is a one-dimensional face. By [Ove20, Proposition 10.4], every edge is parallel to a coordinate vector 𝒆i\bm{e}_{i} or a difference 𝒆i−𝒆j\bm{e}_{i}-\bm{e}_{j}. Consequently, a linear objective with no improving addition, deletion, or exchange within supp⁡ω\supp\omega is globally optimal: these moves include every incident edge. Starting at A0A_{0}, minimize |C∖A|+|A∩O||C\setminus A|+|A\cap O| by such moves. At most nn improvements, each found with O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) queries, either produce a feasible set or certify infeasibility. The convex hull of the feasible incidence vectors is a face of PP and inherits its edge directions. Greedy additions and deletions within this face therefore reach the maximum and minimum cardinalities, visiting every intervening size in O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) further queries. ∎

A.3 Optimality of the curvature threshold

Proof of Remark 1.18.

We reduce counting proper two-colourings of a 33-uniform hypergraph to subset convolution. Deciding whether such a colouring exists is 𝖭𝖯\mathsf{NP}-complete [DRS05]. Fix δ>0\delta>0 and a rational constant 0<c<min⁡{1,δ/2}0<c<\min\{1,\delta/2\}. For a 33-uniform hypergraph ℋ=(𝒰,ℱ)\mathcal{H}=({\mathcal{U}},\mathcal{F}) with n≔|𝒰|≥1n\coloneqq|{\mathcal{U}}|\geq 1, put a≔c/na\coloneqq c/n and define

ℐ\displaystyle\mathcal{I} ≔{S⊆𝒰:F⊈S​ for every ​F∈ℱ},\displaystyle\coloneqq\{S\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}:F\nsubseteq S\text{ for every }F\in\mathcal{F}\},
μ⁡(S)=ν⁡(S)\displaystyle\mu(S)=\nu(S) ≔a|S|𝟏[S∈ℐ].\displaystyle\coloneqq a^{|S|}\mathbf{1}[S\in\mathcal{I}].

The two colour classes form a proper colouring exactly when both belong to ℐ\mathcal{I}. Consequently,

[𝒙𝒰]​(gμ​(𝒙)​gν​(𝒙))\displaystyle[\bm{x}^{{\mathcal{U}}}]\bigl(g_{\mu}(\bm{x})g_{\nu}(\bm{x})\bigr) =an​#​{proper two-colourings of ​ℋ}.\displaystyle=a^{n}\,\#\{\text{proper two-colourings of }\mathcal{H}\}.

Since ana^{n} is known, it remains to verify the promised curvature and oracle bounds.

Fix S∈ℐS\in\mathcal{I}, and let JS≔{u∈𝒰∖S:S+u∈ℐ}J_{S}\coloneqq\{u\in{\mathcal{U}}\setminus S:S+u\in\mathcal{I}\} be its feasible additions. On JSJ_{S}, define the symmetric matrix

BS​(u,v)\displaystyle B_{S}(u,v) ≔𝟏[u≠v,S+u+v∉ℐ].\displaystyle\coloneqq\mathbf{1}[u\neq v,\ S+u+v\notin\mathcal{I}].

Each row of BSB_{S} has at most n−1n-1 nonzero entries, all equal to one, so BS⪰−(n−1)​IB_{S}\succeq-(n-1)I. Substituting the weight ratios into Definition 1.10 gives

ASμ,−c|JS×JS\displaystyle A_{S}^{\mu,-c}\big|_{J_{S}\times J_{S}} =a2​(I+BS)+c​a​I=a2​((n+1)​I+BS)⪰2​a2​I.\displaystyle=a^{2}(I+B_{S})+caI=a^{2}\bigl((n+1)I+B_{S}\bigr)\succeq 2a^{2}I.

All other rows and columns vanish by downward closure. Thus both measures have upward curvature −c-c, and we may take η=κ=−c\eta=\kappa=-c, giving η+κ=−2​c>−δ\eta+\kappa=-2c>-\delta. Their common support is downward closed, their rational weights are computable in polynomial time, and

log⁡(ℛμ​ℛν)\displaystyle\log({\mathcal{R}}_{\mu}{\mathcal{R}}_{\nu}) ≤2​n​log⁡(1/a)=2​n​log⁡(n/c)=O⁡(n​log⁡n).\displaystyle\leq 2n\log(1/a)=2n\log(n/c)=O(n\log n).

An 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} on these instances would therefore give a bounded-error polynomial-time test for hypergraph two-colourability. By reducing the decision queries in the usual 𝖲𝖠𝖳\mathsf{SAT} self-reduction to this problem, amplifying their success probabilities, and verifying the resulting assignment, we obtain an 𝖱𝖯\mathsf{RP} algorithm for 𝖲𝖠𝖳\mathsf{SAT}. Hence 𝖭𝖯=𝖱𝖯\mathsf{NP}=\mathsf{RP}. ∎

A.5 Arithmetic for the counting algorithm

The field-finding and counting algorithms use only arithmetic operations. Ceilings of binary logarithms are computed by repeated doubling; other logarithms in sample counts can be replaced by these upper bounds, changing only absolute constants. In the coordinate-descent application, L=σ=1L=\sigma=1. Take s=log⁡(1+η/8)s=\log(1+\eta/8), which lies in [η/16,η/8][\eta/16,\eta/8], and maintain zuz_{u} directly: an update multiplies or divides one field coordinate zuz_{u} by 1+η/81+\eta/8. Each update costs O⁡(1)O(1) operations, and neither ss nor 𝒚\bm{y} needs to be evaluated. The self-reduction uses membership tests, empirical frequencies, and products and quotients of oracle values, fields, and integer powers of tt, so it requires no further logarithms or exponentials.

Remark A.4 (Bit complexity).

For rational input parameters and polynomial-time value oracles returning rationals of polynomial encoding length, the algorithm in Theorem 1.6 has an implementation whose running time is polynomial in the input length and ε−1\varepsilon^{-1} on every execution. Indeed, the update rule above gives zu=(1+1/(32​n))kuz_{u}=(1+1/(32n))^{k_{u}} for integers kuk_{u}, and the field bound Eq. 23 implies ∑u|ku|=O⁡(n2​B)\sum_{u}|k_{u}|=O(n^{2}B). Each field coordinate can therefore be stored using polynomially many bits. The probabilities for choosing which element to add back are ratios of sums of at most nn weighted oracle values, and empirical frequencies are ratios of sample counts. The final estimate uses products and ratios of these numbers, fields, and powers of tt. All these numbers have polynomially many bits.

We simulate the required rational probabilities using fair coin flips; see [NP05, Proposition 13]. Each binary choice can be simulated with probability at most 2−r2^{-r} of requiring more than rr bits. If NN is a polynomial bound on the total number of binary choices in the homogeneous algorithm, aborting and returning zero when any choice needs more than ⌈log2⁡(64​N)⌉\lceil\log_{2}(64N)\rceil bits adds at most 1/641/64 to its failure probability. The success probability proved in Section 5 is at least 15/1615/16, so it remains above 3/43/4. Conditioning, amplification, and summation over homogeneous layers preserve polynomial bit complexity. In particular, the rational six-vertex instances in Section C.7 satisfy these oracle assumptions.

=−α−2​∇𝒙2​log⁡q⁡(x1α,…,xnα)|𝒙=𝟏⪰0,\displaystyle=-\alpha^{-2}\left.\nabla_{\bm{x}}^{2}\log q(x_{1}^{\alpha},\ldots,x_{n}^{\alpha})\right|_{\bm{x}=\mathbf{1}}\succeq 0,

which proves the asserted curvature bound.

It remains to verify that nonzero coordinate derivatives preserve fractional log-concavity. We use the limiting argument of [Ali+21, Section 1.5]. Writing 𝒙α≔(x1α,…,xnα)\bm{x}^{\alpha}\coloneqq(x_{1}^{\alpha},\ldots,x_{n}^{\alpha}), multiaffinity gives

(∂ip)​(𝒙α)\displaystyle(\partial_{i}p)(\bm{x}^{\alpha}) =lims→∞s−α​p​((𝒙+s​𝒆i)α).\displaystyle=\lim_{s\to\infty}s^{-\alpha}p\bigl((\bm{x}+s\bm{e}_{i})^{\alpha}\bigr).

Each function on the right is a positive multiple of a translate of 𝒙↦p⁡(𝒙α)\bm{x}\mapsto p(\bm{x}^{\alpha}), hence is log-concave. The log-concavity inequality is preserved under the limit. Iterating proves the assertion for every nonzero ∂Sp\partial_{S}p. ∎

A.7 Examples of spectral curvature

We show that every κ∈ℝ\kappa\in{\mathbb{R}} is the largest admissible curvature of some distribution. For a positive value, take the product measure μ⁡(S)∝λ|S|\mu(S)\propto\lambda^{|S|} with λ>0\lambda>0: the curvature matrix on coordinates outside SS is λ⁡(λ−κ)​I\lambda(\lambda-\kappa)I, so the largest admissible κ\kappa is λ\lambda. For a nonpositive value, take 𝒰={1,2}{\mathcal{U}}=\{1,2\} and

(μ⁡(∅),μ⁡({1}),μ⁡({2}),μ⁡({1,2}))=(1,1,1,M)3+M,M≥2.\bigl(\mu(\varnothing),\mu(\{1\}),\mu(\{2\}),\mu(\{1,2\})\bigr)=\frac{(1,1,1,M)}{3+M},\qquad M\geq 2.

The smallest eigenvalue of A∅μ,κA_{\varnothing}^{\mu,\kappa} is 2−M−κ2-M-\kappa, and the singleton matrices are positive semidefinite exactly when κ≤M\kappa\leq M. Thus the largest admissible κ\kappa is 2−M2-M, giving every nonpositive value.

Appendix B Background for Applications

We recall the background used in Appendix C; see [Oxl11] for standard matroid facts.

B.1 Further matroid terminology and examples

We use the definitions and notation from Section 3.2. A set is spanning if it contains a basis. An element ee is a loop if 𝗋𝗄ℳ​({e})=0{\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{M}}}}(\{e\})=0; distinct nonloops e,fe,f are parallel if 𝗋𝗄ℳ​({e,f})=1{\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{M}}}}(\{e,f\})=1. Together with equality, this partitions the nonloops into parallel classes.

In a partition matroid, 𝒰=⨆iEi{\mathcal{U}}=\bigsqcup_{i}E_{i} and independence means |I∩Ei|≤bi|I\cap E_{i}|\leq b_{i} for prescribed nonnegative integer bounds. In a graphic matroid, independent edge sets are forests and bases are spanning forests, one tree per connected component. In a column matroid, independent sets index linearly independent columns of a matrix over a field.

B.2 Operations and oracles

The restriction ℳ|A{\mathcal{M}}|_{A} keeps the independent sets contained in AA; deletion of AA is restriction to 𝒰∖A{\mathcal{U}}\setminus A. The contraction ℳ/A{\mathcal{M}}/A has ground set 𝒰∖A{\mathcal{U}}\setminus A. The ranks of the dual and contraction satisfy

𝗋𝗄ℳ∗​(T)\displaystyle{\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{M}}^{*}}}(T) =|T|+𝗋𝗄ℳ​(𝒰∖T)−𝗋𝗄ℳ​(𝒰),\displaystyle=|T|+{\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{M}}}}({\mathcal{U}}\setminus T)-{\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{M}}}}({\mathcal{U}}), (29)
𝗋𝗄ℳ/A​(S)\displaystyle{\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{M}}/A}}(S) =𝗋𝗄ℳ(S∪A)−𝗋𝗄ℳ(A)(S⊆𝒰∖A).\displaystyle={\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{M}}}}(S\cup A)-{\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{M}}}}(A)\qquad(S\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}\setminus A).

Thus TT is independent in ℳ∗{\mathcal{M}}^{*} exactly when its complement is spanning. If BAB_{A} is a basis of ℳ|A{\mathcal{M}}|_{A}, contraction independence is tested by BA∪S∈ℐ⁡(ℳ)B_{A}\cup S\in{\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{M}}), even when AA is dependent.

The direct sum of matroids on disjoint ground sets has independent sets whose restriction to each component is independent. The union of matroids on a common ground set has independent sets admitting a partition I=I1⊔⋯⊔IkI=I_{1}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup I_{k}, with Ii∈ℐ⁡(ℳi)I_{i}\in{\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{M}}_{i}).

The rank formulas above, together with the greedy rank computation in Section 3.2, give independence oracles for duals and contractions. With separate independence oracles, matroid intersection finds a maximum common independent set in polynomial time [Edm79], and matroid union has a polynomial-time independence oracle [BF10, Section 4.1].

B.3 Submodularity and integral polymatroids

A set function f:2[m]→ℝf:2^{[m]}\to\mathbb{R} is submodular if

f⁡(A)+f⁡(B)≥f⁡(A∪B)+f⁡(A∩B)(A,B⊆[m]).f(A)+f(B)\geq f(A\cup B)+f(A\cap B)\qquad(A,B\subseteq[m]).

It is monotone if A⊆BA\subseteq B implies f⁡(A)≤f⁡(B)f(A)\leq f(B), and normalized if f⁡(∅)=0f(\varnothing)=0. Matroid rank functions are a special case of normalized monotone submodular functions. For such an integer-valued ff, the polymatroid base polytope is

B(f)≔{𝒙∈ℝ≥0m:∑i=1mxi=f([m]),∑i∈Axi≤f(A)∀A⊆[m]}.B(f)\coloneqq\left\{\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{m}:{\sum_{i=1}^{m}x_{i}}=f([m]),\quad{\sum_{i\in A}x_{i}}\leq f(A)\ \forall A\subseteq[m]\right\}.

Its vertices are integral [FM19, Section 2]. For f=𝗋𝗄ℳf=\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{M}}}, its integer points are exactly the basis indicators.

B.4 Log-concave and Lorentzian polynomials

Positive element weights preserve the log-concavity of the basis polynomial recalled in Section 3.2, by variable rescaling:

∑B∈ℬ⁡(ℳ)(∏e∈Bwe)​𝒙B=gℳ​((we​xe)e∈𝒰).\sum_{B\in{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{M}})}\left(\prod_{e\in B}w_{e}\right)\bm{x}^{B}=g_{{\mathcal{M}}}((w_{e}x_{e})_{e\in{\mathcal{U}}}).

Zero weights are handled by deletion; if the original rank drops, the weighted polynomial is zero. Products on disjoint variable sets also preserve log-concavity and multiaffinity.

A nonzero homogeneous polynomial with nonnegative coefficients is Lorentzian if every iterated coordinate partial derivative, including order zero, is either zero or log-concave on the positive orthant [BH20, Theorem 2.30]. For a polynomial p⁡(z1,…,zm)p(z_{1},\ldots,z_{m}), choose positive integers cic_{i} with degzi⁡p≤ci\deg_{z_{i}}p\leq c_{i} and new variables xi,1,…,xi,cix_{i,1},\ldots,x_{i,c_{i}}. Its polarization applies the rule

zik⟼1(cik)​∑J⊆[ci]|J|=k∏j∈Jxi,j,0≤k≤ci,z_{i}^{k}\ \longmapsto\ \frac{1}{\binom{c_{i}}{k}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}J\subseteq[c_{i}]\\ |J|=k\end{subarray}}\prod_{j\in J}x_{i,j},\qquad 0\leq k\leq c_{i},

to each variable in each monomial and extends linearly. This operation preserves the Lorentzian property [BH20, Proposition 3.1].

A nonzero, finitely supported weight ω:ℤ≥0m→ℝ≥0\omega:\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{m}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} is log-M\mathrm{M}-concave if, for some integer rr, ∑iki=r\sum_{i}k_{i}=r for every 𝒌∈supp⁡ω\bm{k}\in\supp\omega, and, for every 𝒙,𝒚∈supp⁡ω\bm{x},\bm{y}\in\supp\omega and every ii with xi>yix_{i}>y_{i}, there is a jj with xj<yjx_{j}<y_{j} such that

ω⁡(𝒙)​ω​(𝒚)\displaystyle\omega(\bm{x})\omega(\bm{y}) ≤ω⁡(𝒙−𝒆i+𝒆j)​ω​(𝒚+𝒆i−𝒆j).\displaystyle\leq\omega(\bm{x}-\bm{e}_{i}+\bm{e}_{j})\omega(\bm{y}+\bm{e}_{i}-\bm{e}_{j}). (30)

Here 𝒆i\bm{e}_{i} is the iith coordinate unit vector. For such a weight ω\omega, the polynomial ∑𝒌ω⁡(𝒌)​𝒛𝒌/𝒌!\sum_{\bm{k}}\omega(\bm{k})\bm{z}^{\bm{k}}/\bm{k}! is Lorentzian, where 𝒌!=∏iki!\bm{k}!=\prod_{i}k_{i}! [BH20, Corollary 3.16].

Appendix C Applications

We apply the subset-convolution framework to counting and approximation problems involving graphs, determinants, and partition functions. The common step is to encode the relevant weights and constraints in two measures that satisfy the log-concavity or spectral-curvature hypotheses of our convolution theorems. The shared matroid and log-concavity preliminaries are collected in Appendix B.

Figure 2 summarizes the reductions to Theorems 1.6 and 1.16. The corollaries below give the precise assumptions and guarantees. We group the applications by the reductions they share.

Unless stated otherwise, running-time statements below use the arithmetic model of Theorems 1.6 and 1.16; we omit bit-complexity analysis for simplicity. The EPR-in-𝖡𝖯𝖯\mathsf{BPP} conclusion still uses the bit-complexity bound in Remark A.4. We first record two reductions used throughout the appendix. Products of polynomially many rational input weights, determinants of rational input matrices, and factorials of polynomially bounded integers have polynomial bit length. We use this observation below to bound the logarithmic ranges of positive coefficients.

Lemma C.1.

Let ω:2𝒰→ℝ≥0\omega:2^{{\mathcal{U}}}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} have a log-concave generating polynomial, an evaluation oracle, a given set in supp⁡ω\supp\omega, and a supplied bound on ℛω{\mathcal{R}}_{\omega}, as in Theorem 1.6. For any matroid ℳ{\mathcal{M}} on 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} given by an independence oracle, there is an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for

∑S∈ℬ⁡(ℳ)ω⁡(S),\sum_{S\in{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{M}})}\omega(S),

with running time polynomial in |𝒰||{\mathcal{U}}|, log⁡ℛω\log{\mathcal{R}}_{\omega}, and the inverse accuracy, counting oracle calls as single operations.

Proof.

Set ν(T)≔𝟏[𝒰∖T∈ℬ(ℳ)]\nu(T)\coloneqq\mathbf{1}[{\mathcal{U}}\setminus T\in{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{M}})]. Its generating polynomial is the basis polynomial of ℳ∗{\mathcal{M}}^{*}, hence is log-concave, and ℛν=1{\mathcal{R}}_{\nu}=1. The complement of a greedy basis initializes ν\nu, and [𝒙𝒰]​(gω​gν)[\bm{x}^{{\mathcal{U}}}](g_{\omega}g_{\nu}) is the desired sum. Apply Theorem 1.6. ∎

Corollary C.2.

Let ℳ,𝒩{\mathcal{M}},{\mathcal{N}} be matroids of the same rank rr on 𝒰{\mathcal{U}}, given by independence oracles, and let wew_{e} be nonnegative rational element weights. There is an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for

∑S∈ℬ⁡(ℳ)∩ℬ⁡(𝒩)∏e∈Swe.\sum_{S\in{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{M}})\cap{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{N}})}\prod_{e\in S}w_{e}.
Proof.

Delete zero-weight elements; if either rank drops below rr, return zero. The weight ω(S)≔𝟏[S∈ℬ(ℳ)]∏e∈Swe\omega(S)\coloneqq\mathbf{1}[S\in{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{M}})]\prod_{e\in S}w_{e} has a log-concave generating polynomial by positive variable rescaling. A greedy basis initializes it, and its logarithmic coefficient range is polynomial in the weight encoding length. Apply Lemma C.1 with the matroid 𝒩{\mathcal{N}}. ∎

To count random subsets that contain a common basis, we use the following consequence of Rado’s theorem [Rad42].

Theorem C.3 (Rado matroids [Oxl11, Theorem 11.2.12]).

Let GG be a finite bipartite graph with left vertex set LL and right vertex set RR, and let ℛ\mathcal{R} be a matroid on RR. There is a matroid ℒ\mathcal{L} on LL such that A⊆LA\subseteq L is an independent set of ℒ\mathcal{L} exactly when GG has a matching whose left endpoints are exactly AA and whose right endpoints form an independent set of ℛ\mathcal{R}.

Lemma C.4.

Let ℳ,𝒩{\mathcal{M}},{\mathcal{N}} be matroids of the same rank on 𝒰{\mathcal{U}}, given by independence oracles. Retain each element uu independently with rational probability pu∈[0,1]p_{u}\in[0,1]. There is an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for the probability that the retained set contains a common basis.

Proof.

We encode the event by weighted common bases of two new matroids. Put m≔|𝒰|m\coloneqq|{\mathcal{U}}|, and let 𝒰+={u+:u∈𝒰}{\mathcal{U}}^{+}=\{u^{+}:u\in{\mathcal{U}}\} and 𝒰−={u−:u∈𝒰}{\mathcal{U}}^{-}=\{u^{-}:u\in{\mathcal{U}}\} be two disjoint copies of 𝒰{\mathcal{U}}. Let ℋ\mathcal{H} be the direct sum of copies of ℳ{\mathcal{M}} and 𝒩∗{\mathcal{N}}^{*} on 𝒰+{\mathcal{U}}^{+} and 𝒰−{\mathcal{U}}^{-}, respectively; it has rank mm. Form a bipartite graph with left vertex set 𝒳≔{xu0,xu1:u∈𝒰}\mathcal{X}\coloneqq\{x_{u}^{0},x_{u}^{1}:u\in{\mathcal{U}}\} and right vertex set 𝒰+∪𝒰−{\mathcal{U}}^{+}\cup{\mathcal{U}}^{-}. The new elements xu0,xu1x_{u}^{0},x_{u}^{1} represent uu being absent or retained, respectively. Join xu0x_{u}^{0} only to u−u^{-}, and join xu1x_{u}^{1} to both u−u^{-} and u+u^{+}.

Apply Theorem C.3 with L=𝒳L=\mathcal{X}, R=𝒰+∪𝒰−R={\mathcal{U}}^{+}\cup{\mathcal{U}}^{-}, and ℛ=ℋ\mathcal{R}=\mathcal{H}, and denote the resulting matroid ℒ\mathcal{L} by 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. A subset is independent in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} exactly when it can be matched to an independent set of ℋ\mathcal{H}. Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} be the partition matroid on 𝒳\mathcal{X} allowing at most one of xu0,xu1x_{u}^{0},x_{u}^{1} for each uu. Both matroids have rank mm: any basis of ℋ\mathcal{H} can be matched to distinct left vertices by matching u+u^{+} to xu1x_{u}^{1} and u−u^{-} to xu0x_{u}^{0}.

The retained set F⊆𝒰F\subseteq{\mathcal{U}} has the unique representation XF≔{xu1:u∈F}∪{xu0:u∉F}X_{F}\coloneqq\{x_{u}^{1}:u\in F\}\cup\{x_{u}^{0}:u\notin F\}. Since |XF|=m=𝗋𝗄⁡(ℋ)|X_{F}|=m={\mathsf{rk}}(\mathcal{H}), XFX_{F} is independent in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} exactly when it can be matched to a basis of ℋ\mathcal{H}. A matching covering XFX_{F} uses exactly one of u+u^{+} and u−u^{-} for each element uu, so its matched right vertices form a set B+∪(𝒰∖B)−B^{+}\cup({\mathcal{U}}\setminus B)^{-} with B⊆FB\subseteq F. This set is a basis of ℋ\mathcal{H} exactly when BB is a common basis of ℳ,𝒩{\mathcal{M}},{\mathcal{N}}. Consequently,

XF∈ℬ(𝒫)∩ℬ(𝒬)⟺F contains a common basis of ℳ,𝒩.X_{F}\in{\mathcal{B}}(\mathcal{P})\cap{\mathcal{B}}(\mathcal{Q})\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\text{ contains a common basis of }{\mathcal{M}},{\mathcal{N}}.

Giving xu1,xu0x_{u}^{1},x_{u}^{0} weights pu,1−pup_{u},1-p_{u} makes the weighted common-bases sum the required probability. Each FF is counted once, regardless of the number of common bases it contains.

It remains to implement an independence oracle for 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. We do so by matroid intersection on restrictions and contractions of ℳ{\mathcal{M}} and 𝒩{\mathcal{N}}. For a queried set Y⊆𝒳Y\subseteq\mathcal{X}, let S2S_{2} contain the elements uu for which both xu0,xu1x_{u}^{0},x_{u}^{1} belong to YY, let S0S_{0} contain those for which neither belongs to YY, and let S1≔{u:xu1∈Y,xu0∉Y}S_{1}\coloneqq\{u:x_{u}^{1}\in Y,\ x_{u}^{0}\notin Y\}. The possible sets of right endpoints of a matching with left endpoint set YY are exactly

(S2∪B)+∪(𝒰∖(S0∪B))−,B⊆S1.(S_{2}\cup B)^{+}\cup\bigl({\mathcal{U}}\setminus(S_{0}\cup B)\bigr)^{-},\qquad B\subseteq S_{1}.

Here BB consists of the elements u∈S1u\in S_{1} for which xu1x_{u}^{1} is matched to u+∈𝒰+u^{+}\in{\mathcal{U}}^{+}. By duality, the displayed set is independent in ℋ\mathcal{H} exactly when S2∪BS_{2}\cup B is independent in ℳ{\mathcal{M}} and S0∪BS_{0}\cup B contains a basis of 𝒩{\mathcal{N}}.

Reject if S2S_{2} is dependent in ℳ{\mathcal{M}}. Otherwise, apply matroid intersection to (ℳ/S2)|S1({\mathcal{M}}/S_{2})|_{S_{1}} and (𝒩/S0)|S1({\mathcal{N}}/S_{0})|_{S_{1}}, and accept exactly when they have a common independent set of size k≔𝗋𝗄𝒩​(𝒰)−𝗋𝗄𝒩​(S0)k\coloneqq{\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}}({\mathcal{U}})-{\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}}(S_{0}), where 𝗋𝗄𝒩{\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}} is the rank function of 𝒩{\mathcal{N}}. The required oracles use only the original independence oracles: test I⊆S1I\subseteq S_{1} in ℳ/S2{\mathcal{M}}/S_{2} by testing S2∪IS_{2}\cup I in ℳ{\mathcal{M}}, and test it in 𝒩/S0{\mathcal{N}}/S_{0} by testing B0∪IB_{0}\cup I in 𝒩{\mathcal{N}}, where B0B_{0} is a basis of 𝒩|S0{\mathcal{N}}|_{S_{0}} found greedily. This gives a polynomial-time oracle for 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, so Corollary C.2 applies. ∎

C.1 Strong orientations

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a loopless undirected multigraph, with |V|≥2|V|\geq 2, and let k≥1k\geq 1 be an integer. An orientation of the edges of GG is kk-arc-connected if for every nonempty proper subset X⊊VX\subsetneq V, there are at least kk arcs directed from V∖XV\setminus X into XX. Give each direction of each labeled edge a nonnegative rational weight we,vw_{e,v}, where vv is its head. Define

Zk​(G,𝒘)≔∑D​ a ​k​-arc-connected orientation∏e∈Ewe,headD⁡(e).Z_{k}(G;\bm{w})\coloneqq\sum_{D\text{ a }k\text{-arc-connected orientation}}\prod_{e\in E}w_{e,\operatorname{head}_{D}(e)}.

The case k=1k=1 counts strong orientations, and zero weights allow fixed directions.

Corollary C.5.

There is an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for Zk​(G,𝐰)Z_{k}(G;\bm{w}), even when kk is part of the input in binary.

The following form of the classical common-bases representation [Goe12, Lecture 16] follows from the indegree characterization in [FM19] and the matroid construction of McDiarmid [McD73]; see also [BCF23, Theorem 2.1].

Lemma C.6 (Common bases for strong orientations).

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a loopless undirected multigraph with |V|≥2|V|\geq 2, and let k≥1k\geq 1 be an integer. Suppose every nontrivial undirected cut has size at least 2​k2k. Put m≔|E|m\coloneqq|E|, and define

𝒰≔{(e,v):e∈E,v∈e},𝒰X≔{(e,v)∈𝒰:v∈X}.{\mathcal{U}}\coloneqq\{(e,v):e\in E,\ v\in e\},\qquad{\mathcal{U}}_{X}\coloneqq\{(e,v)\in{\mathcal{U}}:v\in X\}.

For an orientation DD, let dD−​(v)d^{-}_{D}(v) be the number of edges directed into vv. The function

f⁡(X)≔max⁡∑v∈XD​ a ​k​-arc-connected orientation⁡dD−​(v)(X⊆V)f(X)\coloneqq\max_{D\text{ a }k\text{-arc-connected orientation}}\sum_{v\in X}d^{-}_{D}(v)\qquad(X\subseteq V)

is integer-valued, monotone, and submodular, with f⁡(∅)=0f(\varnothing)=0 and f⁡(V)=mf(V)=m. Let ℳ{\mathcal{M}} be the partition matroid on 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} allowing at most one incidence per edge. There is a matroid 𝒩{\mathcal{N}} on 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} with rank function

𝗋𝗄𝒩​(Y)=minX⊆V⁡(f⁡(X)+|Y∖𝒰X|)(Y⊆𝒰).{\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}}(Y)=\min_{X\subseteq V}\bigl(f(X)+|Y\setminus{\mathcal{U}}_{X}|\bigr)\qquad(Y\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}).

Both matroids have rank mm, and the map

D⟼AD≔{(e,headD⁡(e)):e∈E}D\longmapsto A_{D}\coloneqq\{(e,\operatorname{head}_{D}(e)):e\in E\}

is a bijection from the kk-arc-connected orientations of GG to ℬ⁡(ℳ)∩ℬ⁡(𝒩){\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{M}})\cap{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{N}}).

Proof of Corollary C.5.

We apply Corollary C.2 to the matroids in Lemma C.6. First, by the orientation theorem of Nash-Williams [Nas60, Theorem 1], a kk-arc-connected orientation exists exactly when every nontrivial undirected cut has size at least 2​k2k. Check this by a minimum cut, returning zero if it fails, and put m≔|E|m\coloneqq|E|.

Give incidence (e,v)(e,v) weight we,vw_{e,v}. The bijection in Lemma C.6 preserves the product of weights, so the weighted common-bases sum is exactly Zk​(G,𝒘)Z_{k}(G;\bm{w}). It remains to implement the two independence oracles. For ℳ{\mathcal{M}}, check that the queried set contains at most one incidence per edge.

For 𝒩{\mathcal{N}}, given any Y⊆𝒰Y\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}, compute 𝗋𝗄𝒩​(Y){\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}}(Y) using the lemma’s rank formula and accept exactly when 𝗋𝗄𝒩​(Y)=|Y|{\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}}(Y)=|Y|. For fixed YY, the term

|Y∖𝒰X|=|Y|−∑v∈X|Y∩𝒰{v}||Y\setminus{\mathcal{U}}_{X}|=|Y|-\sum_{v\in X}|Y\cap{\mathcal{U}}_{\{v\}}|

is a constant minus a sum of fixed vertex weights. Adding it to f⁡(X)f(X) therefore preserves submodularity, so the rank formula can be evaluated by submodular minimization [Sch00]. To supply the required values f⁡(X)f(X), assign cost zero to directions whose heads lie in XX and cost one to the others. The minimum cost of a kk-arc-connected orientation is m−f⁡(X)m-f(X), and it can be found in polynomial time [IK05]. Thus every value query, and hence each independence query, takes polynomial time.

With these oracles, Corollary C.2 gives the claimed 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS}. If kk is part of the input in binary, the successful minimum-cut test bounds kk by mm, so the oracle implementations still take polynomial time in the input length. ∎

C.2 Undirected Euler tours

Let GG be a connected 44-regular multigraph. Each edge has two ends, called half-edges; a loop contributes two distinct half-edges at the same vertex. A transition at a vertex pairs its four incident half-edges into two pairs; there are three choices. Entering along either half-edge of a pair is followed by leaving along the other. A closed trail is a closed walk that does not repeat edges. Choosing a transition at every vertex partitions the edges into closed trails. We count the choices that give a single closed trail, or equivalently Euler tours up to cyclic shift and reversal. For each vertex vv and each of its three transitions τ\tau, give the whole pairing τ\tau a nonnegative rational weight wv​(τ)w_{v}(\tau). These three weights may be chosen arbitrarily at each vertex. The total weight of Euler tours is

∑P∏v∈V⁡(G)wv​(Pv),\sum_{P}\prod_{v\in V(G)}w_{v}(P_{v}),

where the sum ranges over all Euler tours PP, and PvP_{v} is the transition used by PP at vv. Thus the weights are attached to local pairings, not to individual edge directions.

Corollary C.7 (Weighted Euler tours).

Let GG be a connected 44-regular multigraph with nonnegative rational weights on its local transitions. There is an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for the total weight of Euler tours in GG.

Proof.

We encode the weighted Euler tours in GG as weighted common bases of two matroids and apply Corollary C.2. Fix an Euler tour CC, viewed as a cyclic sequence of vertex visits. Each vertex occurs twice because GG is 44-regular. Two distinct vertices u,vu,v alternate along CC if, after ignoring visits to all other vertices, their cyclic order is u,v,u,vu,v,u,v. The interlace matrix A∈𝔽2V⁡(G)×V⁡(G)A\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{V(G)\times V(G)} is defined by Au​v=1A_{uv}=1 when uu and vv alternate, and Au​v=0A_{uv}=0 otherwise; in particular, Au​u=0A_{uu}=0 [Tra09, p. 2]. Choose a direction for traversing CC and orient every edge accordingly. At a vertex vv, label the two incoming half-edges a1,a2a_{1},a_{2} and the two outgoing half-edges b1,b2b_{1},b_{2} so that CC enters through aia_{i} and leaves through bib_{i} on its iith visit, for i=1,2i=1,2. Define

ϕv\displaystyle\phi_{v} ≔{{a1,b1},{a2,b2}},\displaystyle\coloneqq\bigl\{\{a_{1},b_{1}\},\{a_{2},b_{2}\}\bigr\},
χv\displaystyle\chi_{v} ≔{{a1,b2},{a2,b1}},\displaystyle\coloneqq\bigl\{\{a_{1},b_{2}\},\{a_{2},b_{1}\}\bigr\},
ψv\displaystyle\psi_{v} ≔{{a1,a2},{b1,b2}}.\displaystyle\coloneqq\bigl\{\{a_{1},a_{2}\},\{b_{1},b_{2}\}\bigr\}.

Only ϕv\phi_{v} is used by CC. The alternative χv\chi_{v} also pairs each incoming half-edge with an outgoing half-edge, but switches which outgoing half-edge follows each incoming one. The transition ψv\psi_{v} pairs the two incoming half-edges together and the two outgoing half-edges together. Associate these choices with the labeled columns

ϕv⟷𝒆v,χv⟷𝑨v,ψv⟷𝒆v+𝑨vof ​[I​∣A∣​I+A]​ over ​𝔽2.\phi_{v}\longleftrightarrow\bm{e}_{v},\qquad\chi_{v}\longleftrightarrow\bm{A}_{v},\qquad\psi_{v}\longleftrightarrow\bm{e}_{v}+\bm{A}_{v}\quad\text{of }[\,I\mid A\mid I+A\,]\text{ over }\mathbb{F}_{2}.

For a transition choice PP, let KPK_{P} contain its selected columns. The extended Cohn–Lempel equality [Tra09, Theorem 4] gives

#⁡{closed trails of ​P}=1+nullity⁡KP.{\#\{\text{closed trails of }P\}}=1+\operatorname{nullity}K_{P}.

Indeed, deleting the identity choices leaves the principal interlace matrix with a diagonal one at each ψ\psi choice, which is the matrix in that equality. Hence PP is an Euler tour precisely when it is a common basis of the column matroid and the partition matroid choosing one column from each vertex triple. Giving each column its transition weight preserves the weight and counts each tour once. Gaussian elimination and checking that at most one column is selected from each vertex triple give the independence oracles, so Corollary C.2 applies. ∎

Ge and Štefankovič [GŠ10, Theorem 4] give an approximation-preserving reduction from counting Euler tours in general undirected graphs to counting AA-trails in 44-regular graphs with prescribed cyclic orders.

In a 44-regular multigraph, suppose that a cyclic order of the four half-edges is specified separately at each vertex. An AA-trail is an Euler tour such that, at every visit to a vertex, the entering and leaving half-edges are adjacent in that vertex’s cyclic order. Either direction through an adjacent pair is allowed. For cyclic order h1,h2,h3,h4h_{1},h_{2},h_{3},h_{4}, the allowed arrival–departure pairs are the unordered pairs

{h1,h2},{h2,h3},{h3,h4},{h4,h1}.\{h_{1},h_{2}\},\qquad\{h_{2},h_{3}\},\qquad\{h_{3},h_{4}\},\qquad\{h_{4},h_{1}\}.

For example, entering through h1h_{1} and leaving through h2h_{2} is allowed, as is entering through h2h_{2} and leaving through h1h_{1}. The transition at that vertex must therefore be one of

{{h1,h2},{h3,h4}}or{{h1,h4},{h2,h3}}.\bigl\{\{h_{1},h_{2}\},\{h_{3},h_{4}\}\bigr\}\qquad\text{or}\qquad\bigl\{\{h_{1},h_{4}\},\{h_{2},h_{3}\}\bigr\}.

The remaining pairing {{h1,h3},{h2,h4}}\{\{h_{1},h_{3}\},\{h_{2},h_{4}\}\} is forbidden.

Counting AA-trails is a special case of weighted Euler-tour counting: assign weight one to each allowed transition and zero to each forbidden transition. Every AA-trail then has weight one, and every other Euler tour has weight zero. By Corollary C.7, this count admits an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS}. Composing that algorithm with the reduction gives the following corollary.

Corollary C.8 (Euler tours in general graphs).

There is an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for the unweighted number of Euler tours in general undirected graphs.

C.3 Network reliability and disjoint linkages

Definition C.9 (SS–TT linkage).

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a directed or undirected graph, and let S,T⊆VS,T\subseteq V be disjoint terminal sets with |S|=|T|=k≥1|S|=|T|=k\geq 1. An SS–TT linkage consists of kk paths that share no vertices. Each path joins a vertex of SS to a vertex of TT, and every vertex of SS and TT is used as an endpoint exactly once. We do not specify which vertex of SS is joined to which vertex of TT. If GG is directed, all paths must follow edge directions from SS to TT.

Corollary C.10 (SS–TT Network reliability).

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a directed or undirected graph, and let S,T⊆VS,T\subseteq V be disjoint terminal sets with |S|=|T|=k≥1|S|=|T|=k\geq 1. Retain each edge ee independently with given rational probability pe∈[0,1]p_{e}\in[0,1]. There is an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for

RelS,T⁡(G,𝒑)\displaystyle\operatorname{Rel}_{S,T}(G;\bm{p}) ≔∑F⊆E:(V,F)​ admits an ​S​–​T​ linkage∏e∈Fpe∏e∈E∖F(1−pe).\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}F\subseteq E:\\ (V,F)\text{ admits an }S\text{--}T\text{ linkage}\end{subarray}}\prod_{e\in F}p_{e}\prod_{e\in E\setminus F}(1-p_{e}). (31)
Remark C.11.

Taking S={s}S=\{s\} and T={t}T=\{t\} in an undirected graph recovers the 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for ss–tt reliability in [FFG26] with worse running time.

Proof of Corollary C.10.

We first encode directed linkage as the existence of a perfect matching in a random bipartite graph, then apply Lemma C.4. An undirected edge gadget gives the undirected case.

For a directed graph, discard loops, arcs entering SS, and arcs leaving TT. Form a bipartite graph with vertex classes

VL\displaystyle V_{L} ≔{ℓv:v∈V∖T},\displaystyle\coloneqq\{\ell_{v}:v\in V\setminus T\}, VR\displaystyle V_{R} ≔{rv:v∈V∖S}.\displaystyle\coloneqq\{r_{v}:v\in V\setminus S\}.

Replace each remaining arc u→vu\to v by the edge ℓu​rv\ell_{u}r_{v}. Keep this edge with the same probability as the original arc. Add an always-present edge ℓv​rv\ell_{v}r_{v} for each v∉S∪Tv\notin S\cup T. A linkage gives a perfect matching by selecting its path edges and the diagonal edges at unused vertices. Conversely, following a perfect matching from each source reaches a distinct sink: entering a cycle or another source’s path would give a vertex two selected incoming edges. Thus, for every retained edge set,

the directed graph admits an SS–TT linkage ⟺the bipartite graph has a perfect matching.\displaystyle\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{the bipartite graph has a perfect matching}.

Let ℳ,𝒩{\mathcal{M}},{\mathcal{N}} be the partition matroids on the bipartite edge set, allowing at most one edge at each left and right endpoint, respectively. If the full bipartite graph has no perfect matching, return zero. Otherwise both matroids have rank |V|−k|V|-k, and a retained edge set contains a perfect matching exactly when it contains a common basis. Thus Lemma C.4 approximates the desired probability, including the always-present diagonal edges.

Finally, for an undirected edge e={u,v}e=\{u,v\}, introduce new vertices ae,bea_{e},b_{e} and arcs

u→ae,v→ae,ae→be,be→u,be→v.\displaystyle u\to a_{e},\quad v\to a_{e},\quad a_{e}\to b_{e},\quad b_{e}\to u,\quad b_{e}\to v.

Only ae→bea_{e}\to b_{e} is random, with retention probability pep_{e}; the other four arcs are always present. Vertex-disjoint undirected paths lift to vertex-disjoint directed paths. Conversely, simple directed paths project to vertex-disjoint undirected paths, since returning through the gadget to the vertex where the path entered would repeat that vertex. This preserves the linkage event for every choice of retained original edges and uses one independent random variable per original edge. The directed result therefore also proves the undirected case. ∎

C.4 Directed root-to-all reliability

Let D=(V,E)D=(V,E) be a directed multigraph with root rr, and retain each arc ee independently with rational probability pe∈[0,1]p_{e}\in[0,1]. For each F⊆EF\subseteq E, let Λ⁡(V,F)∈ℝV×V\Lambda(V,F)\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times V} be the matrix whose entry Λ​(V,F)u,v\Lambda(V,F)_{u,v}, for u≠vu\neq v, is the maximum number of arc-disjoint directed paths from uu to vv in (V,F)(V,F). Set its diagonal entries to zero. For an integer k≥1k\geq 1, define

Rk(D,r;𝒑)≔∑F⊆E:Λ​(V,F)r,v≥k∀v≠r∏e∈Fpe∏e∉F(1−pe).R_{k}(D,r;\bm{p})\coloneqq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}F\subseteq E:\\ {\Lambda(V,F)_{r,v}}\geq k\\ \forall v\neq r\end{subarray}}\prod_{e\in F}p_{e}\prod_{e\notin F}(1-p_{e}).

The paths to different target vertices need not be mutually disjoint. In particular, k=1k=1 asks that the root reach every vertex. Reversing the arcs gives the all-to-root version.

Corollary C.12.

There is an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for Rk​(D,r,𝐩)R_{k}(D,r;\bm{p}), even when kk is part of the input in binary.

Proof.

We express the event as containment of a common basis and apply Lemma C.4. Delete loops and arcs entering rr, which do not affect this event. The one-vertex case has probability one. Otherwise put q≔k⁡(|V|−1)q\coloneqq k(|V|-1), and return zero if q>|E|q>|E|. Let ℳ{\mathcal{M}} be the union of kk copies of the graphic matroid of the underlying undirected multigraph. A set is independent in ℳ{\mathcal{M}} exactly when it can be partitioned into kk forests after ignoring the arc directions. Let 𝒩{\mathcal{N}} be the partition matroid allowing at most kk arcs entering each nonroot vertex. The polynomial-time matroid-union algorithm [BF10, Section 4.1] gives an independence oracle for ℳ{\mathcal{M}}, using cycle detection to test independence in each graphic matroid. For 𝒩{\mathcal{N}}, we count the queried arcs entering each nonroot vertex and check that every count is at most kk. If either rank is less than qq, the event is impossible; otherwise both ranks equal qq.

For each F⊆EF\subseteq E, we have

Λ(V,F)r,v≥kfor all v≠r⟺F contains a common basis of ℳ,𝒩.\Lambda(V,F)_{r,v}\geq k\ \text{for all }v\neq r\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\text{ contains a common basis of }{\mathcal{M}},{\mathcal{N}}.

Edmonds’s arborescence-packing theorem [Edm73] (see also [BF10, Theorem 1.1]) equates the left-hand condition with the existence in FF of kk arc-disjoint spanning out-arborescences rooted at rr, that is, directed spanning trees in which rr reaches every vertex. The standard matroid representation [BF10, Section 4.1] identifies the unions of kk such arborescences with the common bases of ℳ,𝒩{\mathcal{M}},{\mathcal{N}}.

Applying Lemma C.4 now gives the claimed approximation. The preliminary bound k⁡(|V|−1)≤|E|k(|V|-1)\leq|E| ensures polynomial size even when kk is given in binary. ∎

C.5 Mixed discriminants and determinantal point processes

The matrices defining the counting problems below are rational and positive semidefinite. For a matrix LL indexed by 𝒰{\mathcal{U}}, write L⁡[S]L[S] for its principal submatrix on SS, with the convention detL⁡[∅]=1\det L[\varnothing]=1. The determinantal point process with matrix LL assigns probability detL⁡[S]/det(I+L)\det L[S]/\det(I+L) to S⊆𝒰S\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}.

Corollary C.13.

There is an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for each of the following quantities:

  1. (a)

    For a rational positive semidefinite matrix LL indexed by 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} and a matroid ℳ{\mathcal{M}} on 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} given by an independence oracle,

    Zℳ​(L)≔∑S∈ℬ⁡(ℳ)detL⁡[S].Z_{{\mathcal{M}}}(L)\coloneqq\sum_{S\in{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{M}})}\det L[S].
  2. (b)

    For rational positive semidefinite matrices A,BA,B indexed by the same set 𝒰{\mathcal{U}},

    Z⁡(A,B)≔∑S⊆𝒰detA⁡[S]​detB⁡[S].Z(A,B)\coloneqq\sum_{S\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}}\det A[S]\det B[S].
  3. (c)

    For rational positive semidefinite d×dd\times d matrices A1,…,AdA_{1},\ldots,A_{d}, the mixed discriminant

    Δ(A1,…,Ad)≔[x1⋯xd]det(∑i=1dxiAi).\Delta(A_{1},\ldots,A_{d})\coloneqq[x_{1}\cdots x_{d}]\det\left(\sum_{i=1}^{d}x_{i}A_{i}\right).

Before proving Corollary C.13, we recall the following standard determinant identity.

Proposition C.14 (Cauchy–Binet formula [Sta13, Theorem 9.4]).

Let A∈ℝd×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n} and B∈ℝn×dB\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}, where n≥dn\geq d. For S⊆[n]S\subseteq[n] with |S|=d|S|=d, let A:,SA_{:,S} be the d×dd\times d matrix formed by the columns of AA indexed by SS, and let BS,:B_{S,:} be the d×dd\times d matrix formed by the rows of BB indexed by SS, both in increasing order. Then

det(AB)=∑S⊆[n]|S|=ddet(A:,S)det(BS,:).\det(AB)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq[n]\\ |S|=d\end{subarray}}\det(A_{:,S})\det(B_{S,:}).
Proof of Corollary C.13.

The first two reductions use the principal-minor identities (see [BBL09, Section 3.2])

pL​(𝒙)≔∑SdetL⁡[S]​𝒙S\displaystyle p_{L}(\bm{x})\coloneqq\sum_{S}\det L[S]\bm{x}^{S} =det(I+L​D𝒙)=det(I+L1/2​D𝒙​L1/2),\displaystyle={\det(I+LD_{\bm{x}})=}\det(I+L^{1/2}D_{\bm{x}}L^{1/2}),
qL​(𝒙)≔∑TdetL⁡[𝒰∖T]​𝒙T\displaystyle q_{L}(\bm{x})\coloneqq\sum_{T}\det L[{\mathcal{U}}\setminus T]\bm{x}^{T} =det(L+D𝒙),\displaystyle=\det(L+D_{\bm{x}}),

where D𝒙≔diag⁡(𝒙)D_{\bm{x}}\coloneqq\operatorname{diag}(\bm{x}). To obtain the first expansion, use multilinearity of the determinant in its columns: choosing columns from L​D𝒙LD_{\bm{x}} at indices in SS and from II elsewhere contributes detL⁡[S]​𝒙S\det L[S]\bm{x}^{S}. Similarly, choosing columns from D𝒙D_{\bm{x}} at indices in TT and from LL elsewhere contributes detL⁡[𝒰∖T]​𝒙T\det L[{\mathcal{U}}\setminus T]\bm{x}^{T}, giving the second expansion. The last equality for pLp_{L} follows from Sylvester’s identity det(I+A​B)=det(I+B​A)\det(I+AB)=\det(I+BA).

Both polynomials are log-concave. Indeed, the matrices I+L1/2​D𝒙​L1/2I+L^{1/2}D_{\bm{x}}L^{1/2} and L+D𝒙L+D_{\bm{x}} are affine functions of 𝒙\bm{x} and positive definite when 𝒙>𝟎\bm{x}>\mathbf{0}, even if LL is singular. The function X↦logdetXX\mapsto\log\det X is concave on positive definite matrices [BV04, Section 3.1.5, p. 74]. Composing a concave function with an affine map preserves concavity, so log⁡pL​(𝒙)\log p_{L}(\bm{x}) and log⁡qL​(𝒙)\log q_{L}(\bm{x}) are concave.

For Item 1, apply Lemma C.1 with ω⁡(S)≔detL⁡[S]\omega(S)\coloneqq\det L[S], initialized at ∅\varnothing.

For Item 2, use

Z⁡(A,B)=[𝒙𝒰]​(pA​(𝒙)​qB​(𝒙))Z(A,B)=[\bm{x}^{{\mathcal{U}}}]\bigl(p_{A}(\bm{x})q_{B}(\bm{x})\bigr)

and apply Theorem 1.6, with initial sets ∅\varnothing and 𝒰{\mathcal{U}}. This is the normalizing constant for the product of two DPPs [OM21]; dividing by det(I+A)​det(I+B)\det(I+A)\det(I+B) gives their agreement probability.

For Item 3, use the partition-matroid reduction of [Cel+17, Section 4.1]. Here EiE_{i} indexes the rank-one terms of AiA_{i}; we take these index sets to be pairwise disjoint. If Ei=∅E_{i}=\varnothing for some ii, then Ai=0A_{i}=0 and Δ=0\Delta=0. Otherwise put E≔⋃i=1dEiE\coloneqq\bigcup_{i=1}^{d}E_{i}, let VV have columns 𝒗e\bm{v}_{e}, and let ℳ{\mathcal{M}} be the partition matroid on EE whose bases contain exactly one element from each EiE_{i}. Thus a basis selects one rank-one term from each matrix AiA_{i}.

Then ∑i=1dxi​Ai=V​D​(𝒙)​V𝖳\sum_{i=1}^{d}x_{i}A_{i}=VD(\bm{x})V^{\mathsf{T}}. For S⊆ES\subseteq E with |S|=d|S|=d, write VSV_{S} for the d×dd\times d matrix formed by the columns of VV indexed by SS. Applying Proposition C.14 with A=V​D​(𝒙)A=VD(\bm{x}) and B=V𝖳B=V^{\mathsf{T}} gives

det(∑i=1dxi​Ai)=∑S⊆E|S|=ddet(VS)2​(∏e∈Sce)​∏i=1dxi|S∩Ei|.\det\left(\sum_{i=1}^{d}x_{i}A_{i}\right)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq E\\ |S|=d\end{subarray}}\det(V_{S})^{2}\left(\prod_{e\in S}c_{e}\right)\prod_{i=1}^{d}x_{i}^{|S\cap E_{i}|}.

Here det(VS)2=det(VS𝖳​VS)=det((V𝖳​V)​[S])\det(V_{S})^{2}=\det(V_{S}^{\mathsf{T}}V_{S})=\det((V^{\mathsf{T}}V)[S]). The monomial ∏i=1dxi|S∩Ei|\prod_{i=1}^{d}x_{i}^{|S\cap E_{i}|} equals x1⋯xdx_{1}\cdots x_{d} exactly when SS contains one element of each EiE_{i}, that is, when SS is a basis of ℳ{\mathcal{M}}. Extracting this coefficient therefore gives

Δ⁡(A1,…,Ad)=∑S∈ℬ⁡(ℳ)det((V𝖳​V)​[S])​∏e∈Sce.\Delta(A_{1},\ldots,A_{d})=\sum_{S\in{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{M}})}\det((V^{\mathsf{T}}V)[S])\prod_{e\in S}c_{e}.

Apply Lemma C.1 to this determinant weight: the factors cec_{e} are external fields, so log-concavity persists, and ∅\varnothing is again an initial set. All coefficient queries and decompositions use rational arithmetic of polynomial bit length. The square roots in pLp_{L} serve only to prove log-concavity. ∎

C.6 The six-vertex model

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a loopless 44-regular multigraph, with the four incident edges at each vertex labeled 1,2,3,41,2,3,4. We consider Eulerian orientations DD of the edges, meaning that exactly two edges are directed into each vertex. Let Iv​(D)⊆{1,2,3,4}I_{v}(D)\subseteq\{1,2,3,4\} be the labels of the two edges entering vv. The weight wv​(I)w_{v}(I) assigned to an incoming pair II is ava_{v} for I={1,2}I=\{1,2\} or {3,4}\{3,4\}, bvb_{v} for I={1,3}I=\{1,3\} or {2,4}\{2,4\}, and cvc_{v} for I={1,4}I=\{1,4\} or {2,3}\{2,3\}. The partition function is

∑D​ an Eulerianorientation of ​G∏v∈V⁡(G)wv​(Iv​(D)).\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}D\text{ an Eulerian}\\ \text{orientation of }G\end{subarray}}\prod_{v\in V(G)}w_{v}(I_{v}(D)).

These are joint weights for the incoming pair; no factorization into individual edge-direction weights is assumed [CLL19].

Remark C.15.

An Eulerian orientation specifies the direction of each edge, with equal indegree and outdegree at every vertex. If GG is connected, this guarantees the existence of a directed Euler tour; otherwise, each connected component admits one. The six-vertex partition function includes one term per orientation, regardless of how many directed Euler tours it admits.

The Euler-tour weights in Section C.2 depend on the whole pairing of the four incident half-edges, whereas the six-vertex weights depend only on the incoming pair. For example, if edges 1,21,2 enter a vertex and 3,43,4 leave it, the compatible local pairings

{{1,3},{2,4}}and{{1,4},{2,3}}\bigl\{\{1,3\},\{2,4\}\bigr\}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bigl\{\{1,4\},\{2,3\}\bigr\}

may receive different transition weights in Section C.2. Both have incoming pair {1,2}\{1,2\} under this orientation, so the six-vertex weight is ava_{v} in either case.

Corollary C.16.

For every loopless 44-regular multigraph GG, there is an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for its six-vertex partition function when the local pair weights av,bv,cva_{v},b_{v},c_{v} are nonnegative rationals satisfying

av≤bv+cv,bv≤av+cv,cv≤av+bvfor every ​v∈V⁡(G).a_{v}\leq b_{v}+c_{v},\qquad b_{v}\leq a_{v}+c_{v},\qquad c_{v}\leq a_{v}+b_{v}\quad\text{for every }v\in V(G).
Proof.

Use the incidences 𝒰≔{(v,e):v∈e}{\mathcal{U}}\coloneqq\{(v,e):v\in e\} as the ground set, and let ℳ{\mathcal{M}} be the partition matroid choosing one incidence of each edge. Assign to S⊆𝒰S\subseteq{\mathcal{U}} the product of its local incoming-pair weights, with weight zero unless SS has two incidences at every vertex. Then bases of ℳ{\mathcal{M}} with positive weight are exactly the six-vertex orientations, with their prescribed weights. We apply Lemma C.1 to this weight.

Its generating polynomial is ∏vqv\prod_{v}q_{v}, where

qv​(𝒙)=av​(x1​x2+x3​x4)+bv​(x1​x3+x2​x4)+cv​(x1​x4+x2​x3).q_{v}(\bm{x})=a_{v}(x_{1}x_{2}+x_{3}x_{4})+b_{v}(x_{1}x_{3}+x_{2}x_{4})+c_{v}(x_{1}x_{4}+x_{2}x_{3}).

An all-zero local triple gives partition function zero. Otherwise the Hessian of qvq_{v} has eigenvalues av+bv+cva_{v}+b_{v}+c_{v}, av−bv−cva_{v}-b_{v}-c_{v}, −av+bv−cv-a_{v}+b_{v}-c_{v}, and −av−bv+cv-a_{v}-b_{v}+c_{v}. The triangle inequalities leave at most one positive eigenvalue, which is the log-concavity criterion for a nonzero homogeneous quadratic with nonnegative coefficients [BH20, Section 2]. Hence the product is log-concave. Choosing any positive incoming pair at each vertex gives an initial set, and coefficient queries are products of the given local weights. Thus Lemma C.1 applies, including equality in the triangle inequalities. ∎

The earlier 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} of [CLL19] requires the stronger inequalities av2≤bv2+cv2a_{v}^{2}\leq b_{v}^{2}+c_{v}^{2} and their permutations.

C.7 Bipartite Quantum Max-Cut and the EPR model

The Pauli matrices are

X≔(0110),Y≔(0−ii0),Z≔(100−1),X\coloneqq\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Y\coloneqq\begin{pmatrix}0&-\mathrm{i}\\ \mathrm{i}&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Z\coloneqq\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&-1\end{pmatrix},

with i2=−1\mathrm{i}^{2}=-1. A ket |𝝍⟩|\bm{\psi}\rangle denotes a column vector, and the bra ⟨𝝍|\langle\bm{\psi}| is its conjugate transpose. For a,b∈{0,1}a,b\in\{0,1\}, set

|0⟩≔(10),|1⟩≔(01),|a​b⟩≔|a⟩⊗|b⟩,|0\rangle\coloneqq\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 0\end{pmatrix},\qquad|1\rangle\coloneqq\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 1\end{pmatrix},\qquad|ab\rangle\coloneqq|a\rangle\otimes|b\rangle,

where ⊗\otimes denotes the tensor product. Thus

|𝚽+⟩≔|00⟩+|11⟩2=12​(1001),|\bm{\Phi}^{+}\rangle\coloneqq\frac{|00\rangle+|11\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 0\\ 0\\ 1\end{pmatrix},

and the local matrix

P≔|𝚽+⟩​⟨𝚽+|∈ℂ4×4P\coloneqq|\bm{\Phi}^{+}\rangle\langle\bm{\Phi}^{+}|\in\mathbb{C}^{4\times 4}

is the orthogonal projector onto its span.

For a vertex set V={1,…,n}V=\{1,\ldots,n\}, the operators act on ⨂v=1nℂ2\bigotimes_{v=1}^{n}\mathbb{C}^{2}, with one factor for each vertex. The subscript uu means that a matrix acts on the factor at vertex uu and as the identity on every other factor; explicitly,

Xu≔I2⊗(u−1)⊗X⊗I2⊗(n−u),X_{u}\coloneqq I_{2}^{\otimes(u-1)}\otimes X\otimes I_{2}^{\otimes(n-u)},

where I2I_{2} is the 2×22\times 2 identity matrix and zero tensor powers are omitted. Define Yu,ZuY_{u},Z_{u} similarly, and let I=I2⊗nI=I_{2}^{\otimes n}. Thus Xu​XvX_{u}X_{v} applies XX at both vertices u,vu,v. For example, when n=3n=3, X1​X3=X⊗I2⊗XX_{1}X_{3}=X\otimes I_{2}\otimes X.

For a∈{0,1}a\in\{0,1\}, the ket |a⟩u|a\rangle_{u} denotes |a⟩|a\rangle in the copy of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} at vertex uu. For u<vu<v, the notation

|𝚽+⟩u​v≔|0⟩u⊗|0⟩v+|1⟩u⊗|1⟩v2|\bm{\Phi}^{+}\rangle_{uv}\coloneqq\frac{|0\rangle_{u}\otimes|0\rangle_{v}+|1\rangle_{u}\otimes|1\rangle_{v}}{\sqrt{2}}

denotes a vector on these two vertex factors. Let Pu​v∈ℂ2n×2nP_{uv}\in\mathbb{C}^{2^{n}\times 2^{n}} act as PP on the factors at u,vu,v and as the identity on all remaining factors. For example, when n=3n=3,

P12=P⊗I2,P23=I2⊗P.P_{12}=P\otimes I_{2},\qquad P_{23}=I_{2}\otimes P.

For a loopless graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) with nonnegative rational edge weights wew_{e}, let

Qcut≔∑e=u​vwe​I−Xu​Xv−Yu​Yv−Zu​Zv4,QEPR≔∑e=u​vwe​Pu​v.Q_{\mathrm{cut}}\coloneqq\sum_{e=uv}w_{e}\frac{I-X_{u}X_{v}-Y_{u}Y_{v}-Z_{u}Z_{v}}{4},\qquad Q_{\mathrm{EPR}}\coloneqq\sum_{e=uv}w_{e}{P_{uv}}.

For a Hermitian matrix MM and β>0\beta>0, define its partition function by

Zβ​(M)≔Tr⁡eβ​M.Z_{\beta}(M)\coloneqq\operatorname{Tr}\mathrm{e}^{\beta M}.

We consider approximating this quantity and the largest eigenvalue of MM. For background on the two problems, see [TSC24, MS26]. Write W≔∑eweW\coloneqq\sum_{e}w_{e}.

Corollary C.17.

Given a loopless graph GG with nonnegative rational edge weights, there is an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for λmax​(QEPR)\lambda_{\max}(Q_{\mathrm{EPR}}). For rational β>0\beta>0, there is also an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for Zβ​(QEPR)Z_{\beta}(Q_{\mathrm{EPR}}) when β​W\beta W is polynomially bounded in the input length. More precisely, a randomized algorithm approximates this partition function with relative error at most ε\varepsilon in time polynomial in the input length, β​W\beta W, and ε−1\varepsilon^{-1}.

If GG is bipartite, the same claims hold for λmax​(Qcut)\lambda_{\max}(Q_{\mathrm{cut}}) and Zβ​(Qcut)Z_{\beta}(Q_{\mathrm{cut}}).

Proof.

We first prove the EPR claims by reducing them to the six-vertex partition function in Section C.6. We then deduce the Quantum Max-Cut claims by an explicit change of basis.

The EPR matrix: eigenvalue estimation.

Fix 0<ε≤10<\varepsilon\leq 1. If W=0W=0, the largest eigenvalue is zero and Zβ​(QEPR)=2nZ_{\beta}(Q_{\mathrm{EPR}})=2^{n}. Otherwise delete zero-weight edges, put pe≔we/Wp_{e}\coloneqq w_{e}/W, and set Q≔QEPR/W=∑e=u​vpe​Pu​vQ\coloneqq Q_{\mathrm{EPR}}/W=\sum_{e=uv}p_{e}P_{uv}. Each Pu​vP_{uv} is an orthogonal projector, and ∑epe=1\sum_{e}p_{e}=1, so 0⪯Q⪯I0\preceq Q\preceq I. For the unit vector |𝝃⟩=|0⟩⊗n|\bm{\xi}\rangle=|0\rangle^{\otimes n}, we have ⟨𝝃|Pu​v|𝝃⟩=1/2\langle\bm{\xi}|P_{uv}|\bm{\xi}\rangle=1/2 for every edge u​vuv. Consequently,

12=12​∑epe=⟨𝝃|Q|𝝃⟩≤λmax​(Q)≤1.\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{e}p_{e}=\langle\bm{\xi}|Q|\bm{\xi}\rangle\leq\lambda_{\max}(Q)\leq 1.

For β>0\beta>0, let λ1=λmax​(Q)≥⋯≥λ2n\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{\max}(Q)\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{2^{n}} be the eigenvalues of QQ. The eigenvalues of eβ​Q\mathrm{e}^{\beta Q} are eβ​λi\mathrm{e}^{\beta\lambda_{i}}, so

eβ​λ1≤Zβ​(Q)=∑i=12neβ​λi≤2n​eβ​λ1.\mathrm{e}^{\beta\lambda_{1}}\leq Z_{\beta}(Q)=\sum_{i=1}^{2^{n}}\mathrm{e}^{\beta\lambda_{i}}\leq 2^{n}\mathrm{e}^{\beta\lambda_{1}}.

The lower bound keeps only the i=1i=1 term; the upper bound replaces each term by eβ​λ1\mathrm{e}^{\beta\lambda_{1}}. Taking logarithms and dividing by β\beta gives

λmax​(Q)≤log⁡Zβ​(Q)β≤λmax​(Q)+n​log⁡2β.\lambda_{\max}(Q)\leq\frac{\log{Z_{\beta}(Q)}}{\beta}\leq\lambda_{\max}(Q)+\frac{n\log 2}{\beta}.

Thus β≔8​(n+1)/ε\beta\coloneqq 8(n+1)/\varepsilon and an estimate of Zβ​(Q)Z_{\beta}(Q) with relative error at most 1/41/4 suffice for additive error ε/4\varepsilon/4 in λmax​(Q)\lambda_{\max}(Q), including the error from evaluating the logarithm to sufficiently many bits. Since λmax​(Q)≥1/2\lambda_{\max}(Q)\geq 1/2, this gives relative error at most ε\varepsilon after multiplying by WW.

The EPR matrix: a six-vertex instance.

We next transform QQ into a matrix AA with the same eigenvalues, so that Zβ​(Q)=Tr⁡eβ​AZ_{\beta}(Q)=\operatorname{Tr}\mathrm{e}^{\beta A}, and approximate this trace using Corollary C.16. Put

K≔I2−i​X2,|𝚿+⟩≔|01⟩+|10⟩2,R≔|𝚿+⟩​⟨𝚿+|.K\coloneqq\frac{I_{2}-\mathrm{i}X}{\sqrt{2}},\qquad|\bm{\Psi}^{+}\rangle\coloneqq\frac{|01\rangle+|10\rangle}{\sqrt{2}},\qquad R\coloneqq|\bm{\Psi}^{+}\rangle\langle\bm{\Psi}^{+}|.

The matrix KK is unitary and (K⊗K)​|𝚽+⟩=−i⁡|𝚿+⟩(K\otimes K)|\bm{\Phi}^{+}\rangle=-\mathrm{i}|\bm{\Psi}^{+}\rangle. For e=u​ve=uv, let Re≔Ru​vR_{e}\coloneqq R_{uv} be the extension of RR to the full space by the same convention as Pu​vP_{uv}. Thus

A≔K⊗n​Q​(K∗)⊗n=∑epe​Re,Tr⁡eβ​A=Zβ​(Q).A\coloneqq K^{\otimes n}Q(K^{*})^{\otimes n}=\sum_{e}p_{e}R_{e},\qquad\operatorname{Tr}\mathrm{e}^{\beta A}=Z_{\beta}(Q).

Here K∗K^{*} is the conjugate transpose of KK.

Fix rational β>0\beta>0 and a target relative error 0<η≤10<\eta\leq 1. Set m≔⌈max⁡{1,4​β,20​β2/η}⌉m\coloneqq\lceil\max\{1,4\beta,20\beta^{2}/\eta\}\rceil and δ≔β/m\delta\coloneqq\beta/m. Label the edges 1,…,|E|1,\ldots,|E| in any order, and multiply their matrices in this order and then in reverse order:

B≔(∏e=1|E|(I+δ​pe2​Re))​(∏e=|E|1(I+δ​pe2​Re)).B\coloneqq\left(\prod_{e=1}^{|E|}\left(I+\frac{\delta p_{e}}{2}{R_{e}}\right)\right)\left(\prod_{e=|E|}^{1}\left(I+\frac{\delta p_{e}}{2}{R_{e}}\right)\right).

We claim the following bound:

B≻0,‖log⁡B−δ​A‖≤5​δ2,B\succ 0,\qquad\|\log B-\delta A\|\leq 5\delta^{2}, (32)

where ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| denotes the operator norm. The matrix logarithm log⁡B\log B is obtained by applying the scalar logarithm to the positive eigenvalues of BB in an orthonormal eigenbasis. The intuition comes from the scalar approximation log⁡(1+δ​x)−δ​x=O⁡(δ2​x2)\log(1+\delta x)-\delta x=O(\delta^{2}x^{2}) as δ​x→0\delta x\to 0: the linear terms sum to δ​A\delta A, and we expect an error quadratic in δ\delta. We will verify Eq. 32 at the end of the proof, accounting for the order of the matrix factors. Assuming this estimate, our choice of mm gives

‖m​log⁡B−β​A‖≤5​m​δ2=5​β2m≤η4.\|m\log B-\beta A\|\leq 5m\delta^{2}=\frac{5\beta^{2}}{m}\leq\frac{\eta}{4}.

Let μ1≥⋯≥μ2n\mu_{1}\geq\cdots\geq\mu_{2^{n}} and ν1≥⋯≥ν2n\nu_{1}\geq\cdots\geq\nu_{2^{n}} be the eigenvalues of m​log⁡Bm\log B and β​A\beta A, respectively. These matrices are Hermitian, so the norm bound implies

β​A−η4​I⪯m​log⁡B⪯β​A+η4​I.\beta A-\frac{\eta}{4}I\preceq m\log B\preceq\beta A+\frac{\eta}{4}I.

The min–max principle for eigenvalues therefore gives

νi−η4≤μi≤νi+η4(1≤i≤2n).\nu_{i}-\frac{\eta}{4}\leq\mu_{i}\leq\nu_{i}+\frac{\eta}{4}\qquad(1\leq i\leq 2^{n}).

Exponentiating these scalar inequalities and summing over ii gives

e−η/4∑ieνi≤∑ieμi≤eη/4∑ieνi.\mathrm{e}^{-\eta/4}\sum_{i}\mathrm{e}^{\nu_{i}}\leq\sum_{i}\mathrm{e}^{\mu_{i}}\leq\mathrm{e}^{\eta/4}\sum_{i}\mathrm{e}^{\nu_{i}}.

Since

∑ieμi=Tr⁡em​log⁡B=Tr⁡(Bm),∑ieνi=Tr⁡eβ​A=Zβ​(Q),\sum_{i}\mathrm{e}^{\mu_{i}}=\operatorname{Tr}\mathrm{e}^{m\log B}=\operatorname{Tr}(B^{m}),\qquad\sum_{i}\mathrm{e}^{\nu_{i}}=\operatorname{Tr}\mathrm{e}^{\beta A}=Z_{\beta}(Q),

we obtain

e−η/4Zβ(Q)≤Tr(Bm)≤eη/4Zβ(Q).\mathrm{e}^{-\eta/4}Z_{\beta}(Q)\leq\operatorname{Tr}(B^{m})\leq\mathrm{e}^{\eta/4}Z_{\beta}(Q).

For each edge ee, write se≔δ​pe/2s_{e}\coloneqq\delta p_{e}/2 and Fe≔I+se​ReF_{e}\coloneqq I+s_{e}R_{e} for its matrix in BB. Writing I4I_{4} for the 4×44\times 4 identity matrix, the local table of FeF_{e} in row and column order 00,01,10,1100,01,10,11 is

I4+se​R=(100001+se/2se/200se/21+se/200001).{I_{4}+s_{e}R}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0&0\\ 0&1+s_{e}/2&s_{e}/2&0\\ 0&s_{e}/2&1+s_{e}/2&0\\ 0&0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.

The product BmB^{m} uses each edge 2​m2m times. Each use gives one node carrying the displayed 4×44\times 4 table. At a node for e=u​ve=uv, two edge ends specify the first and second bits of the row label, corresponding to u,vu,v; another two specify the first and second bits of the column label. For each original vertex uu, connect its column end at each node to its row end at the next node involving uu, following the order in BmB^{m} and connecting the last such node back to the first. This defines the tensor network.

A configuration σ\sigma assigns a bit 00 or 11 to every network edge. The four incident bits select one entry at each node tt; call this entry its weight wt​(σ)w_{t}(\sigma). The partition function sums the product of node weights over all configurations:

ZTN≔∑σ∏nodes ​twt​(σ).Z_{\mathrm{TN}}\coloneqq\sum_{\sigma}\prod_{\text{nodes }t}w_{t}(\sigma).

Expanding the trace sums the same products of node weights. Matrices for edges not incident to uu leave its bit unchanged, while each isolated vertex of GG contributes two choices for its bit. Hence, if GG has hh isolated vertices,

Tr⁡(Bm)=2h​ZTN.\operatorname{Tr}(B^{m})=2^{h}Z_{\mathrm{TN}}.

This tensor network has the same partition function as a six-vertex model; see Fig. 3 for an illustrated example.

There are 2​m​|E|2m|E| nodes in the network, with rational weights of polynomial encoding length. An estimate of Tr⁡(Bm)\operatorname{Tr}(B^{m}) with relative error at most η/4\eta/4, obtained from Corollary C.16, together with the displayed trace bound, gives an estimate of Zβ​(Q)Z_{\beta}(Q) with relative error at most η\eta: indeed, (1+η/4)​eη/4≤1+η(1+\eta/4)\mathrm{e}^{\eta/4}\leq 1+\eta and (1−η/4)e−η/4≥1−η(1-\eta/4)\mathrm{e}^{-\eta/4}\geq 1-\eta. The running time is polynomial in the input length, β\beta, and η−1\eta^{-1}. Since

Zβ​(QEPR)=Zβ​W​(Q),Z_{\beta}(Q_{\mathrm{EPR}})=Z_{\beta W}(Q),

this proves the partition-function claim with running time polynomial in the input length, β​W\beta W, and η−1\eta^{-1}. Taking η=1/4\eta=1/4 and β=8​(n+1)/ε\beta=8(n+1)/\varepsilon for the normalized matrix QQ also completes the largest-eigenvalue approximation described above.

The Quantum Max-Cut matrix.

Now suppose GG is bipartite, with V=V0⊔V1V=V_{0}\sqcup V_{1}. We show that QcutQ_{\mathrm{cut}} has the same eigenvalues as QEPRQ_{\mathrm{EPR}} on the same weighted graph. Define the unitary matrix

U≔⨂v∈VUv,Uv≔{I2,v∈V0,Y,v∈V1.U\coloneqq\bigotimes_{v\in V}U_{v},\qquad U_{v}\coloneqq\begin{cases}I_{2},&v\in V_{0},\\ Y,&v\in V_{1}.\end{cases}

Since Y​X​Y=−XYXY=-X, Y​Y​Y=YYYY=Y, and Y​Z​Y=−ZYZY=-Z, conjugation by UU gives

U​Qcut​U∗=∑e=u​vwe​I+Xu​Xv−Yu​Yv+Zu​Zv4=∑e=u​vwe​Pu​v=QEPR.UQ_{\mathrm{cut}}U^{*}=\sum_{e=uv}w_{e}\frac{I+X_{u}X_{v}-Y_{u}Y_{v}+Z_{u}Z_{v}}{4}=\sum_{e=uv}w_{e}P_{uv}=Q_{\mathrm{EPR}}.

The second equality follows by multiplying the displayed Pauli matrices. Therefore

λmax​(Qcut)=λmax​(QEPR),Zβ​(Qcut)=Zβ​(QEPR).\lambda_{\max}(Q_{\mathrm{cut}})=\lambda_{\max}(Q_{\mathrm{EPR}}),\qquad Z_{\beta}(Q_{\mathrm{cut}})=Z_{\beta}(Q_{\mathrm{EPR}}).

The EPR algorithms prove both remaining claims.

Verification of Eq. 32.

We return to the EPR product BB on an arbitrary graph. Let FF be the first parenthesized product in the definition of BB. Each factor is Hermitian and positive definite, with eigenvalues 11 and 1+δ​pe/21+\delta p_{e}/2. Thus FF is invertible, the reverse product is F∗F^{*}, and B=F​F∗≻0B=FF^{*}\succ 0.

To bound B−I−δ​AB-I-\delta A, list the matrices δ​pe​Re/2\delta p_{e}R_{e}/2 in their order of occurrence in BB as H1,…,HNH_{1},\ldots,H_{N}, where N=2​|E|N=2|E|, and put hj≔‖Hj‖h_{j}\coloneqq\|H_{j}\|. Each edge occurs twice, so

B=∏j=1N(I+Hj),∑j=1NHj=δ​A,∑j=1Nhj=δ​∑epe=δ.B=\prod_{j=1}^{N}(I+H_{j}),\qquad\sum_{j=1}^{N}H_{j}=\delta A,\qquad\sum_{j=1}^{N}h_{j}=\delta\sum_{e}p_{e}=\delta.

Expand the product by choosing either II or HjH_{j} at each position, keeping the chosen matrices in their original order. The term with no chosen HjH_{j} is II, while the terms with exactly one chosen HjH_{j} sum to ∑jHj=δ​A\sum_{j}H_{j}=\delta A. Subtracting these terms therefore leaves

B−I−δA=∑k=2N∑1≤i1<⋯<ik≤NHi1⋯Hik.B-I-\delta A=\sum_{k=2}^{N}\;\sum_{1\leq i_{1}<\cdots<i_{k}\leq N}H_{i_{1}}\cdots H_{i_{k}}.

The norm of a matrix product is at most the product of the norms of its matrices:

∥Hi1⋯Hik∥≤∥Hi1∥⋯∥Hik∥=hi1⋯hik.\|H_{i_{1}}\cdots H_{i_{k}}\|\leq\|H_{i_{1}}\|\cdots\|H_{i_{k}}\|=h_{i_{1}}\cdots h_{i_{k}}.

Applying the triangle inequality to the displayed remainder now yields

‖B−I−δ​A‖\displaystyle\|B-I-\delta A\| ≤∑k=2N∑1≤i1<⋯<ik≤Nhi1⋯hik\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=2}^{N}\;\sum_{1\leq i_{1}<\cdots<i_{k}\leq N}h_{i_{1}}\cdots h_{i_{k}}
=∏j=1N(1+hj)−1−∑j=1Nhj\displaystyle=\prod_{j=1}^{N}(1+h_{j})-1-\sum_{j=1}^{N}h_{j}
≤eδ−1−δ.\displaystyle\leq\mathrm{e}^{\delta}-1-\delta.

The equality uses the scalar expansion of ∏j(1+hj)\prod_{j}(1+h_{j}), with its constant term 11 and linear terms ∑jhj\sum_{j}h_{j} removed. The last inequality uses 1+hj≤ehj1+h_{j}\leq\mathrm{e}^{h_{j}} and ∑jhj=δ\sum_{j}h_{j}=\delta. Similarly, subtracting only II keeps all terms with k≥1k\geq 1, so

‖B−I‖\displaystyle\|B-I\| ≤∑k=1N∑1≤i1<⋯<ik≤Nhi1⋯hik\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=1}^{N}\;\sum_{1\leq i_{1}<\cdots<i_{k}\leq N}h_{i_{1}}\cdots h_{i_{k}}
=∏j=1N(1+hj)−1≤eδ−1.\displaystyle=\prod_{j=1}^{N}(1+h_{j})-1\leq\mathrm{e}^{\delta}-1.

Set D≔B−ID\coloneqq B-I. Since δ≤1/4\delta\leq 1/4, the scalar exponential series gives

eδ−1≤δ1−δ≤2​δ,eδ−1−δ≤δ22​(1−δ)≤δ2.\mathrm{e}^{\delta}-1\leq\frac{\delta}{1-\delta}\leq 2\delta,\qquad\mathrm{e}^{\delta}-1-\delta\leq\frac{\delta^{2}}{2(1-\delta)}\leq\delta^{2}.

Hence ‖D‖≤2​δ≤1/2\|D\|\leq 2\delta\leq 1/2 and ‖D−δ​A‖≤δ2\|D-\delta A\|\leq\delta^{2}. Applying the scalar series for log⁡(1+x)\log(1+x) in an orthonormal eigenbasis of DD gives the absolutely convergent matrix series

log⁡B\displaystyle\log B =D+∑k=2∞(−1)k+1k​Dk,\displaystyle=D+\sum_{k=2}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{k+1}}{k}D^{k},
‖log⁡B−D‖\displaystyle\|\log B-D\| ≤∑k=2∞‖D‖kk≤‖D‖22​(1−‖D‖)≤4​δ2.\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=2}^{\infty}\frac{\|D\|^{k}}{k}\leq\frac{\|D\|^{2}}{2(1-\|D\|)}\leq 4\delta^{2}.

Combining the two remainder bounds proves

‖log⁡B−δ​A‖≤‖log⁡B−D‖+|D−δ​A|≤5​δ2.\|\log B-\delta A\|\leq\|\log B-D\|+\|D-\delta A\|\leq 5\delta^{2}.

This proves Eq. 32 and completes the proof.
