C.8 Matroid-congestion Gibbs distributions

Let p,q≥1p,q\geq 1. There are pp labeled players, each choosing a basis BiB_{i} of a matroid ℳi{\mathcal{M}}_{i} on the same ground set EE of size qq, given by an independence oracle. A profile B=(B1,…,Bp)B=(B_{1},\ldots,B_{p}) records all players’ choices. The load of an element e∈Ee\in E is the number of bases containing it, ℓe​(B)≔|{i:e∈Bi}|\ell_{e}(B)\coloneqq|\{i:e\in B_{i}\}|. For each element, supply a table of nonnegative rational weights ae​(0),…,ae​(p)a_{e}(0),\ldots,a_{e}(p) that are positive exactly for le≤k≤uel_{e}\leq k\leq u_{e}, where 0≤le≤ue≤p0\leq l_{e}\leq u_{e}\leq p are integers. Assume these weights are log-concave: ae​(k)2≥ae​(k−1)​ae​(k+1)a_{e}(k)^{2}\geq a_{e}(k-1)a_{e}(k+1) for 1≤k<p1\leq k<p. The partition function is

Z⁡(a)≔∑Bi∈ℬ⁡(ℳi), 1≤i≤p∏e∈Eae​(ℓe​(B)).\displaystyle Z(a)\coloneqq\sum_{B_{i}\in{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{M}}_{i}),\ 1\leq i\leq p}\prod_{e\in E}a_{e}(\ell_{e}(B)). (33)

Thus a profile has positive weight exactly when le≤ℓe​(B)≤uel_{e}\leq\ell_{e}(B)\leq u_{e} for every element ee.

Corollary C.18.

For the matroids and rational log-concave tables above, there is an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for Z⁡(a)Z(a) with running time polynomial in p​qpq, the table encoding length, and ε−1\varepsilon^{-1}.

Proof.

We apply Lemma C.1 on the set 𝒰≔[p]×E{\mathcal{U}}\coloneqq[p]\times E of ordered pairs (i,e)(i,e): the first entry i∈[p]i\in[p] is a player index, and the second entry e∈Ee\in E is an element. Including (i,e)(i,e) records that player ii uses element ee. Let ℳ{\mathcal{M}} be the matroid whose bases are precisely {(i,e):1≤i≤p,e∈Bi}\{(i,e):1\leq i\leq p,\ e\in B_{i}\} as each BiB_{i} ranges over the bases of ℳi{\mathcal{M}}_{i}. Thus its rank is R≔∑i𝗋𝗄⁡(ℳi)R\coloneqq\sum_{i}{\mathsf{rk}}({\mathcal{M}}_{i}). Put Ve≔[p]×{e}V_{e}\coloneqq[p]\times\{e\} and define

ω(X)≔𝟏[|X|=R]∏eae(|X∩Ve|).\omega(X)\coloneqq\mathbf{1}[|X|=R]\prod_{e}a_{e}(|X\cap V_{e}|).

Each basis of ℳ{\mathcal{M}} specifies one profile, so Z⁡(a)=∑X∈ℬ⁡(ℳ)ω⁡(X)Z(a)=\sum_{X\in{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{M}})}\omega(X).

To show that the generating polynomial of ω\omega is log-concave, we use the following sufficient condition [BH20, Corollary 3.16 and Theorem 2.30]: for every X,YX,Y with ω⁡(X),ω⁡(Y)>0\omega(X),\omega(Y)>0 and every a∈X∖Ya\in X\setminus Y, some b∈Y∖Xb\in Y\setminus X satisfies

ω⁡(X)​ω​(Y)≤ω⁡(X−a+b)​ω​(Y+a−b).\omega(X)\omega(Y)\leq\omega(X-a+b)\omega(Y+a-b). (34)

Here X−a+bX-a+b means (X∖{a})∪{b}(X\setminus\{a\})\cup\{b\}, and similarly for Y+a−bY+a-b. The sets X,YX,Y in this condition need only have positive ω\omega-weight; they are not required to be bases of ℳ{\mathcal{M}}. For each element g∈Eg\in E, write xg=|X∩Vg|x_{g}=|X\cap V_{g}| and yg=|Y∩Vg|y_{g}=|Y\cap V_{g}|. Fix a∈Vea\in V_{e} for some element ee. If xe≤yex_{e}\leq y_{e}, the fact that a∈(X∖Y)∩Vea\in(X\setminus Y)\cap V_{e} gives

|(Y∖X)∩Ve|=ye−xe+|(X∖Y)∩Ve|≥1.|(Y\setminus X)\cap V_{e}|=y_{e}-x_{e}+|(X\setminus Y)\cap V_{e}|\geq 1.

Thus we can choose b∈(Y∖X)∩Veb\in(Y\setminus X)\cap V_{e} simply by counting; no matroid property is needed. Exchanging aa and bb leaves every load unchanged, so ω⁡(X−a+b)=ω⁡(X)\omega(X-a+b)=\omega(X) and ω⁡(Y+a−b)=ω⁡(Y)\omega(Y+a-b)=\omega(Y). Otherwise xe>yex_{e}>y_{e}. Since ∑gxg=|X|=|Y|=∑gyg\sum_{g}x_{g}=|X|=|Y|=\sum_{g}y_{g}, there must be a different element f≠ef\neq e with xf<yfx_{f}<y_{f}. Choose b∈(Y∖X)∩Vfb\in(Y\setminus X)\cap V_{f}. Since Vf=[p]×{f}V_{f}=[p]\times\{f\}, the first entry of bb is a player index and its second entry is the fixed element ff. This choice is possible because YY contains more pairs in VfV_{f} than XX. Exchanging aa and bb changes the loads at ee from (xe,ye)(x_{e},y_{e}) to (xe−1,ye+1)(x_{e}-1,y_{e}+1), and at ff from (xf,yf)(x_{f},y_{f}) to (xf+1,yf−1)(x_{f}+1,y_{f}-1). These loads stay within their allowed intervals, and the log-concavity of ae,afa_{e},a_{f} gives Eq. 34.

To find a set of positive weight, choose integers ke∈[le,ue]k_{e}\in[l_{e},u_{e}] with ∑eke=R\sum_{e}k_{e}=R and select kek_{e} elements from each VeV_{e}. Such integers exist exactly when ∑ele≤R≤∑eue\sum_{e}l_{e}\leq R\leq\sum_{e}u_{e}; otherwise Z⁡(a)=0Z(a)=0. We evaluate ω⁡(X)\omega(X) by checking |X|=R|X|=R, counting |X∩Ve||X\cap V_{e}| for each element, and multiplying the corresponding weights. The ratio of its largest to smallest positive weight satisfies

ℛω≤∏emaxle≤k≤ue⁡ae​(k)minle≤k≤ue⁡ae​(k).{\mathcal{R}}_{\omega}\leq\prod_{e}\frac{\max_{l_{e}\leq k\leq u_{e}}a_{e}(k)}{\min_{l_{e}\leq k\leq u_{e}}a_{e}(k)}.

Thus Lemma C.1 applies. ∎

Weights specified by costs.

For the same matroids and integers le,uel_{e},u_{e} as in Corollary C.18, suppose we are given a rational β≥0\beta\geq 0 and rational costs ce​(1)≤⋯≤ce​(p)c_{e}(1)\leq\cdots\leq c_{e}(p), where ce​(k)c_{e}(k) is the cost to each player using element ee at load kk. Define the tables by

ae​(k)≔{exp(−β∑j=1kce(j)),le≤k≤ue,0,otherwise,a_{e}(k)\coloneqq\begin{cases}\exp\bigl(-\beta\sum_{j=1}^{k}c_{e}(j)\bigr),&l_{e}\leq k\leq u_{e},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}

with the empty sum equal to zero. We use the same partition function Z⁡(a)Z(a) as in Eq. 33. When Z⁡(a)>0Z(a)>0, the Gibbs distribution assigns probability ∏eae​(ℓe​(B))/Z⁡(a)\prod_{e}a_{e}(\ell_{e}(B))/Z(a) to profile BB. When le=0l_{e}=0 and ue=pu_{e}=p for every ee, sampling from this distribution is the question posed in [Kle23, Section 1.3].

If each real weight can be evaluated exactly in one operation, this is already an application of the proof of Corollary C.18: the ratios ae​(k)/ae​(k−1)=e−β​ce​(k)a_{e}(k)/a_{e}(k-1)=e^{-\beta c_{e}(k)}, for le<k≤uel_{e}<k\leq u_{e}, are nonincreasing in kk, so the tables are log-concave. Sampling follows by using approximate counts to make the players’ choices one element at a time. The next corollary handles the fact that these weights need not be rational: we approximate them by rational log-concave tables and control the resulting error. To state the running time, put

Λ≔∑elog⁡maxle≤k≤ue⁡ae​(k)minle≤k≤ue⁡ae​(k).\Lambda\coloneqq\sum_{e}\log\frac{\max_{l_{e}\leq k\leq u_{e}}a_{e}(k)}{\min_{l_{e}\leq k\leq u_{e}}a_{e}(k)}.

This value is rational and can be computed exactly from the costs. The weight-ratio bound in the preceding proof gives log⁡ℛω≤Λ\log{\mathcal{R}}_{\omega}\leq\Lambda, so even with exact evaluation the running-time bound depends polynomially on the numerical value of Λ\Lambda. Maxima below range over le≤k≤uel_{e}\leq k\leq u_{e}.

Corollary C.19.

For the matroids and rational numbers ce​(1)≤⋯≤ce​(p)c_{e}(1)\leq\cdots\leq c_{e}(p) and β≥0\beta\geq 0 specified above, restrict the profiles BB to those satisfying le≤ℓe​(B)≤uel_{e}\leq\ell_{e}(B)\leq u_{e} for every e∈Ee\in E. A randomized algorithm returns an estimate of Z⁡(a)Z(a) with relative error at most ε\varepsilon, with probability at least 3/43/4, in the form (∏emaxk⁡ae​(k))​Z^\bigl(\prod_{e}\max_{k}a_{e}(k)\bigr)\widehat{Z}, where Z^\widehat{Z} is rational and the exponential factor is specified by its exact rational exponent. If Z⁡(a)>0Z(a)>0, there is also a sampler within total variation distance ε\varepsilon of the Gibbs distribution. The running times are polynomial in p​qpq, the input encoding length, ε−1\varepsilon^{-1}, and the numerical value of Λ\Lambda. If the costs are nonnegative and every le=0l_{e}=0, then maxk⁡ae​(k)=ae​(0)=1\max_{k}a_{e}(k)=a_{e}(0)=1 for every ee, so the estimate is rational.

Proof.

It suffices to approximate the partition function and sample after dividing each table by its largest entry. Indeed, put

a¯e​(k)≔ae​(k)maxj⁡ae​(j).\bar{a}_{e}(k)\coloneqq\frac{a_{e}(k)}{\max_{j}a_{e}(j)}.

This leaves the Gibbs distribution unchanged, and Z⁡(a)=(∏emaxk⁡ae​(k))​Z​(a¯)Z(a)=\bigl(\prod_{e}\max_{k}a_{e}(k)\bigr)Z(\bar{a}). The logarithm of this factor is rational and can be computed exactly from the given costs. We replace a¯e\bar{a}_{e} by rational log-concave tables with nearly the same weights. For 0<ε≤10<\varepsilon\leq 1, set τ≔ε/[64​q​(p+1)2]\tau\coloneqq\varepsilon/[64q(p+1)^{2}] and r≔1+τr\coloneqq 1+\tau. For each le≤k≤uel_{e}\leq k\leq u_{e}, write a¯e​(k)=e−x\bar{a}_{e}(k)=e^{-x}, where x=−log⁡a¯e​(k)∈[0,Λ]x=-\log\bar{a}_{e}(k)\in[0,\Lambda] is rational and computable exactly from the costs. Standard algorithms for evaluating the exponential function [BZ10, Sections 4.3–4.4] compute a positive rational approximation a~e​(k)\widetilde{a}_{e}(k) satisfying

|log⁡a~e​(k)a¯e​(k)|≤τ/16\left|\log\frac{\widetilde{a}_{e}(k)}{\bar{a}_{e}(k)}\right|\leq\tau/16

in time polynomial in the input encoding length, Λ\Lambda, and log⁡(τ−1)\log(\tau^{-1}).

The rational approximation may lose log-concavity. To ensure log-concavity, we make a further small adjustment: define be​(k)≔a~e​(k)​r−k2b_{e}(k)\coloneqq\widetilde{a}_{e}(k)r^{-k^{2}} on the allowed interval and zero outside it. For every le<k<uel_{e}<k<u_{e},

log⁡be​(k)2be​(k−1)​be​(k+1)≥2​log⁡r−τ/4>0.\log\frac{b_{e}(k)^{2}}{b_{e}(k-1)b_{e}(k+1)}\geq 2\log r-\tau/4>0.

Thus beb_{e} is log-concave, and every profile BB with le≤ℓe​(B)≤uel_{e}\leq\ell_{e}(B)\leq u_{e} for every e∈Ee\in E obeys

|log⁡∏ebe​(ℓe​(B))∏ea¯e​(ℓe​(B))|≤q​τ/16+q​p2​log⁡r≤ε/64.{\left|\log\frac{\prod_{e}b_{e}(\ell_{e}(B))}{\prod_{e}\bar{a}_{e}(\ell_{e}(B))}\right|}\leq q\tau/16+qp^{2}\log r\leq\varepsilon/64.

Consequently the sums Z⁡(b)Z(b) and Z⁡(a¯)Z(\bar{a}) differ by a factor at most eε/64e^{\varepsilon/64} in either direction. When these sums are positive, dividing the profile weights by their respective sums gives two probability distributions whose total variation distance is at most eε/32−1<ε/16e^{\varepsilon/32}-1<\varepsilon/16. Applying Corollary C.18 with accuracy ε/4\varepsilon/4 gives an estimate of Z⁡(a¯)Z(\bar{a}) with relative error at most ε\varepsilon. Multiplying by ∏emaxk⁡ae​(k)\prod_{e}\max_{k}a_{e}(k) gives the required estimate of Z⁡(a)Z(a). For sampling, decide for each pair (i,e)(i,e) whether e∈Bie\in B_{i}, using approximate counts to estimate the total weight of each choice [JVV86]. Fixing these choices deletes or contracts elements of the player matroids. For each element, it also shifts the load index by the number of players already required to use it and removes infeasible entries. The resulting tables remain log-concave, so Corollary C.18 applies at every step. Sampling from the distribution defined by the rational tables beb_{e} within total variation distance ε/4\varepsilon/4 then gives the desired approximate Gibbs sample. The rational tables have encoding length polynomial in Λ\Lambda, the input encoding length, and ε−1\varepsilon^{-1}, which gives the stated running time. ∎

C.9 Integer polymatroid intersections, contingency tables, and bounded flows

We first reduce weighted intersections of integer families to subset convolution. Each integer coordinate is encoded by a subset of a block of labeled elements; factorial weights compensate for the multiple encodings of the same integer vector. This gives an approximate counting algorithm for intersections of integral polymatroid bases. We next obtain an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for contingency tables with log-concave entry weights by separating their row-sum and column-sum constraints. A weight-preserving bijection then gives the result for bounded integer flows. In Section C.10, the flow result yields an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for vertices of network-matrix polytopes.

We use log-M\mathrm{M}-concave weights and polarization as defined in Section B.4. A nonempty finite family 𝒜⊆ℤ≥0m\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{m} is M\mathrm{M}-convex if its indicator weight is log-M\mathrm{M}-concave: all vectors have the same coordinate sum, and both exchanged vectors in Eq. 30 belong to 𝒜\mathcal{A}. In particular, the integer points of an integral polymatroid base polytope form such a family [BH20].

Proposition C.20 (Counting weighted intersections of integer families).

Let 𝐜∈ℤ≥1m\bm{c}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}^{m} be given in unary, meaning that each cic_{i} is represented by cic_{i} copies of the symbol 11. Let μ,ν:[𝟎,𝐜]∩ℤm→ℝ≥0\mu,\nu:[\bm{0},\bm{c}]\cap\mathbb{Z}^{m}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} be log-M\mathrm{M}-concave weights, extended by zero outside the box, given by evaluation oracles. Suppose we are given initial vectors 𝐱0,𝐲0\bm{x}_{0},\bm{y}_{0} with μ⁡(𝐱0)>0\mu(\bm{x}_{0})>0 and ν⁡(𝐲0)>0\nu(\bm{y}_{0})>0, and upper bounds on their coefficient ranges whose logarithms are polynomial in the input length. Then there is an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for

Z≔∑𝒌∈[𝟎,𝒄]∩ℤmμ⁡(𝒌)​ν​(𝒌)\displaystyle Z\coloneqq\sum_{\bm{k}\in[\bm{0},\bm{c}]\cap\mathbb{Z}^{m}}\mu(\bm{k})\nu(\bm{k})

in the arithmetic model of Theorem 1.6. In particular, membership oracles and one point in each of two M\mathrm{M}-convex families 𝒜,𝒟\mathcal{A},\mathcal{D} in the box suffice to approximate |𝒜∩𝒟||\mathcal{A}\cap\mathcal{D}|.

Proof.

We construct two subset weights whose convolution is Z/𝒄!Z/\bm{c}!, where 𝒌!≔∏iki!\bm{k}!\coloneqq\prod_{i}k_{i}!. We then show that their generating polynomials are log-concave and apply Theorem 1.6. If the coordinate sums of the two initial vectors differ, the supports are disjoint and Z=0Z=0, so assume these sums agree.

Encoding the integer vectors. Take disjoint sets 𝒰i{\mathcal{U}}_{i} with |𝒰i|=ci|{\mathcal{U}}_{i}|=c_{i} and put 𝒰≔⨆i𝒰i{\mathcal{U}}\coloneqq\bigsqcup_{i}{\mathcal{U}}_{i}. For S⊆𝒰S\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}, write ki​(S)≔|S∩𝒰i|k_{i}(S)\coloneqq|S\cap{\mathcal{U}}_{i}| and define

μ^​(S)\displaystyle\widehat{\mu}(S) ≔μ⁡(𝒌⁡(S))​(𝒄−𝒌⁡(S))!𝒄!,\displaystyle\coloneqq\mu(\bm{k}(S))\frac{(\bm{c}-\bm{k}(S))!}{\bm{c}!}, (35)
ν^​(S)\displaystyle\widehat{\nu}(S) ≔ν⁡(𝒄−𝒌⁡(S))​(𝒄−𝒌⁡(S))!𝒄!.\displaystyle\coloneqq\nu(\bm{c}-\bm{k}(S))\frac{(\bm{c}-\bm{k}(S))!}{\bm{c}!}.

In the convolution, μ^​(S)\widehat{\mu}(S) and ν^​(𝒰∖S)\widehat{\nu}({\mathcal{U}}\setminus S) use the same integer vector 𝒌⁡(S)\bm{k}(S). Exactly (𝒄𝒌)≔∏i(ciki)\binom{\bm{c}}{\bm{k}}\coloneqq\prod_{i}\binom{c_{i}}{k_{i}} subsets encode 𝒌\bm{k}, and the factorial weights cancel this multiplicity:

(μ^∗ν^)​(𝒰)\displaystyle(\widehat{\mu}*\widehat{\nu})({\mathcal{U}}) =∑𝟎≤𝒌≤𝒄(𝒄𝒌)​μ​(𝒌)​ν​(𝒌)​(𝒄−𝒌)!​𝒌!(𝒄!)2=Z𝒄!.\displaystyle=\sum_{\bm{0}\leq\bm{k}\leq\bm{c}}\binom{\bm{c}}{\bm{k}}\mu(\bm{k})\nu(\bm{k})\frac{(\bm{c}-\bm{k})!\,\bm{k}!}{(\bm{c}!)^{2}}=\frac{Z}{\bm{c}!}. (36)

Log-concavity of the generating polynomials. We use the weighted exchange condition in Eq. 30 for ν\nu; log-concavity of its generating polynomial alone would not provide this condition. Put ν¯​(𝒌)≔ν​(𝒄−𝒌)\bar{\nu}(\bm{k})\coloneqq\nu(\bm{c}-\bm{k}) for integer vectors 𝒌\bm{k} satisfying 0≤ki≤ci0\leq k_{i}\leq c_{i} for every ii, and set ν¯​(𝒌)=0\bar{\nu}(\bm{k})=0 otherwise. We first verify that ν¯\bar{\nu} is also log-M\mathrm{M}-concave. Take 𝒙,𝒚∈supp⁡ν¯\bm{x},\bm{y}\in\supp\bar{\nu} with xi>yix_{i}>y_{i}. Then 𝒄−𝒚,𝒄−𝒙∈supp⁡ν\bm{c}-\bm{y},\bm{c}-\bm{x}\in\supp\nu and (𝒄−𝒚)i>(𝒄−𝒙)i(\bm{c}-\bm{y})_{i}>(\bm{c}-\bm{x})_{i}. Apply Eq. 30 to these two vectors in this order. It gives an index jj with (𝒄−𝒚)j<(𝒄−𝒙)j(\bm{c}-\bm{y})_{j}<(\bm{c}-\bm{x})_{j}, equivalently xj<yjx_{j}<y_{j}, and

ν¯​(𝒙)​ν¯​(𝒚)\displaystyle\bar{\nu}(\bm{x})\bar{\nu}(\bm{y}) =ν⁡(𝒄−𝒚)​ν​(𝒄−𝒙)\displaystyle=\nu(\bm{c}-\bm{y})\nu(\bm{c}-\bm{x})
≤ν⁡(𝒄−𝒚−𝒆i+𝒆j)​ν​(𝒄−𝒙+𝒆i−𝒆j)\displaystyle\leq\nu(\bm{c}-\bm{y}-\bm{e}_{i}+\bm{e}_{j})\nu(\bm{c}-\bm{x}+\bm{e}_{i}-\bm{e}_{j})
=ν¯​(𝒙−𝒆i+𝒆j)​ν¯​(𝒚+𝒆i−𝒆j).\displaystyle=\bar{\nu}(\bm{x}-\bm{e}_{i}+\bm{e}_{j})\bar{\nu}(\bm{y}+\bm{e}_{i}-\bm{e}_{j}).

Moreover, if the vectors in supp⁡ν\supp\nu have coordinate sum rr, then those in supp⁡ν¯\supp\bar{\nu} have coordinate sum ∑ici−r\sum_{i}c_{i}-r. Thus ν¯\bar{\nu} satisfies both parts of the definition.

By [BH20, Corollary 3.16], the exponential generating polynomial of a log-M\mathrm{M}-concave weight is Lorentzian. Applying this separately to μ\mu and ν¯\bar{\nu} gives two Lorentzian polynomials:

gμexp​(𝒙)\displaystyle g_{\mu}^{\mathrm{exp}}(\bm{x}) ≔∑𝟎≤𝒌≤𝒄μ⁡(𝒌)𝒌!​𝒙𝒌,\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{\bm{0}\leq\bm{k}\leq\bm{c}}\frac{\mu(\bm{k})}{\bm{k}!}\bm{x}^{\bm{k}},
gν¯exp​(𝒙)\displaystyle g_{\bar{\nu}}^{\mathrm{exp}}(\bm{x}) ≔∑𝟎≤𝒌≤𝒄ν¯​(𝒌)𝒌!​𝒙𝒌=∑𝟎≤𝒌≤𝒄ν⁡(𝒌)(𝒄−𝒌)!​𝒙𝒄−𝒌.\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{\bm{0}\leq\bm{k}\leq\bm{c}}\frac{\bar{\nu}(\bm{k})}{\bm{k}!}\bm{x}^{\bm{k}}=\sum_{\bm{0}\leq\bm{k}\leq\bm{c}}\frac{\nu(\bm{k})}{(\bm{c}-\bm{k})!}\bm{x}^{\bm{c}-\bm{k}}.

Apply polarization from Section B.4, with the new variables for coordinate ii indexed by 𝒰i{\mathcal{U}}_{i}. Since 1/(k!​(cik))=(ci−k)!/ci!1/(k!\binom{c_{i}}{k})=(c_{i}-k)!/c_{i}!, the resulting polynomials are exactly gμ^g_{\widehat{\mu}} and gν^g_{\widehat{\nu}} from Eq. 35. These are multiaffine log-concave polynomials because polarization preserves the Lorentzian property [BH20, Proposition 3.1 and Theorem 2.30].

Oracle access and running time. Choose S0,T0⊆𝒰S_{0},T_{0}\subseteq{\mathcal{U}} with |S0∩𝒰i|=(x0)i|S_{0}\cap{\mathcal{U}}_{i}|=(x_{0})_{i} and |T0∩𝒰i|=ci−(y0)i|T_{0}\cap{\mathcal{U}}_{i}|=c_{i}-(y_{0})_{i} for every ii. These satisfy μ^​(S0)>0\widehat{\mu}(S_{0})>0 and ν^​(T0)>0\widehat{\nu}(T_{0})>0. The input length is at least ∑ici=|𝒰|\sum_{i}c_{i}=|{\mathcal{U}}| under the stated encoding. Factorials can be precomputed and the weights μ^\widehat{\mu} and ν^\widehat{\nu} evaluated in polynomial time. Their coefficient ranges increase by at most a factor of 𝒄!\bm{c}!, whose logarithm is also polynomial in the input length. Apply Theorem 1.6 and multiply the estimate by 𝒄!\bm{c}!, using Eq. 36, to obtain the claimed 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS}. ∎

The proposition allows a separate log-concave weight on each coordinate. Indeed, if 𝒜\mathcal{A} is M\mathrm{M}-convex and each aia_{i} is log-concave with interval support, then, whenever nonzero,

ω(𝒌)≔𝟏{𝒌∈𝒜}∏iai(ki)\displaystyle\omega(\bm{k})\coloneqq\mathbf{1}_{\{\bm{k}\in\mathcal{A}\}}\prod_{i}a_{i}(k_{i})

satisfies Eq. 30. For the exchange indices i,ji,j, log-concavity gives ai​(xi)​ai​(yi)≤ai​(xi−1)​ai​(yi+1)a_{i}(x_{i})a_{i}(y_{i})\leq a_{i}(x_{i}-1)a_{i}(y_{i}+1) and the analogous inequality with jj increased in 𝒙\bm{x} and decreased in 𝒚\bm{y}. Thus the proposition counts weighted integer points in the intersection of two integral polymatroid base polytopes.

A contingency table is a nonnegative integer matrix with specified row and column sums. The next corollary allows both entrywise upper bounds and a separate log-concave weight on each entry.

Corollary C.21 (Contingency tables with log-concave entry weights).

The input consists of row sums 𝐫∈ℤ≥0m\bm{r}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{m}, column sums 𝐜∈ℤ≥0n\bm{c}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}, entrywise upper bounds ui​j∈ℤ≥0u_{ij}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, and nonzero nonnegative log-concave tables wi​j​(0),…,wi​j​(ui​j)w_{ij}(0),\ldots,w_{ij}(u_{ij}) with interval support. There is an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for

Z𝒓,𝒄≔∑X∈ℤ≥0m×n,Xi​j≤ui​j∑jXi​j=ri​(i∈[m])∑iXi​j=cj​(j∈[n])∏i=1m∏j=1nwi​j​(Xi​j)\displaystyle Z_{\bm{r},\bm{c}}\coloneqq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}X\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{m\times n},\ X_{ij}\leq u_{ij}\\ \sum_{j}X_{ij}=r_{i}\ (i\in[m])\\ \sum_{i}X_{ij}=c_{j}\ (j\in[n])\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{m}\prod_{j=1}^{n}w_{ij}(X_{ij})

C.10 Vertices of network-matrix polytopes

We now apply Corollary C.22 to count vertices of network-matrix polytopes. The vertices correspond to integer flows; the key point is that their binary coordinates let us bound the total flow capacity by a polynomial in the matrix dimensions.

A network matrix records signed paths in a directed tree. More precisely, let TT be a directed tree with mm edges, and let EE consist of nn additional labeled directed edges on the same vertex set. Write VV for this vertex set, so |V|=m+1|V|=m+1. For each directed edge e=(u→v)e=(u\to v), its incidence entry in row ww is bw,e=𝟏{w=u}−𝟏{w=v}b_{w,e}=\mathbf{1}_{\{w=u\}}-\mathbf{1}_{\{w=v\}}. Choose any vertex r∈Vr\in V and define

BT\displaystyle B_{T} =(bw,e)w∈V∖{r},e∈E⁡(T)∈ℝm×m,\displaystyle=(b_{w,e})_{w\in V\setminus\{r\},\ e\in E(T)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m},
BE\displaystyle B_{E} =(bw,e)w∈V∖{r},e∈E∈ℝm×n.\displaystyle=(b_{w,e})_{w\in V\setminus\{r\},\ e\in E}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}.

Thus we omit the row for vertex rr from both incidence matrices and keep all other vertex rows in the same order. To see that the square matrix BTB_{T} is invertible, let 𝒛∈ℝV∖{r}\bm{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{V\setminus\{r\}} satisfy BT𝖳​𝒛=𝟎B_{T}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{z}=\bm{0}, and put zr=0z_{r}=0. For every tree edge e=(u→v)e=(u\to v),

0=(BT𝖳​𝒛)e=zu−zv.0=(B_{T}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{z})_{e}=z_{u}-z_{v}.

Every vertex is joined to rr by a path when edge directions are ignored, so these equalities give zw=zr=0z_{w}=z_{r}=0 for every w∈Vw\in V. Thus BT𝖳​𝒛=𝟎B_{T}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{z}=\bm{0} has only the zero solution, proving that BTB_{T} is invertible. The matrix A=BT−1​BEA=B_{T}^{-1}B_{E} is a network matrix. Given only a network matrix AA, one can find in polynomial time a directed tree TT and additional directed edges EE such that A=BT−1​BEA=B_{T}^{-1}B_{E} [BC80]. Network matrices are totally unimodular, so in particular their entries lie in {0,±1}\{0,\pm 1\}. Consequently, for integral bounds ℓ,𝒖\bm{\ell},\bm{u}, the vertices of

P={𝒙∈[0,1]n:ℓ≤A​𝒙≤𝒖}P=\{\bm{x}\in[0,1]^{n}:\bm{\ell}\leq A\bm{x}\leq\bm{u}\}

are exactly its binary points: integrality gives one direction, and every binary point of a polytope contained in the cube is a vertex.

The following result answers the network-matrix case posed in [GJ23, Problem 4.3]. It follows by combining their reduction to integer flows [GJ23, Section 4] with Corollary C.22.

Corollary C.23.

There is an 𝖥𝖯𝖱𝖠𝖲\mathsf{FPRAS} for the number of vertices of PP above, with running time polynomial in the input length and ε−1\varepsilon^{-1} in the arithmetic model of Theorem 1.6. This includes a polytope {𝐱:A​𝐱≤𝐛}\{\bm{x}:A\bm{x}\leq\bm{b}\} promised to have only binary vertices, for a network matrix AA and integral 𝐛\bm{b}.

We recall the reduction of Guo and Jerrum [GJ23, Section 4] and apply Corollary C.22 with unit weights. We verify the bijection from vertices to flows and bound the total capacity in terms of the dimensions of AA.

The vertices of PP are exactly its binary points. For each such point 𝒙\bm{x}, set 𝒚=A​𝒙\bm{y}=A\bm{x}. The identity A=BT−1​BEA=B_{T}^{-1}B_{E} gives

𝒚=A𝒙⟺BT𝒚−BE𝒙=𝟎.\displaystyle\bm{y}=A\bm{x}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad B_{T}\bm{y}-B_{E}\bm{x}=\bm{0}.

The enlargement is polynomial in nn and ε−1\varepsilon^{-1}.

Degree checks and greedy rank queries evaluate both measures using the dual-rank identity above. Both are positive at the empty set, and

log⁡(ℛμq​ℛνq)≤2​n​log⁡(1/q)+∑e∈Elog⁡(1/we).\log({\mathcal{R}}_{\mu_{q}}{\mathcal{R}}_{\nu_{q}})\leq 2n\log(1/q)+\sum_{e\in E}\log(1/w_{e}).

This bound and χ=8​n/ε\chi=8n/\varepsilon are polynomial in the input length and ε−1\varepsilon^{-1}. Apply Theorem 1.16 with relative error ε/2\varepsilon/2 and divide its coefficient estimate by q𝗋𝗄𝒩​(E)q^{{\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}}(E)}. This gives an estimate of ZqZ_{q} with relative error at most ε/2\varepsilon/2, and hence an estimate of Z0Z_{0} with relative error at most ε\varepsilon. ∎

Appendix D Miscellaneous Aspects of Theorem 1.14

D.1 A Matroid Intersection Analog of the Monomer-Dimer Model

In this section, we consider a generalization of the classical monomer-dimer model over matchings of a graph to matroid intersection. We use Theorem 1.14 to prove a spectral gap for the standard heat-bath Glauber dynamics that decays smoothly as the parameter λ\lambda grows. In particular, the model does not exhibit a dynamical phase transition in λ\lambda. The motivation for studying this problem was discussed in Section 1.5.

Let ℳ,𝒩{\mathcal{M}},{\mathcal{N}} be two matroids on a common ground set, and fix a parameter λ≥0\lambda\geq 0. We consider the following probability measure over common independent sets of all sizes:

μλ​(S)∝λ|S|,∀S∈ℐ⁡(ℳ)∩ℐ⁡(𝒩).\displaystyle\mu_{\lambda}(S)\propto\lambda^{\left|{S}\right|},\qquad\forall S\in{\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{M}})\cap{\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{N}}).

The discrete-time heat-bath Glauber dynamics is a Markov chain whose evolution can be described as follows: If the state at time step tt is StS_{t}, then we transition to St+1S_{t+1} by

  1. (a)

    sampling a uniformly random element u∈𝒰u\in{\mathcal{U}}, and

  2. (b)

    resampling the in/out status of uu conditioned on all other elements. More specifically, if u∈Stu\in S_{t}, then set St+1=St−uS_{t+1}=S_{t}-u with probability 11+λ\frac{1}{1+\lambda}. Otherwise, if u∉Stu\notin S_{t} and St+u∈ℐ⁡(ℳ)∩ℐ⁡(𝒩)S_{t}+u\in{\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{M}})\cap{\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{N}}), then set St+1=St+uS_{t+1}=S_{t}+u with probability λ1+λ\frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda}. In all other cases, set St+1=StS_{t+1}=S_{t}.

Let PλP_{\lambda} denote the corresponding transition probability matrix, and let ℒλ≔I−Pλ{\mathcal{L}}_{\lambda}\coloneqq I-P_{\lambda}. It is straightforward to verify that Pλ,ℒλP_{\lambda},{\mathcal{L}}_{\lambda} are reversible with respect to μλ\mu_{\lambda}. For λ>0\lambda>0, the chain is irreducible since every state can reach ∅\varnothing by deletions, and each such path can be reversed.

Theorem D.1.

For every ℳ,𝒩{\mathcal{M}},{\mathcal{N}} with n=|𝒰|≥1n=\left|{{\mathcal{U}}}\right|\geq 1 and every λ≥0\lambda\geq 0, we have the spectral gap lower bound

γ⁡(ℒλ)≥1n⋅(1+λ)⋅(1+λ⋅(n−1)).\displaystyle\gamma({\mathcal{L}}_{\lambda})\geq\frac{1}{n\cdot(1+\lambda)\cdot(1+\lambda\cdot(n-1))}.

Following the strategy used above for common bases, we first establish a Poincaré inequality for a softened version of μλ\mu_{\lambda} using Theorem 1.14. We then deduce Theorem D.1 by a direct comparison of Dirichlet forms.

Lemma D.2.

For 0≤t≤10\leq t\leq 1, define the distribution

μλ(t)​(S)∝λ|S|⋅t|S|−𝗋𝗄𝒩​(S),∀S∈ℐ⁡(ℳ).\displaystyle\mu_{\lambda}^{(t)}(S)\propto\lambda^{\left|{S}\right|}\cdot t^{\left|{S}\right|-\mathsf{rk}_{{\mathcal{N}}}(S)},\qquad\forall S\in{\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{M}}).

Then for every f:ℐ⁡(ℳ)→ℝf:{\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{M}})\to{\mathbb{R}}, we have the Poincaré Inequality

𝐕𝐚𝐫μλ(t)​[f]≤ℰλ(t)​(f,f)≔λ⋅∑S∈ℐ⁡(ℳ)∑u∉SS+u∈ℐ⁡(ℳ)μλ(t)​(S)⋅(f⁡(S+u)−f⁡(S))2.\displaystyle\mathbf{Var}_{\mu_{\lambda}^{(t)}}\left[f\right]\leq{\mathcal{E}}_{\lambda}^{(t)}(f,f)\coloneqq\lambda\cdot\sum_{S\in{\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{M}})}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}u\notin S\\ S+u\in{\mathcal{I}}({\mathcal{M}})\end{subarray}}\mu_{\lambda}^{(t)}(S)\cdot\left({f(S+u)-f(S)}\right)^{2}.

As discussed in Remark 2.6, the “softening” of μλ\mu_{\lambda} into μλ(t)\mu_{\lambda}^{(t)} can be viewed as a generalization of the “softening” used in the proof of Theorem 2.2.
